LILIES AND THE RIVER. at' The lilies grew on a silent pool, Un ler the alders deep and cool, And they said to the rushing river— " Why dost thou hurry away, away? 14, Stay with us, beautiful fiver, stay, And sing to us here for ever." Tb river crept under the alders' shade, And fresh sweet lips to the lilies laid, And kissed them in loving wonder. "I may not linger," it murmured low, "For ever and ever I onward flow To the ocean which calleth yonder." • Then the river sped on with its flashing feet, So deep and strong, and so:pure and sweet, t•."-;it_ The beautiful shining river. And, skirting many a stately town, It carried all dark defilements down SZI, To be lost in the sea for ever. w.f.? And the lilies rocked on the fairy pool Under the alders, dark and cool, tIRIMM.• Watching the rushing river, " And whispered to me of the infinite Love, And infinite Peace of the Land above Where earth's sins will be lost for ever. ...He,len Marion Burnside in the Girls' Own Paper.

r AN AUSTRALIAN SONG OF PROGRESS. In sunshine golden comes the glad New Year, Another link in Time's eternal chain, That brings each sad and weary heart more .near Its welcome rest from earthly care and pain; And bids us seek, as we have sought of old, ' To do the good that each to each can do, And with united love and strength uphold ". The cause divine of Progress pure and true. ot ours the strife of earthly passion born, That clouds with hate this world of beauty rare, Till, crushed with cynic mockery and scorn, a But few to hope for brighter days may dare. We fl(dit as fought the knights in ancient time Against the ills that lowly souls oppress And, panoplied with- Truth and Faith sublime, E'er strive the rugged path of Toil to bless. What nobler task? What grander, prouder aim Thin this, which e'en the weakest heart may share, To light afresh the warm and glowing flame 0: brotherhood—to bear and fond forbear; : And as each fleeting year rolls into space, Behold the tiny seed that we have sown The thorns of life with buds and fruit replace, And erring Man more Christ-like—God-like grown. Sydney, New South Wales. JOHN PM:WIER.

Were wo as eloquent as angels, we should Please some more by listening than by talking. Our ancestors, the monkeys, couldn't have been so ignorant after all; they were all educated in the higher branches. Scene—House in the West End. Mrs. Robertson (with six eligible daughters, to old bachelor) : "Mr. Jones, why do you never get married ?" Mr. Jones:' "Became I wouldn't marry a lady I couldn't respect, and I couldn't respect any lady that would marry me." " Now, Johnny, speak your proverb," sweetly spoke a school marm at the annual exhibition. "Please, marm, I forget," lisped Johnny. "I will refresh your memory. 'People who live in glass houses —' Now, finish it." "People who live in glass houses must pull down the blinds." Johnny took the first prize. Mrs. Parvenu was at a very exclusive affair on Six- teenth-street the other evening, and the hostess was asking aboxt her daughter, whose 'health has not been good. "Oh," said the lady, "Mollie is not improving as I should like to have her. You see, the doctor told me she ought to try calisthenics, and I've been to every drug store in the town but can't find a bit anywhere." THE QUET-V.B FIRST NIGHT AT OSBORNE.—There is 3 touching incident in connection with the Queen's first sojourn at Osborne House, which had been purchased chiefly in order to make a quiet and retired home for the training of the Royal Family. Lady Lyttelton, writing of the first night spent there, tells us:—" The Prince Consort, after dinner, said, very naturally and simply, but seriously, We have a hymn' (he called it a psalm) for such occasions; it begins—', and then he repeated twe I:nes in German, which I could not quote right, meaning a prayer to bless our going out and coming in. It was dry and quaint, being Luther's; we all perceived that he was feeling it. And truly, entering a new house, a new palace, is a solemn thing to do, to those whose probable space of life in it is long, and, in spite of rank, and health, and youth, downhill now. The verse the Prince quoted has been thus translated into English : God bless our going out, nor less Our coming in. and make them sure; God bless our daily bread, and bless Whate'er we do. whate'er endure; In death unto His peace awake us, And heirs of His salvation make us." FAWCETT AS A MAN.—He was utterly a stranger to finesse, to trick, to any form of over-reaching. He would always play fair,rand expected others to do the same; this was one of the secrets of his popularity. In this he was a thorough Englishman. He was utterly healthy, without a.ffec-ation or pretension. He enjoyed a joke at his own expense quite as much as a joke at another's. Mr. Stephe.! assures us that he was no more ashamed of his deEienck?s as a scholar than of theshape of his nose. "He h‘arilv enjoyed all the good things of life," writes his biograph r; "a good glass of wine, a good cigar, or a bit of downright gossip not less than more intellectual recreations. One of the first things I remember about him.' s, yi his wife, was his saying how keenly he en- joyed life. He expressed,' she adds, some impatience with people who avowed or affected weariness of life.' 'There is only one thing :thtt I ever regret.' he would say, and that is to have missed a chance of enjoyment.' He would, for instance, seriously ponder at the end of a frost whether he coul i not have contrived another hour's skating. He intended, he would tell me, to live to be ninety, and to relish every day of his life. Should any- one be • ffended at a doctrine which seems to be more sound than easy to put in practice, he must remember that all Fawcett's enjoyments were wholesome and in- nocent, that they emphatically included a strenuous exertion of all his faculties, and excluded with equal emphasis every tinge of ill-nature. He never enjoyed anything which could give pain to others. • . There -was only one thing, he told his sister, which he dreaded —viz., a loss of energy. Life might become a burden to him if life no longer meant action."—Gentleman's Maga- zine.

INSTINCT AS AN ELEMENT OF HUMAN LlFE.—Even 'centuries of cultivation and the highest hereditary ad- vantages fail utterly to eliminate or destroy the inherent property of instinct in man; for not only is it displayed in the common shrinking from death and the avoidance of injury and suffering, but it manifests itself in count- less other instances in daily life. Let us regard the union of sexes as one: how frequently is the choice of a partner in life made through nothing less than a blind instinct, often apart from any reasoning process, so much so, that the fact has passed into a proverb that "Love is blind." And in the common affairs of life, it is often possible to trace an independent course of action pur- sued without reference to a reasoning faculty, rather by a blind adherence to an unseen hidden principle, which is undoubtedly instinct guiding rather than reason. And this obedience to an unknown faculty has doubtless, in the history of the world, played important parts; espe- cially when, in prehistoric times, man was essentially a predatory animal. On this instinctive love of fighting for personal aggrandisement, and his instinctive love of the chase for providing food and clothing, his very ex- istence in a great measure depended. Indeed, the mo- tives which influence and direct men's lives are only, after all, the attributes of instinct, as we commonly ob- serve pourtrayed in civilised Society; thus, in one, the 1 instinct of commercial enterprise pushes towards specu- lation; in another, the instinct of self-preservation in- duces precautions of benefit to the community; again, the instinct of need prompts measures for procuring supplies of food and clothing. On all hands, human in- stinct is an active agent and irrepressible. And further, we may find the instinct of an unseen yet overruling power dominant in one form or another among the whole human race; even where, degraded by numberless superstitions, it exists among the dusky tribes of Africa, the Red American Indians, or in the countless mytholo- gical legends of nations long passed away, the instinctive belief in a God holds universal sway. In the common affairs of life, too, the teaching of instinct is displayed, as in presentiments,which,like impulses, have frequently no rational basis, but by the observance of which, our lives are not uncommonly modified in their effects and made subservient to the unseen. It is indeed possible, were the chapters of human lives actually recorded, it would be found in how many important instances and numberless occasions the exercise of instinct prevails above that of reason. It is, however, to be noted, that in proportion as the exercise of intellectual force is stimulated by education and strengthened by practice, instinctive action becomes more and more influenced by ' reason; and just as particular muscles, by long use, in- crease in bulk, so the repeated receptivity of ideas by the higher organism of the brain leads to the reflective powers being increased; and, as a natural consequence, the actions thus performed betoken the connection of ideas from which they spring, and are consequently at- tributed to reason.—f hambers's Journal. When weariness comes, take a breathing-spell. Of one thing be sure—to-day's work well done will prepare you for to-morrow. Purpose ennobles everything, and the man or woman who has worthy purposes in life finds nothing that they demand trivial or menial. Take, for example, domestic life, made up as it is of numberless little things all demanding attention. There are some men so shallow and unnhilosophical as to deem the ordering of a family an easy and trivial occupation that anybody could suc- ceed in. As they leave their own cares, and come to their own homes for rest or leisure, they imagine that the life of those who preside over them and make them what they are must be all rest and leisure. On the contrary, it is only as the wife and mother is thoughtful and large- hearted enough to realise the grand purposes of home life, and to direct all efforts to subserve those purposes, that she can gather up its thousand details and give to each one its due proportion of attention.

INATTENTIVE Jung—Fs.—Between Sugden and Brougham there were repeated "rows in court." Sometimes Sug- den distinctly got the better; sometimes it was other- wise. Lord Brougham would write his letters while listening to the address of counsel. We have seen judges deliberately reading newspapers while counsel have been making their speeches. But on this occasion Sugden was addressing judge and jury, not a jury alone. Sug- den stopped • short in the middle of a sentence. "Go on, Sir Edmund, lam listening to you," said Brougham. "I observe that your lordship is engaged in writing, and not favouring me with your attention." The Chancellor neatly stopped him. "I am signing papers of mere form. You may as well say that I am not to blow my nose or to take snuff while you speak." On this occasion the laugh was against Sir Edmund. But on other occasions the laugh was all on his side. Sugden hated Brougham. Towards a Chancellor whom he liked he could be as sweet as summer. We think it was Lord Cottenham who actually fell asleep. Sir Edmnnd immediately paused. The cessation of sound had the customary effect of awakening the Chancellor. "Why don't you go on, Sir Edmund ?" "I thought your lordship might be looking over your notes," was the bland re- sponse. This would please Lord Coftenham, who was very liable to doze, and hated anybody noticing it. Sug- den took his revenge on Brougham in the famous bon- mot, that it was a pity he did not know a little law, and then he would have a smattering of everything. To a man of his great knowledge, a discursive mind like Lord Brougham's would be very distasteful, and they were also separated by many political and personal differences.

SOME CURES FOR SEA SICKNESS.:—A very good remedy for sea-sickness is chloral, but whether it acts by simply benumbing the nerves of the stomach, or by reducing the susceptibility of the whole nervous system, we do not know. At all events, a passenger may take thirty grains of chloral at Dover, fall into a drowsy, half-con- scious state, and find himself at Calais free from sick- ness. Sometimes one or two drops of pure chloroform taken in a wine-glass of water will prove efficacious. Hypodermic injections of morphia are occasionally re- sorted to, but their use is not justifiable until other reme- dies have been tried and failed. The substance known as petroleum mineral naphtha, or rock oil, enjoys .a high reputation in the treatment of sea-sickness. It should be taken on going on board, a drop or two on a small piece of sugar, and repeated every two or three hours. A pill containing three drops of creosote is another good remedy. Ipecacuinha wine, in drop doses, which proves so successful in the treatment of many kinds of vomiting, would probably succeed in sea-sick- ness, although we are not acquainted with the records of any cases in which it has been tried. Recent experi- ments seem to show that cocaine is a promising and harmless remedy against sea-sickness. An authority on the subject recommends that the drug be administered I in doses of 4to of a grain, dissolved in water (1 in 10) three times a day, with a small piece of ice. A surgeon on board one of the vessels of the White Star line re- cently informed us that in obstinate cases he had often obtained relief by the use of iced dry champagne. It is essential, he says, that the wine should be dry, for sweet champagne only makes matters worse. In the Levant the daily internal use of iron is a very common cure for sea-sickness. Sailors, when suffering from this com- plaint, obtain their iron in a very primitive manner, for they scrape off a portion of the rust adhering to the anchor and anchor-chain, and then swallow it in a little water.—The Family Physician. A PEDAGOGUE OF THE OLDEN TIME.,—The master of our school (writes a contributor to Bentley's Magazine) was an eccentric pedagogue, very learned, as we thought, very formal, as we saw, very severe, as we felt; and among his eccentricities there was none more laughable and cryable than his manner of inflicting punishment. It was a maxim with him that justice should not only be done, but acknowledged; and thus such scenes as the following were of frequent occurrence :—Pedagogue: John Smith ?—John: Here, sir !—Ped.: Come from your " Here " hither. (John moves slowly and reluctantly up to the rostrum). John Smith, you have been guilty of throwing stones, which I forbade. (John hangs his head disconsolately). John Smith, it is of no use look- ing sorrowfully now, you should have thought of sorrow before you committed the offence (reaching down the cane). You are aware, John Smith, that those who do evil must be punished; and you, John, must therefore be punished. Is it not so ?—John : Oh, sir, I will never do it again.—Ped.: I hope you will not, John; but as you forgot the prohibition when left to your own un- assisted memory, the smart of the remembrance now to be administered will be the more likely to prevent any relapse in future. Hold out your hand. (Whack).— John: Oh, sir! oh, sir! I will never do it again.—Ped. : I hope not; hold out your hand again. (Whack, and a screech from John). Now, John, you begin to perceive the consequences of disobedienceF—John : Oh, yes sir— enough sir, enough sir !—Ped : By no means, John. You are somewhat convinced of your error, but not yet sen- sible of the justice of your punishment, and the quan- Itum due to you. Hold out your other hand (whack and scream).—John: Mercy, sir, I will never—(blubbering) —Ped. : It is all for your good, John; hold out your left hand again. Even-handed justice! Why don't you do as you are bid, sir, eh? (A slash across the shoulders). John: Oh! oh !—Ped. : That's a good boy! (Whack on the hand again). That's a good boy! (Whack). Now, John, you feel that it is all for your good ?—.John: Oh, no, sir—oh, no! it is very bad, sir, very sore.—Ped. : Dear, me, John. Hold out again, sir. I must convince you that it is justice, and all for your good. (A rain of stripes on hands and back, John bellowing all the while). Yoir must feel it is for your good, my boy !---John: Oh, yes, sir—oh, ves-s-s-s-s.—Ped.: That's a good lad; you're right again.—John: It is all for my good, sir; it is all for my good.—Ped. : Indeed it is, my dear. There! (Whack, whack). Now thank me, John. (John hesi- tates—whack, whack)—John Ah, ah ! Thank you, sir— thank you very much. I will never do it; thank you, sir. Oh, sir, tha-a-a-nks.—Ped : That's a dear good boy. Now you may go to your place, and sit down and cry as much as you wish, but without making a noise. And then you must learn your lesson. And John, you will not forget my orders again. You will be grateful for the instruction I have bestowed upon you. You will feel that justice is a great and certain principle. You will feel it, John. You may see, also, how much your companions may be benefited by your example. Go and sit down; there's a good boy. John, there are punish- ments in this school more disgraceful and severe than that you have just undergone.—John, bowing: Yes, sir thank ye, sir.

The price of the above machine, fitted for power, is £2B; but one has been recently adapted to work by hand, the price of which is £l5. Afterwards the butter is put in a hardening box for some hours. It is a good plan to make butter in the afternoon , or evening, and leave it in the hardening box all night. Since the foregoing was in type, we have received the following official description of the soft cheeses (the first alluded to in our notes) called "Neufchatel," or "Swiss Double Creme :"—" These cheeses are made with equal pavb3 of milk and cream. A gallon of the mixture at the temperature of the air is set, with only one drop of Hansen's rennet, diluted with three drops of water, or ' in the proportion of one drop of rennet to 10,000 drops of the milk and cream. The object of the maker is to obtain a rich and smooth curd; he must not, therefore, use more rennet than is absolutely necessary to convert the milk and cream very slowly into curd. The quan- tity of the rennet required will vary with its strength, with the season and temperature, and with the age and condition of the milk. Warm poor, or stale milk will require less rennet; cold milk, or milk enriched with cream, requires more. The exact quantity required ' under varying circumstances can only be ascertained by experience. The curd is formed in twenty-four hours; it is then put into a cloth in a light wooden square frame to drain for twelve hours, and gently strained two or three times, when the cloth is then changed and the curd pressed. When the whey has been pressed out the curd is worked smooth in the cloth with a flat trowel, and put into moulds lined with paper, when it can be turned out at once, and disposed of as soon as the cheese is sufficiently firm to bear packing. It will be observed that the principles of manufacture of these and other soft cheeses is directly opposed to that which regulates the making of English hard cheeses, such as Cheddar, Cheshire, Derbyshire, Gloucestershire, &c., as follows :- 1. The quantity of rennet applied is very small indeed. 2. The temperature is not raised. 3. The curd is, there- fore, a long time in coagulating. 4. The curd is neither cooked nor cut. 5. The curd is carefully and gently lifted from one draining cloth to another."

~. , MILK DILUTION.—A correspondent, who-lends his ad- dress, writes as follows :—" I should feel greatly obliged if you could inform me how much added water a farmer is allowed by law to put in his milk, before starting it away for London. Also, if you tell a purchaser before be purchases that 'this milk contains water,' whether you are liable to be prosecuted? Also, what amount (if any) of added water can be sold in milk, if it is sold as new milk ?" We cannot help you; nor do we care to tell any man how far he may do wrong without risk of de- tection.

THE WEATHER AND THE CROPS.—During the past few days we have.had showery weather, and some thunder. On Wednesday morning the temperature was very high, and in the afternoon rain descended in torrents, accom- panied by thunder and lightning. The brooks were sud- denly swollen, watercourses were blocked, and low-lying lands were in several districts under water for some hours. The exceedingly fine weather of Monday and Tuesday enabled the farmers to get in a large quantity of hay. The corn crops have greatly benefited by the great heat of the past few weeks. We hear of several experiments in ensilage in the district. The result of 1 the feeding with ensiled fodder last year proved most satisfactory, especially on those farms where there are no green crops. A correspondent writes :—" Again I can report favourably of farming prospects, and though those who are late with their hay may have had it damped by passing showers, still the rain has done a world of good to all other crops. I noticed a few fields of oats this week in the Irlam district that were re- markably forward, and: the wheat has now shot, and is freshened up and very much improved in appearance. I never remember less grumbling amongst farmers about the weather, which shows conclusively that they find that all is making satisfactory progress. Farmers are now very busy weeding their turnips and potatoes, which has been rendered much easier owing to the heavy dews and rains having moistened the soil. During the dry period a few weeks ago it was simply impossible to get the ground clean and clear of weed, as it was in many cases, especially on stiff land, as hard as a board. I noticed last week in a walk through Ashley and Mob- berley that roots were looking very well, particularly swecl.s. Beans seem healthy, but are not being grown in any great quantity. We have had during the last fortnight some aerial phenomena well worth noting by those who desire to forecast the weather. Of the sun- sets of the last ten days a note should be taken. Perhaps the most remarkable was that of Monday, the 12th, for though the sky was covered with fantastic cloud forms and wreaths of mist, all these forms were of an ashy white, and for a long time there was not a shade of yel- low to be traced even where the sun was sinking behind a bank of dark cloud. This strange appearance was no doubt owing in some measure to the fact that the moon was high in the heavens. On Friday and again on Mon- day, we had a full glow of crimson red and yellow for a shorter or longer time. On several days last week at sundown the sky was covered with what the country people call 'mares' tails' and 'hen scrats'—long lines of light clouds across the heavens—a sure precursor, they say, of wind.

THE WORKING D 4IRY AT NORWICH. To withdraw the working dairy from the Royal show- yard would be to rob it of one of its chief attractions. Every day the dairy drew together a large number of in- terested spectators, and many and varied were the ques- tions which they addressed to Miss Smithard, the chief dairymaid. In general arrangement the building was erected on the same plan as in previous years; but an added interest was produced by a new division styled the "cheese dairy," where the manufacture of two kinds of soft cheese, which become rapidly fit for consumption, was illustrated at intervals during each day. Brief descriptions of the methods employed may here be given. They are so simple that it is hard to understand why it should have been found necessary to secure the services of a lad from France, M. Paul Mispolet, to perform the operations. The Royal Agricultural Society endeavoured to induce an English dairywoman to demonstrate how the soft cheeses of the St. Ives district are made, but no one could be prevailed upon to undertake this duty. Two distinct kinds of cheese were made in the show- yard—one from an equal quantity of cream and new milk, and the other from fresh separated milk. In the former case the mode pursued was as follows :—A gallon of cream and a gallon of new milk having been thoroughly mixed together, and brought to a tempera- ture of 62 deg., a very small quantity of Hansen's ex- tract of rennet (mixed with water in the proportion of one drop of rennet to ten drops of water) is added and well stirred in, the whole being then allowed to stand for twenty-four hours. At the expiration of this time it is pnt in a thick cloth, the ends of which are well twisted or rolled. The cloth and its contents are then put in a wooden crate of convenient size, and on the top is placed a block of wood. In this way the curd is left to drain. After standing twenty-four hours the cloth is changed, and the curd is allowed to stand in the same way for another twenty-four hours. By this time it is ready to put in the moulds, which are of the well- known Neufchatel shape. Before this operation is per- formed small strips of paper are placed round the inside of the moulds, the latter being composed of zinc, with eighteen moulds fixed together. In putting the curd into the moulds great care must be taken to thoroughly fill every mould, but a little practice would enable any- one to become an expert in this, as in all other opera- tions In France, where very large quantities are made, the moulds are filled by steam-power. The cheeses, with the paper around them, are immediately taken out of the moulds and placed in boxes, each containing twelve. In the showyard they are offered for sale at 3s. a box; and as thirty-six cheeses were made from a gallon of cream and a gallon of milk, it will not be difficult to esti- mate the profit, assuming, of course, that a ready sale could be found for such cheeses at 3d. a piece. On the latter point, however, we are by no means sanguine. Some of the cheeses made at Norwich were certainly far too soft, as Miss Smithard and other officials were will- ing to admit; but, on the other hand, we must make allowance for the difficulties to be encountered in con- ducting such operations in an open shed. The other French soft cheeses, made from separated milk, were not unlike the white York curd cheese, which meet a certain , demand in London and other large towns. They may be sold either whole or cut into pieces. In the latter way they are sold in France at about id. a lump. The separated milk when at 62deg. to 63deg. is curded with Hansen's rennet, pains being taken to use no more than is necessary. The milk then stands for twenty-four hours, when the curd is taken off very thinly with an ordinary skimmer, Placed in sieves or wickerwork baskets of the required size, and left for twenty-four hours. There is no pressure beyond the weight of the curd. Great care must be taken on no account to break the curd; in fact, this is the great secret in the manu- facture of the article. Of course, cheeses of this descrip- tion require to be eaten up very soon after being made, otherwise they would become hard and indigestible. It need scarcely be said that cheese from whole milk could be made in exactly the same way. The demonstrations of butter-making, accompanied by Miss Smithard's running commentary, were a source of unfailing interest. As she very truthfully remarked, there are a great many reasons for bad butter in England. One is that cows are not kept clean, and every care taken to prevent milk being tainted. Especially now that ensilage is in vogue, means should be taken to prevent its smell penetrating to the dairy. Before commencing their task the milkers should always scour their hands, and then rinse them in cold water. One of the secrets of good butter is, that the cream should be taken off while the milk is perfectly, sweet. If it stands too long a cheesy flavour is deve- loped, and is imparted to the butter. After the cream is obtained the proper plan is to ripen it but if required for immediate use it should be cooled it, obtained by a cream separator), and then heated to the proper tem- perature for churning. From 24 to 30 hours is enough to ripen cream; more than the latter ought not to be allowed. After the cream is ripened, Miss Smithafd's practice is to strain it, and then test it with a small creamometer ; she considers that no dairy is complete without this instrument. If the cream is tested and brought to the right temperature (58 deg. or 60 deg.), the butter will come in its proper time—half an hour, or not more than ten minutes longer. If the tempera- ture is not right, the best plan is to put the cream in a small cylinder, and then dip it in warm or cold water, as may be required. Miss Smithard greatly objects to colouring butter, but if colouring is necessary in order to suit customers, she considers carrot juice the best for , the purpose. At first she churns slowly, taking out the I stopper occasionally to ventilate the churn. After a few minutes, churning is proceeded with at a steady pace for 20 minutes or so. Then it is well to look in the churn. The great thing is to stop churning directly the butter comes. The next process is to take away all the butter- milk—and this requires great patience on the part of the dairymaid—and then proceed to wash the butter three or four times. Miss Smithard prefers not to dry-salt the butter, but to use a nice brine made by mixing 1 lb. or 11 lb. of salt in a gallon of water. Of course the hand should not be used at all, because the hand naturally is porous, and experience teaches that butter does not keep so well if touched by the hand. After use all dairy uten- siLs should be thoroughly scalded, and lie in boiling water for about ten minutes. It is very important to preserve the grain of the butter. When taken out of the churn the butter is worked in an " Albany " or other butter-worker, or in the Delaiteuse. The action of the machine, briefly described, is as follows :—" The butter, after leaving the churn, is, while still in a granular state, , r, placed—about 16 lb. at a time—in a canvas bag. This bag is then placed in a metal cylinder, perforated with holes, like a colander, which, from motion communicated by the horizontal spindle, is made to revolve rapidly- -700 to 800 turns per minute. Tho result is that the buttermilk, or any other moisture the butter may con- tain, is driven off to the circumference, and thence through the holes into the outer case, whence it passes out by the pipe into a receptacle underneath, the butter remaining in a perfectly dry condition, in imme- diate readiness for being worked up into pats of whatever shape may be required. The whole ope- ration only takes four minutes, and directly one lot of butter is dealt with another may be put in. It follows, then, that, taking five minutes as the time required, changing included, about 14 cwt. of butter can be dealt with in an hour. There is a friction

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

CABBAGE is essentially a poor man's vegetable, and with many it is such a favourite, in conjunction with a few rows of potatoes, that scarcely anything else finds a place in the garden, and the latter consequently pro- duces very • little variety. Sweet, tender cabbage we always enjoy in May and June, but from now on-Wards we prefer sweet turnips, carrots, cauliflowers, peas, and various kinds of beans for a change. The cabbage is one of the most exhaustive crops in the garden, and occu- pies the land for more than twelve months; for those that are.usually sown at this time are rarely in before June, and some of them remain on the ground till August or September, just as the cabbage happens to heart, some sorts doing this much earlier than others. It would therefore appear that if we wish to shorten the season we must pay a little attention to varieties. Non- pareil Improved is a favourite with many gardeners who have this in view, and Wheeler's Imperial is another ex- cellent variety. Cattell's Reliance is another favourite, and we have grown those, and cannot find much differ- ence in point of earliness. Ellam's Dwarf Early Spring is a new variety, and said to be unsurpassed for its earli- ness, compact habit, and hardiness. Those who wish for later and larger varieties should choose Battersea or Ful- ham or Enfield Market, and plant them on the outer side, so as not to interfere with clearing the ground for an- other crop. As so much depends upon the lengthy season that is to follow the sowing, it is advisable to I'make two—one forthwith and another about 10 or 14 idays later' when one is sure to be right, and perhaps ,looth may be found useful. We found the late sowing 1' most useful last season, simply because they were so small that they were not moved out of the bed they were pricked out in. This enabled us to provide them for some weeks with shelter, which was the means of hastening them so that we cut from them first. Select for a seed bed a rich, mellow piece of ground, and scat- ter the seed thinly over the bed, or draw drills half an inch deep and sow in them. In either case the seeds will need about that thickness of soil over them this season of the year; and if the weather is dry and sunny after the operation is completed, the bed would benefit by a slight shade till the seed appears above the soil, and where birds are troublesome some of the seeds should be protected from the first. Leeks: To grow these fine they should have trenches prepared for them, as for celery. One, two, or three rows may be planted; and the growth they will make will as a rule be in propor- tion to the space they occupy. Some excellent stuff may, however, be grown by planting two rows in such a trench as would be calculated to produce one good row of celery.

THE FRONT GARDEN.—Dahlias : Where these are grown from old stools they are apt to throw up a greater I number of shoots than can really be accommodated round a single stake, and it is a question as to whether more stakes are added or the number of shoots reduced. 1 If large flowers be the object, the latter course must be adopted, and two or three will be sufficient for each root. Those who grow for exhibition rely upon cuttings, and a single stem is run up, and when it makesa natural break, the weakest of the shoots are removed and the flower-buds thinned so as to concentrate the whole energy of the plant into the few remaining buds. The plants require much feeding with liquid manureand the surface of the ground round the plants should be mulched with partially decayed cow manure. Some- times this is put on quite fresh, and by frequent;water- ings the fertilising ingredients are in time washed out of it, and when thus freed of its rankness the roots come up to the surface of the soil and enter it. If, however, 'an inch or two of less crude matter is placed under it, the chances are that the roots would enter that at once and ultimately penetrate into the other.—Annuals: These are usually allowed to remain too thick and one spoils the other. It is not easy to give instructions asto the exact distance they should be thinned, inasmuch as the plants grow double their dimensions in some ground, as well as being affected by the season—a moist season being much more conducive to the growth of these as well as other plants. Keep the plants from encroaching upon each other by pulling the weakest out in the earliest stages of their growth, and later by cutting portions from the strongest plants, from time to time as may be required. THE GREENHOUSE.—An amateur acquaintance, who. had exhausted his patience in trying to keep them in health, contemptuowlv characterised the Cyclamen as. the "Sickly Men." "Not an inappropriate appellation this, even when they are seen at times under the care of the professional The corms will now be starting to- grow, and they should be turned out of their pots and the soil shaken away from the roots; potted in sweet loam with one-fourth leaf-mould and one-eighth coarse sand. The corms are buried half their depth in the soil,. which should not be pressed too firmly round them. Some growers after this stand the pots on ashes to pre- vent the ingress of worms, and cover the pots and corms with cocoanut fibre and refuse with sifted leaf soil. They require So little water until they are fairly growing that it is necessary to take some steps to protect them from. the rain. Another method of growing them is to plant them in the same kind of soil in the open ground and lift and pot them in September..

As for the place you were born in, don't find fault with that; you need not be a horse because you were born in a stable. ' King Frederick VI. of Denmark, while travelling through Jutland, one day entered a village school and found the children lively and intelligent and quite ready to answer his questions. "Well, youngsters," he said, "what are the names of the greatest kings of Denmark ?". With one accord they cried out, "Canute the Great, Waldemar, and Christian IV." Just then a little girl, to whom the schoolmaster had whispered something, stood up and raised her hand. "Do you know another ?" asked the King. "Yes. Frederick VI. !" "What great act did he perform ?" The girl hung her head and stam- mered out," I don't know." "Be comforted, my child," said the King, "I don't know either." • BABuLsTEßs—wbose professional labours necessitate long In- tervals between meals—nothing will be found so exhilarating, comforting, and capable of sustaining exhausted natu,e as Cadbury's Cocoa, guaranteed absolutely pure. THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY. POULTRY-HOUSES.—III. The question as to whether the house should be raised from the ground or not is one that has never been fully settled. At one time we were in favour of the plan of raised houses, but we have come to the conclusion that they are not advisable. There can be no doubt that they were first introduced in order to secure two desirable objects, namely, a convenient shelter for the fowls in wet or hot weather at the least expense, and to economise space in crowded places. And it must be admitted that the houses which have the floor raised 30 inches from the ground attain both of these objects. In the case of a small ',run where there is only a very limited amount of ground at the disposal of the poultry-keeper a consider• - able addition is thus made to the run. For instance, if the run is 20ft. long by sft. wide, the having of the run under the house will add about a fifth to the run—a very important addition. And as it is necessary to have some place apart from the house itself where the fowls can go for shelter this serves that object also. Therefore if this were the only consideration the plan would be worthy of universal adoption. Our great objection to the plan is that the fowls are so very much colder in a house like this than in one the floor of which comes to the ground. Instead of the sides only of the house being played upon by the atmosphere, in addition to the roof, there is the floor also, and thus the house is entirely surrounded by a bed of cold air. Not only so. but it is more difficult to make the floor air tight than the sides, and generally the birds are in a direct line of draught. If the temperature of two houses be taken, one of which is made with the run below and the other not, it will be found that what we have here stated is correct. Therefore houses in which the fowls are to be kept during the autumn and winter seasons should not be built with the run below. It is difficult enough to keep wooden houses warm in any case without adding unnecessarily to the difficulty. Of course., for summer houses which are merely to be used during a portion of the year it does not make any matter.

Mention has already been made of the size of poultry- houses, but there is another question which it is always desirable to bear in mind, and that is how the wood will cut, when it is to be built of that material. With bricks and stone it d'oes not matter in the least, but when wood is employed' the less waste there is the cheaper will the house ultimately be. In this country flooring deals are usually cut in twelve lengths. Therefore four, six, or twelve feet Wises prevent any waste. This may seem a small consideration where wood can be had for the cutting, but it is only comparatively few who are so placed, and even this hint may be the means of pre- venting loss. We have just spoken of a twelve feet house. As a riffe it is not desirable to make any house ' twelve feet in one compartment, as this accommodates more fowls than should be kept together. But some- times in a permanent structure it may be desirable or necessary to make a house of that size. In this case it is better to divide it into a couple of compartments, which during the' breeding and chicken rearing seasons will be found much more useful than one larger house. Before commencing the erection itself, it is desirable to decide just what can be done with the houses, should circumstances arise necessitating the selling of them. In the case of small portable erections it is all right, but if the buildings are larger, then the removal of them is a difficult task, and often involves spoiling them unless they are made at first in such a way that they lend themselves to removal. This consideration was pressed upon us very forcibly some time ago. A gentleman who had gone very extensively and expensively into poultry-keeping, wished to sell off his stock of birds and houses. The latterhad cost him large sums, and he did I not realise a tithe of what they had cost, simply because I they were so difficult to remove. In some instances houses which could have been sold over and over again had to be left for this reason, or almost given away. We do not advocate that all houses be made in the way those usually sold by poultry-house vendors are, for that adds to the original cost; but what can be done without any difficulty is 6 put them together in sections, and with sCrews instead of nails. Then, should there arise any need for their sale or removal, in the one case a better price will be realised, and in the other there will be con- siderably less trouble involved in the business. If it is I wished to make the house similar to the portable ones usually sold, the way to do this is to make each side separate and complete, and the roof in two sections. The whole is then put together with bolts, and can be taken to pieces snare-erected very speedily. It is need-- ful in houses like this to make the parts strong and of good material, for if this is not done the taking to pieces will soon destroy. There are many thhigs which appear all right so long as they are not touched, but once come to interfere with them and they reveal at once their. weaknesses. This is specially true in the case of poull try houses.

One of these portable poultry houses will need to be in seven pieces. First, the front, in which there should 'be the window and, if no covered run is provided, the small trap door; second, the side in which the door is placed, which may be that to the right or left, as may be thought best; thircl, the other side; fourth, the back;. fifth, the floor, unless one is dispensed with, as we prefer; sixth and seventh, the roof in two pieces, if a gabled one, but if a sloping roof then it will be only in a single piece. If gabled there will need to be a cap made to fit the apex of the roof running its whole length, so as to make it perfectly water tight. There is another form of poultry house which is often very much used, namely, the lean-to. This is very suit- able for gardens, and where there is a wall which can be utilised for one side or the back. In a cold, unfavourable position it is a great help if there is a wall which can be utilised in this way. We once saw in Scotland a very clever use made of the wall flanking the field that was the fowls' run. This run was on the north side of the wall, and therefore on the cold side. But the houses were erected on the southern side, there being only trap- holes in the wall to allow of communication between the houses and the runs. This is a plan that could be fol- lowed by many with advantage when they are troubled by the same unfavourable conditions. These lean-to houses requite to be well built and to have the joints between the wall and the sides properly made, or they are very liable to let in the rain. In gardens where the amount of space at command for the poultry run is very limited these answer very well indeed, as the house and run need not be more than 4ft. wide, and have just as much length as can be afforded to them. The run should be at one end, or at both ends if there is available ac- commodation, with the attendant's door opening out on to the side.

The principles which we have laid down for the making of poultry-houses will enable those who wish to build such houses to do so in the right manner. Of course it is almost impossible to provide for every case and condition, but it will not be difficult to adapt the general rules to the special circumstances of each par- ticular case.

A DAY IN THE "LAND OF WATER- FALLS." (From Ben Brierley's Journal.) "There never wur sich times as these," exclaims the old grandmother, as she stands at her door, watching the passing of brakes, waggonettes, and nondescript vehicles, each laden with human freight, en route for some distant spot in the country-, where they can form a temporary encampment, and partake of an alfresco feed and jolli- fication. She had never known such things in her younger days; a visit to town with her elder children, a seat in the corner of some taproom—there was no better accommodation in those day-s —there to dispose of the contents of a basket, not the finest quality of viands, and spend the day in gazing at shop windows, was her only holiday. To have dreamt of the possibility of being able to visit any part of the kingdom in a day would have turned her head. As soon would she have thought of flying, and taking wing to the antipodes, if she had ever heard of the other hemisphere. But to hear the continuous rumbling of wheels, the clatter of horses' feet, and the screaming of steam whi ties, where once could only be heard the song of birds, the whetting of scythes, and the lazy jolting of a cart, she might well exclaim, "there never wur sich times as these." Not to be behind others in the race for pleasure, the gentlemen composing the "North Manchester Social Pic- nic" Society, of which your humble servant is the President, entered into an engagement with the L. & Y. Railway Co. to be carrried at cheap rates, and by special train, to Ingleton, a romantic piece of Country in the west of Yorkshire. This was to come off on Wed- nesday, the 30th ult. ; and it did, with every possible eclat, added to as fine a day as was ever vouchsafed to pic-nickers. The company numbered about fifty, and being divided among three first-class saloon carriages, were not packed, as we have seen people on ordinary cheap trips, before railway companies had begun to provide for the com- forts of excursionists. In the centre of these saloons are placed tables, which can be variously employed— lunching," or nap -ing„ or the spreading of newspapers. Often, or we may say, as a rule, these table are de- voted to the shuffling, and dealing of royal portraits on pasteboard. Being a special train we had few stoppings on the way, and what added to our comfort,no changes. We had one pleasant break at Hellifield, and imme- diately the flies were at the sugar. Everyone was bound to be thirsty, especially when the waiting is provokingly slow. But what could two young ladies do for fifty mouths agape, like young starlings,re.ady-fOr the worm? But we are off again. Though our tickets are for Ingle- ton, we agreed to drop off at Clapham, about four miles distant, to give the opportunity to those who had not been before, of visiting the celebrated cave there. Those who had already explored this subterranean wonder, lounged about the village, admiring its trickling water- falls, which the villagers said when the water was pro- perly turned on sent up a roar like Niagara, or a pocket edition of it. Up in the grounds marked "private " there is a tinkling cataract which steals and leaps its , way down its rocky course inviting us to seat ourselves on the parapet of an ornamental bridge, and listen to its drowsy music. At the bottom of-the fall there is a pool that ought to be inhabited by trout, but perhaps the weather was too hot for these wary denizen& of stony waters to show themselves; so that the flies that. hover about the surface of the pool enjoy an immunity from immediate danger. It is not well to linger long on the seat, for fear sleep might overtake us, or we. might feel a sudden impulse to take a dive into the pooL The section of our party returning from the cave, we took conveyances to Ingleton, a pleasant drive if the powdered hmestone had been previously- damped. On the way we had a sight of Penyglient, the highest of the twin mountains which form the " paps " of West York- shire. Anon the other, Ingleborough hove iti sight, and we- had a clear outline of it. We promised ourselves we would' make an ascent some time in the afternoon, but the time' never came. There were some of us whose joints were not so "limber" as they were thirty years ago, and who were constitutionally inclined to laziness. If we could "do the various-waterfalls in the district it would be a good day's work, and more than seine of us would be inclined to do if we had to be paid for it. The fine hotel at In- gleton was the goal of our present desires, as notwith- standing that we had demolished almost a dairy of cheese, and paid for it, there were those amongst us who were ready again. It is evident that mountain air is a better appetiser than the thin breeze blowing from the sea. We reach the-town, if town it can be called, where the bellman; standing in the market-place can be heard at the corner, -and dogs can sleep in the middle of the road, without fear of being disturbed, and the welcome front of the-hotel is-smiling on us. "Luncheon at one 'r was in our programme but it is two already, and we are informed brour hoster:s that the potatoes were spoiled. Were they.' They, were worse spoiled in about ten minutes, for they had disappeared, and so had some- thing besides: The wheels oiled, and our joints re- freshed, we are ready for the "round walk," which some imagine is like treading the " gravel " round a bowling- green, and start out as jauntily as if they did not ex- pect a hair being turned. "I'm not going to do any collar work to-day," says one of the stoutest of our party. "It's too hot.' But he did a little of it that had a perceptible effect on his collar, notwithstanding. It is very-pleasant, and very assuring setting out on that walk. We mount the stile, and fancy we have done the hardest work. The greensward is soft, and we trip, lightly on, admiring the landscape, and wondering why- we have not been before: Surely the place is unknown- to tourists; or they would come m droves. There is a, slight change, and we are less jubilant. The footing gets worse ; and there are ugly bits of knolls that we did not expect to meet with, and these get more irregul?x and more difficult to ascend. How the path could be in wet weather we can only surmise. It is quite enough for us as it is, and 'without ladies to look after. Our guide says that after rain a lady should not attempt the walk without having the company of a gentleman. She would not have mine. She would have to go at "own" risk. What could a gentleman do to assist a lady on a narrow path, at an angle of seventy-five degrees, wading through clay puddle, and over stones worn smooth, and with a prospect of being soused in the Greta, after mowing down a grove of young trees, if he missed his footing? Better stay at home if it be wet. The gentle- men who have caused these walks to be laid out have been very considerate in one sense. The halting places are numerous, and we availed ourselves of every one. They afforded us pleasact opportunity for the telling of old stories that are true, and of fledging new ones that are no less-probable. Taking our pleasure after this 1 manner the afternoon wore on, not very comfortably, except when we were resting, when the "wiper" had to be plied about the face and neck, and the wish was. ex- , pressed that there was something more than seats to swallow. We thought a half-way house, where butter- milk, pop, or something else, could be had, would shorten the road, but make it longer to travel. Our first unpleasant encounter was the "Creeping Steads." What this path was before the Improvement Committee stepped hr can easily be imagined. It isvery awkward to ungainly people even now. But what must it have been when visitors had to "creep," cat-like,, on all fours, to get along it? The path is made more tolerable on hot days by the- shelter which the trees afford, and the occasional glimpses of fine prospect when a rent in this natural screen occurs. After traversing"-Creeping Steads*" we come to a wooden stairway leading, or rather droppihg us* into " Swilla Bottom." From an engraving in-our "-guide" we were led to imagine these stairs to be formidable, if not dangerous. The perspec- tive, if it does not increase the number of steps, pulls the whole arrangement out like a telescope, and we look like going headlong to perdition, if we are not very careful, or lose our head. We found there was no such danger. The stairs are as easy to descend-as-the stairs in a "jerry" house, and so constructed that there is no fear of being thrown forward when we descend, or backward when we ascend. It can easily. be imagined that when the Greta and Doe, whichever is which, are in freshet the scene here would be magnificent; but fortunately, or =fortunately for us, most of the river bed was dry, or the river was lading itself out in tea- cupfuls, to make the best of a show. Perhaps we lin- gered longer here than was necessary to take in the beauty of the scene. Shirt Collars were getting limp already,,and throats were in a state of--" parch-ment." Away I, nor let me loiter in my songs. For waliave many a mountain path to tread. Now we are getting to work, and we struggle silently on. We are going the nearest way, because many a, time we have our backs to the head of the valley, and, our faces towards the place whence we started. Onwards, zig-zag we go, till we reach another resting place. How kind of the Improvement Company, to furnish these opportunities of unloading our portfolios of old tales, and furbished up "cracks," while we got i down the temperature that is making, our linen feel like ' a huge plaster! There is ever a rift in the screens of foliage where these benches are placed; and we. are enabled to make ourselves.familiar with the beauties of the opposite side of the valley, and calculate what would be the effect of an attempt to cross over. Now we are getting much nearer the. sky, and we are wondering how we shall descend. We have now our goal in view, and a little more grunting will brine us to it. Here I would say to a companion, "Do not look down, for fear you might miss your footing, and / might be exiled as. a witness at the inquest, keep your pecker' well on the line and shout 'Excelsior.'" Here is our final resting place—well, so far as our mountaineering is concerned. Ido not mean the other thing. The "Pecos, Falls" are before us, but a good quarter of a mile distant. A nearer approach would spoil their beauty. We can see the silver lacing- that seems to bind the rocks together, until it spreads itself out in a molten state, and tumbles into the poo/ below. Here the last story is told, for we intend having a proper " wind " before we return. We had missed one of our companions at an early stage of our journey. He must have taken another path. Yes, he is yonder, at the bottom of the valley, and near to the Falls. But he cannot telegraph to us the means by which he got there, and avoided so much climbing. But we fancy, the dry,- MSS of some portions of the river bed must have been taken advantage of, or he could not have beaten us by such a disaance. His trousers, wet up to the calf, ex- plained that he had occasion sometimes to follow the trout track.

Yorkshirernert are at to " gush" over the Craven Waterfalls. Our guide tells us that the road along the Pecca "lies perilously near to the margin of the strealst and the roar of the cataracts above, which aro liiddM from sight, is appalling. * * * * The view up and down the ravine from this point is one to remember, being a perfect panorama of wood and water, cascade and torrent. Five of the seven falls are visible, three above, and two below, and as they leeP with deafening noise over the steep rocks that impede their course into the boiling cauldron at the base of each, it is impossible to look on unmoved at the sublimity of the scene where grandeur sits enthroned, and man is but a bubble compared with the mighty forces here dis- played."

(.3ur author assures us at the commencement that ho "shall make no attempt at fine writing ;" but I think there's a touch of it in the foregoing. He might behold some "mighty forces" if he took a trip to Canada, and placed hixaself at the foot of Montmorency Falls, or the Falls of the Chaudierie, or the Lorette. He would se! and hear something there that would be "appalling. If he was not satisfied he might get a little nearer to the States, and gaze upon the placid Niagara, where the water tumbles down in bucketfuls, and is not pumped back again. Bucketfuls! when it is computed that 28,000 tons of water are shot over the falls every second, one may be sure it has something to say about itseif when it strikes the "pool" below. No mere trickle, that. If he would get a little nearer home, and place himself in the shadow that darkens the " Ausabler chasm," he might see and hear some "mighty forces" at work there. If he is not appalled by the dashing and tossing of the falls, he might not feel so complacent at the idea that a slip would project him into a depth of seventy-five feet of river, that has in its time scooped out 200 feet of chasm, walled like the ruins of a castle that has been breached by an army. We did not get up to "Thornton Force," prefering that the younger branches should report to us what the had seen there. Besides, some of us had been there before, and there was a slackne.o of material for making a respectable show. Some of the streams prefer an underground passage, and 01111 emerge into daylight to get their breath. The cunninci stream that supplies the water to " Weathercote Cave? sought to conceal its retreat. It was thought that it stole away by certain "pots "in the vicinity, and piirr suit was baffled. But a genius arose, and made the dis- covery of its destiny by emptying a bag of chaff in diva stream. The morning following the chaff was found in the Lune.

But the retreat of the sun has left one side of the valley in shadow. Ingleborough is preparing its night- cap, and the solitude that surrounds it grows more and more intense. Besides, we fancy we can hear the clatter of plates at the hotel. The fancy has been prompted by hunger, and a desire to be doing something more agree- able than unstarching our linen, and stiffening our joints, we descend cautiously. Were we to attempt pace we might descend more quickly than we bargained for. We reach the level greensward again, and congratulate ourselves that, barring the spoiled work of our laundresSl we are not much the worse for our climbing. "What distance is it to where we have been ?" we inquire. "About a mile," is the answer. "A mile! more lik. three." "A mile as the crow flies. A crow would not be such a d—d fool as to go the road you've been." Nor more he would, we thought. Well, the dinner was the finest artificial attraction Nve had yet seen. It repaid us for all our rambles. But the latter had given us an appetite which could not have been found in the slums of Manchester; and as we len the station on our way home, we heard it boasted that someone had eaten enough for a week. That was a pie - nicker, and no mistake.—BEN BRIBRLEY.

BAZAAR AT WESTON POINT. PRESENTATION TO MR. R. VERDIN, M.P. A bazaar in aid of the funds of Christ Church School, Weston Point, was commenced on Wednes- day, and continued. throughout the week. The opening ceremony was performed by Mr. Robert Verdin, M.P. for the Northwich Division, who was accompanied by Miss Verdin, Miss M. Verdin (9f Liverpool), Miss Cooke (Crewe), and Mr. Verdin Cooke. Amongst the numerous company present were the Revs. J. H. Wilcockson (incumbent), R. Edwards, J. J. Bryant, W. Fielding, B.A. (Aston), and R. Masheder (Salford) ; Dr. Mangan, Dr. Ma- Dougall, Mr. Lightburn, Mr. A. Lighburn, Mrs. Gibson, Mrs. Joynson, Mr. and Mrs. R. Clark, Messrs. Rosenberg, J. Pain, W. Deacon, T. Raynor, R. H. Clark, T. Moore, Griffiths, Weston, Dalton, and J. Barton.

Mr. Verdin, who was cordially greeted, said he willing)! consented to open that bazaar, because be knew that thoee schools had done a good work, and that they were placed under a disadvantage now owing to the River Weaver Trustees wishing to keep within strictly legal bounds, had withdrawn their support from the schools some three years ago. The Trustees had not only erected the schools, but had up to that time supported them. Weston Point was populated by what be might call workers • there was DO residential population from whom they could expect annual subscriptions with which to meet the expenses; and the managers of the schools had found they must early get into debt. At the present time there was a debt of MO, and it was further desired toubtain 60 for the purpose of re- furnishing the schools.. A like sum was also needed for the erection of a wall to enclose the playground. He was pleased that the inhabitants of Weston Point had done cer. tam n work, and then had gone outside for help in connection with that bazaar; And he hoped they would realise not only sufficient to wipe offs, the debt, but also have a handsome sum towards the other objects they had in view. (Applause.) Mr. Verdin then declared the bazaar open. Mr. L. Rosenberg then read the following address " Robert Verdin, Esq., M.P. Dear sir,—We, the under- signed managers of the Weston Point Church School, desire your acceptance of this address as a token of our apprecia- tion of pour kindness in opening the bizaar in aid of our school. Our sense of obligation to you is all the greater knowing, as we do, ,the excitement which you have lately undergone in connection with the Parliamentary elections, and the increased onmtaer of calls made upon your time owing to the onerous public position which you now oc- cupy. We trust your life may long be spared to fill the position to which you have been lately elected, and that you may enjoy many years of happiness and prosperity,—We are, most respectfully yours, J. H. Wilcockson, R. Clark, Rosenberg, T. Jeffs..". The reading of the address, which was beautifully illuminated by Meredith, Ray, and Littler, of Manchester, was received with applause. The Rev. J. H. Wilisockson then made the presentation, and remarked that he thought parsons better out of the arena of politics. He was,,however, certain that Mr. Verdin would represent that division of the county as well as any man could do, and they must rem.mber that he was not the member of a portion of the constituency, but of the whole. k Applause.) He thanked Mr. Verdin for his presence that day, and spoke of the noble manner in which he (Mr. Wileock• son) had been supported by the working claws of Weston point in making that effort to aid the funds of, the school. (.Applause.) The fair vendors then commenced the sale of their wares which were tastefully displayed. The space at the dispo- sal of those whohad arranged the bazaar had:been used to the best advantage, and the appearance of the room was bright and attractive. No. 1 stall was presided over by Mrs H Wilcockson, Miss Jackson, Mrs J H Wilcockson, and Mrs Latterthwaite (of Lancaster) ; (2) Mrs ROsenberg, Mrs F. W. Clark, Mite Jeffs, and Miss K. Rosenberg; (3) Mtn A. Ward, Miss Maud Clarke, Miss Lily- Hayward, Min!' Emily Hayward; Mrs Reese, and Mrs Mather; (4) Mrs 3 McLean, Mrs Fryer, Mrs Dickens, and Miss Ditchfield. The refreshment stall was under the superintendence of Mrs Clarke, assisted by Miss F. Clarke, Miss Pelly Clarke, and Miss Blanche Clarke. The usual entertainments were pro. vided, and. the Mersey Mission Baud and the Weston Church, and Mill Brow Brass Banda- played selections of music during the evening.

To RiNDRR BOOTS AND SOgS WATERPROOF.—A good' composition for winter use, when it is desired to make • boots proof against snow and wet, is composed of one, part mutton suet and twice that quantity of beeswax\ melted together. It should be applied to the leather at night, and the boots wiped with a flannel next morning. Although when the composition is first applied the leather will not polish as well as usual when blacked, yet they will be susceptible of. a brilliant polish after the blacking has been applied a few times. The following composition not only renders the leather capable of re- sisting wet, but also makes it more pliable, softer, and. more durable. Dissolve half an ounce of Burgundy pitch. in half a pint of drying oil mixed with half an ounce of turpentine. To use this fluid the boots should<be mado. slightly warm beforethe fire, and then painted over with the composition by means of a soft brush. Then allow:. them to dry, and paint them over again with the liquid,. The boots should then be placed in a warm and dry place until perfectly dry.. Another composition of a similar kind is made by dissolving an ounce of powdered resin in a quarter .of a pint of linseed oil made hot over the fire in a pipkin. Then add two ounces of mutton suet from the kidney, chopped up small-, and simmer until the materials are well mixed. This composition is applied like th 3 last, but does not require a second ap- plication.—From "Cas.sell's Household Gz.ide." 15,000 PERSONS STARVING. ST. JOHN'S, TUESDLY ETENlNG.—Further details received here from Labrador state that the snowstorm which com- menced there on the 20th inst. has cemented the ice and closed all the trails. Between 10,000 and 15,000 persons are thus cut off, and it is believed cannot escape death. A large number of Polar bears have been driven south by star- vation, and are devastating the country. The Indians are eating their dead companions. The severe cold is caused bv the Arctic ice massed along the shore. Winter sets in in two months, and it is thought imposiible for the ice to dis- appear in the time. A DYNAMITE SCARE IN NEW YORK. NV.' YORK, TllESDAY.—Yeaterday the Coney Island Steamship Conapany entertained Dom Augusto, a Brazilian Prince, and a large number of distinguished citizens of New York. In the evening, while returning in the special steamer from Coney Island, a contrivance resembling a bot- tle with a lighted fuse attached was in the cabin. It was at once seized and thrown overboard amidst great excitement and almost panic. Opinion vary as to whether an elaborate hoax has been played upon the steaniship company, but the manager now admits that he previously received an anonymous letter warning him that if he entertained the representatives of tyranny " revenge" would follow. The letter was signed—" By order of the Social Revolution Committee."

SOUTH AFRICA. WE Towle, JULY 7.—A deputation from the Boer Zulu Republic hal arrived 'in Natal, and had an interview with the Governor on the sth. They claimed official recognition of their independence, 2,269,000 acres of land, and suzerain rights over the whole of Zeluland exclusive of the reserve. The Governor insisted that 250 farms out of 800 acres claimed should be renounced, with all pretensions to suze- rainty. The deputation conceded the latter point, hut in- sisted on keeping the farms. It is reported that 50 to 60 parties of Boers have treklied into Massouna country, and intend occupying land there. Fighting is expected between the Malabeles aid Beers. ABOLITION OF SLAVERY IN CUBA. MADRID, WEDNESDAY.--During the discussion of the Cuban Budget in the enamber of Deputies, last night, Senor Labra brought forward an amendment authorising the Government to free as soon as possible 26,000 Cuban slaves (Patrocenados) who are still under the protection of their former masters. The Government accepted the amendment, and it was unanimously agreed to. The Pre- sident of the Chamber congratulated the House on the adoption of the resolution, which he declared was the crowning of the glorious work of the abolition of sla.very• The sitting was suspended at 2 a.no. DESTRUCTION OF A THEATRE: 100 PERSONS KILLED. MADRAS, WRDNESDAY:--The Hindoo theatre at Tinni- velly has been burnt down, and 100 natives been killed, and many injured.

THE CHOLERA— WEDNBSDAI.—The cholera returns during the past twentv-four hours report 7 cas,s and 3 deaths at Franca- villa Fontana, 3 deaths at Latia.r.o, 29 cases and 5 deaths at Mandurla, 2 cases at Ferrara, 9 cases and 2 deaths at Codi- goro, 9 cases and 6 deaths at Massafiscaglia, and 4 cases and 3 deaths at Lago Santo.

A man may dearly love his wife And from all ill defend her, But still he's apt to plague her life When the beefsteak isn't tender. Boston young lady (visiting in Chicago): I am very agreeably surprised in Chicago. I had no idea that it was a city of so much refinement and culture.—Chicago young lady: Oh, yes; we are making Chicago a very dizzy place for cult?' Education in its true sense, must have two distinct arms—to inform and develop the mind and to inspire and influence fhe heart. The success of each of these depends largely upon the success of the other; and upon their united and harmonious action will depend the strength and excellence of the character and the purity and value of the life. All knowledge is like good seed— it cannot be too highly prized or too widely disssemi- nated ; but to realise its possibilities it must be placed in fruitful soil prepared to rece,iye and vitalise it.
