THE POLITICAL SITUATION. LORD SALISBURY'S ACCEPTANCE OF OFFICE. - EXPECTED PROPOSAL OF CONSERVATIVE

HOME RULE. Lord Randolph Churchill reached Arlington-street shortly after ten o'clock on Saturday, and remained in consultation with Lord Salisbury for over half an hour, when he left. Immediately after his departure Lord Salisbury walked over to Devonshire House in company with Mr. Henry Man- ners, his private secretary. 9n reaching there Lord Salis- bury had an interview with Lord Hartington, with whom be remained some time. On Lord Salisbury's departure Lord Hartington accompanied him to the door, and warmly shook hands with him as he left. Lord Salisbury proceeded to Arlington-street, and left there again at eleven o'clock for Victoria Station. whence he proceeded to Osborne, ac- companied b, Mr. Manners. It is understood that the leader of the Liberal Unionists expressed himself as willing to extend a friendly support to the new Conservative G-overnmeat, but adhered to his refusal to join the Admini- stration. Later in the day a Queen's messenger arrived at Devonshire House with despatches from Osborne, and Lord Derby had an interview with Lord liartington. Lord Salis- bury received further despatches from the Queen before leaving London for the Isle of Wight. In his interview with her Majesty on Saturday, Lard Salisbury intimated his readiness to undertake the forraa- tion of a Cabinet, and before leaving Osborne kissed hands on his appointment as First Lord of the Treasury. His Lordship was able to inform the Queen that Lord Harling- ton, though opposed to a coalition Government, is prepared to support a Conservative Administration. The noble Mar- quis, accompanied by Mr. Manners, his private secretary, arrived at his house in Arlington-street shortly afternoon on Monday, and it was remarked by those who are in the habit of seeing him frequently that he looked somewhat pale and

worn. Lord Randolph Churchill arrived by appointment at four o'clock, after Sir Michael Hiaka-Beach had left. The noble lord, who has palpably benefitted by his short trip to Nor- way, drove up in a hansom amidst the cheers of a small knot of idlers who had by this time collected ia Arlington- street. His interview with Lord Salisbury, at which Lord John Manners was present, lasted just half an hour, and on leaving by the park door he walked towards Picsdilly Circus

. _ smoking a eigarette. There was not much doing at Devonshire House on Mon- day. Lord Hartington remained at borne the greater part of the day, and was visited, amongst others of his followers. by Sir Henry James and Mr. Goschen, each of whom had a long interview with his lordship. Mr. Chamberlain, who , arrived at Devonshire House about three o'clock, was en- ' gaged in consultation with Lord Hartington until nearly , four. Lord Stalbridge, formerly Lord Richard Grosvenor, , also had a beg interview with the noble =rani& It is, says the Central News, AR open secret that Mr. Goschen has received from Lord Salisbury a definite offer of a seat in the new Cabinet. It is, therefore, assumed that the object of his visit to Devonshire House on Monday morning was te •onsult Lord Hartington as to the wisdom of accepting the offer of the Conservative leader. It is probable that Mr. Gladstone, having acted as Lord Privy seal, which office has been in abeyance, will accom- pany to Osborne the other outgoing Ministers who have to deliver up the seals of office. The "Pall Mall Gazette" says :—The following forecast of the constitution of the new Cabinet reaches us from a well-informed authority on the Conservative side. whose proclivities are obvious. We give it, of course, with all

reserve : Prime Minister ....... ...... Lord Salisbury. I Lord Oranbrook (old gang). 7"eign 845erebuT 1 Lord R. Churchili (young gang). Lord Cha•cellor ....... Sir Richard Webster. Home Secretary . ........ Sir John Gorst. Seotch Secretary Mr. Arthur J. Balfour. Lord President of Council Mr. °naplain. Solicitor• General Viceroy of Ireland Commander of Forces in Ireland ...Lord Wo.seley. Chief secretary lir. B. Stanhope. The election of the Speaker will be complete on Friday, August 6th, and it is supposed that the Queen's Message referring to the issue of. writs will sot be read before Monday the oth, that if possible all the writs will be moved for, and if not that the House will adjourn till Thursday the 12th, when it is likely that the issue could be

- eompieted. A usually well-informe4 correspondent writes :—Lord Salisbury will now possibly be able to keep Lord Randolph Churchill out of the Foreign Office, but there is said to be greater difficulty about the leadership of the House of Com- mons. In ordinary times Lord Randolph could push Ms ambition with greater success, but these are not ordinary times. The Conservative leader in the House of Commons will have frequent and very critical relations with Lord Hartington, and this fact is pressing against Lord R. Churchill's claim. Lord Hartington would, there can be no doubt, prefer to do such business with Sir H. Hicks- Beach. They are well known to each other; they are both oountry gentlemen; they have a certain similarity of taste and manner. It was a brief conversation between Lord Hartington and Sir M. Hicks-Beach behind the Speatter's chair, which led to the meeting of Mr. Gladstone and Lord Salisbury, and to the transaction which ended in the joint arrangement of the Seats Act. The Liberal Unionists would distinctly prefer to see Lord Iddesleigh at the For- eign Office and Sir M. Hicks-Beach as leader of the House

of COMMORS. MEETING OF THE CONSERVATIVE PARTY. The Press Association says :—Long before half-past two o'clock on Tuesday afternoon, the hour which had been fixed for the meeting of the members of the Conservative party, the attendance at the Carlton Club was abnormally large. The activity which was observable at that institu- tion attracted a large number of persons to the spot. and these lined Pall Mall on each side of the club. Most of the first arrivals at the meeting were received by Mr. Akers- Douglas in the central ball, and with him were the Marquis at Abergavenney and Mr. H. S. Northcote. The lunch rooms and other apartments were soon crowded with the new arrivals, who proceeded subsequently to the reception room upstairs, where the meeting was appointed to be held. The prominent members of the party began to arrive before two o'clock, and those who were recognised were loudly cheered by a large crowd which surrounded the entrance to the club, and occupied the footpath opposite the building. Amongst the earlier arrivals were Earl De La Warr, Colonel Tottenham, the Hon. Edward Stanhope. Mr. S. Herbert, Lord Cranborne, the Duke of Richmond, Mr. Morgan How- ard, Mr. Heniker •Heaton, Colonel Gardiner, Lord Cran- brook, Mr. Ashmead Bartlett, Sir James Fergusson, Earl Jersey, Sir Algernon Borthwiek. The Hon. H. S. North- cote, Sir Richard Cross, Lord Randolph Churchill, Mr. Boord, Mr. Seeger Hunt, and Sir John M‘Garel-Hogg were the next arrivals. Mr. W. H. Smith, Lord Charles Beres ford, Mr. Chaplin, and Sir Michael Hicks-Beach came next. Lord Charles Beresford was accorded a hearty reception. Mr. Goschen drove past in a hansom, but was not recog- nised. Mr. Howard Vincent, sir George Elliott, Lord Cado- gan, Mr. Kimber, and others followed. At 2-35, Lord Salis- bury accompanied by the chief among his sapporters, entered the reception room, and was received with great cheering by the meeting, which must have numbered, peers and commoners together, over 40e. The cheering was renewed when his lordship rose to speak. The crowd in Pall Mall at this time was very great, and extra police had to be sent for to prevent the people from encroaching on the steps of the club and obstructing the passage thereto— Lord Salisbury arrived shortly before 2-30, and, dismissing his carriage when he reached the edge of the crowd, he walked through the midst of the people, who vociferously cheered and applauded him, many following his lordship right up to the steps of the club. The Prime Minister frequently acknowledged these greeting by turning and raising his hat. Such a demonstration has not before been seen in Pall Mall. Inside the building his lordship's re- ception was warm and hearty. The Hon. E. Stanhope and Sir A. Borthwick were amengst the next arrival., the for- mer being loudly cheered. Lord Winborne, Lord Halsbury, Earl Jersey, Lord Brabourne, Lord Ashhourne, Colonel Duncan, Colonel Walrond, Mr. Sidney Herbert, Baron Henry de Worms. Mr. W. Jackson, Mr. Ainslie, Vicount Barrington. and Lord Bathurst followed shortly after two o'clock. The proceedings were strictly private, hut the Press Association furnishes the following resumti of what took place. Lord Salisbury, who, on rising, was received with load cheers, prefaced his remarks with an earnest appeal to those present to regard the proceedings as strictly confidential. He coneratulated the party on the success which had at- tended their efforts at the recent elections, and especielly on their honourable observance of the compact with the Liberal Unionists. In the existing condition of political controversy, the Conservatives and the Liberal Unionists were ighting the same battle, and he was glad to find that when necessary Conservatives were willing to sacrifice their personal interests rather than give cause for irritation to their allies. It was his desire that this condition of things should continue to exist, and with this view he had had an interview with Lord Hartington and bad made efforts to unite the Conservative party and the Liberal Unionists. It would be a breach of confidence on his part to state what Lord Hartington had said to him, but he was at perfect liberty to tell them what he had said to Lord Hartington. He had given the Liberal Unionist leader an urgent invita- tion either to take the responsibility of forming a Ministry himself, which would have the support of the Conservative party, or to co-operate with him (Lord Salisbury) in the formation of a Cabinet. But with every desire to subor- dinate party interests to the maintenance of the unity of the Empire, Lord Hartington, for patriotic reasons, was disin- clined to dissociate himself from those with whom he had been so long and honourably connected. He therefore de- clined the invitation, which had been made in a spirit of good faith, and refused, in complete consistency with his pre- vious avowals. Lord Hartington was perfectly pronounced on this point; but he promised that the policy of the Go- vernment upon Irish affairs should meet with his cordial support so far as from his point of view it tended in the direction of the unity of the three kingdoms. Lord Salis- bury then invited the attention of the meeting to the work to which Parliament would have to turn its attention on its assembling. There were two courses open to them. In the first place, the House of Commons might be called together for the purpose of swearing in members, and that business being disposed of and the writs for the re-election of Minis- ters being issued, the House might adjourn forthwith for an autumn session. The vote on account granted by the last Parliament was for a sufficiently long period to meet such a contingency. On the other hand the House of Commons might, after its reconstitution, immediately proceed to the consideration of Supply. He suggested that it might be wise and prudent to proceed with the outstanding business immediately after the opening of the session in August, and

that might be done after the rs-eleetions had been moved e4neurreutly with thoee re-elections. He referred in general terms to the question of Ireland, which would recaive at the hands of the Government a most careful attention, and expressed a hope that it might not be necessary to call Parliament together again until the early part of next year, when the Government weuid be in a position to state their views on that important subjeet.—The noble lord, who spoke about twenty minutes, was again loudly cheered as he resumed his seat. Sir John Mowbray followed. In a brief speech he drew attenCou to the high and patriotic motives which had ani- mated Lord Salisbury in the present difficult stite of affairs. He thought his lordship was rendering the highest service to his country, and that they should unite in every way to expedite public business. Mr. Cecil Raikes, while agreeing with the suggestion of Lord Salisbury that they should proceed at once to business pointed out that more time might be occupied with it than the noble maiquis anticipated; but, on the whole, he was certainly strongly in favour of the view Lord Salisbury had taken. _ _
Sir Henry Holland said. he viewed the matter from the sarae standpoint as the last speaker, but he thought the course suggested by the Prime Minister was an the whole the best. ._

Colonel Tottenham asked if some information could net be given as te what measures would be prepared for the protection of life and property in Ireland before the Government brought in any measures dealing with the Irish question. Lord Silisbury said at this particular moment it would be imporsible to state what might be necessary in the case of Ireland in view of measures which would in due course be prepared. Lord Carnarvon expressed his intention of giving his most cordial support to a Conservative Government, which he thought absolutely necessary at the present time, having regard, not only to home affairs, but to the general state of politics in Europe. The proceedings were throughout most harmonious, and In the short discussion which ensued Sir Robert Fowler and others took part. After the conclusion of the meeting Lord Salisbury re- mained at the Carlton for over an hour in consultation with Lord Iddesleigh, Sir Michael Hicks-Beach, Lord Randolph Churchill, Mr. W. H. Smith, and ether prominent Conser- vatives. He left at half-pest four for Arlington-street amid loud cheers and wavieg of hats. The meeting resulted practically in a unanimous decision to diepense with an autumn session unless unexpected de- velopements in Irelaud create a necessity for extraordinary legislation. It is probable, therefore, that members will not be released from their Parliamentary duties until at the earliest the first week in September. A brief adjournment will be required after the formal preliminaries of electing the Speaker, swearing members, Acc , for the re-election of mem- bers accepting certain Government appointments, and there- after Supply will be at once dealt with. Parliament will then stand prorogued until the usual time in February.

div.head: MEETING OF LIBERAL LEADERS.
div.p: MEETING OF LIBERAL LEADERS.

In consequence of the events of Tuesday it was felt de- sirable to hold a meeting of the Liberal leaders on Wednes- day with a view to discuss the action which should be adopted on the assembling of Parliament. It was summoned by special messengers on Wednesday morning, and took place at Lord Granville's residence in Carlton Hones-terrace. The members of the Liberal Ministry present were Mr. Gladstone, the Marquis sbf Ripen, the lilted of Rosebery, Mr. Campbell-Bannerman, Mr. Childers, Mr. Stansfield, Mr. John Morley, Lord Herschel], Sir Wm. Harcourt, and Mr. Mundella. Mr. Arnold Motley, chief Liberal whip, was also present, At the oonclusien of the meeting, which laeted from two o'cloelt until twenty minutes to four, Mr. Gladstone and Mr. Arnold Morley remained for some time In consultation with Lord Granville, after which Mr. Os- borne Morgan called en his lordship. It is stated that it was agreed to await the Queen's Speech before coming to a anal decision as to the eonree which should be pursued by the Opposition leaders. It is under- stood, however, that in the probable event of the Irish ques- tion receiving no mention in the Queen's Speech, an at- tempt will be made by the Oppoeition to elicit from the Conservative leaders a statement as to the precise nature of the policy they intend to adopt in regard to Ireland. Fail- ing a satisfactory reply the matter may be discussed at some length, but it is improbable that a division will be pressed. In regard to the outstanding work to be dealt with by the House of Commons, it is understood that the Liberal leaders will give every assistance in their power to the Go- vernment to facilitate the passage of the remainder of the Estimates.

MISCELLANEOUS. It is announced that Mr. David Davies has decided net to file a petition against the return of his Gladstonian oppo- nent, Mr. Bowen Rowlands, for Cardiganshire. It was stated on Wednesday that Mr. Goechen will shortly be returned to Parliament as member for Dublin University, in room of Mr. Ho'meg, who will be made a judge. The Liberal Unionists have determined to maintain their political organisation on a permanent footing, and it is as- wted that the members of the committee are quite as much afraid of the Tories as they were of Mr. Gladstone on the matte* ef Ireland. ' It was decided at a meeting at the National Liberal Club to enlarge and reconstitute the Gladstone Candidates' Elec- tion Fund Comnaittep, under the title of the "United Kingdom Home Rule League," for the purpose of die. eeminating information on Howe Rule and Liberal prin-

ciples. LORD HARTINOTON AND r °CAL GOVERNMENT. Lord Hartington, answering an inquiry from Mr. Hoare, the Unionist candidate for Orkney and Shetland, regarding a local government scheme. says he is in favour of measures of local government for the three kingdoms, not necessarily identical, but based on similar principles.. PROPOSED AMERICAN TESTIMONIAL TO MR. GLAD- STONE.—The "New York World" proposes that a popular subscription be set on foot in order to present a testimonial to Mr. Gladstone as an expression of the esteem in which he is held by the American people and the sympathy they feel with the struggle in which he is engaged. Mr. Bright has written a letter to a gentleman at Birming- ham denying that he had, as stated be Mr. Gladstone, con- tended in 1866 for a legislature in Dublin. He says the con- cessions to and the Liberal legislation for Ireland by the , united Parliament since the year 1566 are enough to eon- Vines any reasonable man that the interests of the United Kingdom may be left to the Parliament at Westminster. MICHAEL DAVITT AND IRISH DisTRESS. Mr. Michael Devitt, publishing his report of the distribution of the re- I lief fund for the islands on the Irish western sea-board, says I no exceptional distress now remains, but the termination of the relief works does not solve the grave problem. A wet or stormy season at a critical harvest period next year may- once more throw the island upon publie benevolence, and unless the Irish are willing to abide the stigma of becoming a mendicant nationality, steps moat be taken to prevent the recurrence of distress. Pending a complete solo:ion, their condition would be materially improved by the develop- ment of the fisheries and the promotion of cottage indus- tries. He asserts that 30 per cent of the relief subscriptions Ands its way directly or indirectly into the coffers of Irish landlords. NATIONAL RADICAL UNION Maemsgero.—The report of the Executive Committee of the National Radical Union, jrtst published, states that the reunion of the party on the basis of some common Irish policy must be accomplished before they could hope to return to power, and the commit- tee believed that when the irritation and division caused by the dubious tactics and the mistaken policy of the late Go- vernment have died away the Liberal party will recognise In the programme of the eseociation the essential conditions I of any further extension of local self-government to the , various portions of the United Kingdom. In the expecta- tion of being able to assist in this result, the officers pro- posed to direct their attention to the work of organising the &distal party, rendered imperative by the unfortunate and intolerant action of some members of the older Liberal As- sociations. ARCHBISHOP CROILB ON NATIONALIST PROSPECTS. Archbishop Croke, sending £360 as a third contribution, tusking £1,600 subscribed by his clergy and flock to the Irish Parliamentary Fund, writes :—" There is absolutely no ground for despondency in the Nationalist camp. The greatest political strategist of this or, perhaps, of any other age is at our head. The proverbially high courage of our race was never higher or more hopeful than to-day. The sympathies of the whole civilised world are with us. We have a compact party of 300 in the House of Commons. I Close on a million and a half of liberty-loving Englishmen have voted for the restoration of our country's rights a d the hearty fraternisation of the two peoples, and so with the prospect of another electoral campaien in the near future, the time is opportune for replenishing the Parlia- mentary purse." Mr. Gladstone having intimated his intention not to sit for Leith, the Secretary of the Leith Unionist Committee replied on Saturday to the letter of the agents of Air. D. R. *Gregor, which stated that, while that candidate had formerly made no secret of his willingness to retire in favour of Sir George Tre- velvan, he had now resolved to hold the field against all comers. The Secretary of the Unionist sail that, as they had every reason to expect the official support of both sec- tions of the Unionist Committee to the candidature of Sir George Trevelyan, to whom an invitation had been addres- sed, they trusted that Mr. *Gregor would adhere to his Arst \resolution not to remain in the field against the right hon. . gentleman. To this Mr. M'aregor's agents answered, that it is not said that Sir George Trevelyan has Consented to stand, and that apart from Mr. *Gregor's psrsonal feelings in the matter they do not feel justified in calling together his committee and supporters to ask their sanction for any departure from the resolution to hold the field. Meanwhile Mr. Munro Ferguson. of Novar, is addressing meetings of the electors as the Liberal candidate.—A meeting of the Leith Unionist Liberal Committee was held on Monday night, when it was reported that the requisition in favour of Sir George Trevelyan as candidate for Leith Burghs had been extensively signed, but that Sir George was not dis- posed to at present engage in another contest. The meeting passed a resolution expressing regret at Sir George's de- cision, and further resolved to tender their support to Mr. Jacks in the event of his now determining to become the candidate. Mr. Jacks afterwards addressed a meeting, and stated that Sir George having declined to come forward, he should himself meet unquestionably contest the seat.
A. fire occurred shortly after Tuesday midnight, at St. John's Church, Bedford, and considerable damage was done to the chancel. The organ was almost /entirely destroyed.

THE CRAWFORD DIVORCE CASE. It is stated that Sir Charles Mike had made arrangements before the end of the trial for immediately leaving the isountry in the contingency of an adverse verdict. Sir losseph M4lienna M.P., has addressed the following letter to Sir Charles Dilke Dear Sir Charles Dilke,—lt may be of no use that I should write to you on the subject of the recent trial, Crawford v. Crawford, the Queen's Proc- tor intervening, but I feel in some degree bound to do so. I have expressed opinions in other cases when the Govern- ment of which you were then a member was in power, and subsequently the convictions which I called in question were actaally, and so far as possible technically and legally, quashed, and it was shown in each case that a miscarriage of justice had occurred. As in those cases to which I refer I have not questioned the sense of justice of the juries or of the judges who tried them, neither do I now in this case, for I am impressed with the utmost respect for both judge and fury. Nevertheless, I cannot regard the proceedings on the intervention of the Queen's Proctor as a satisfactory trial of your guilt or innocence. You were not sufficiently safe- guarded train a miscarriage of justice without counsel being , heard directly on your behalf. After a careful perusal of the evidence, I may say for myself that I regard it as not only inconclusive against you, but in important—nay, vital —points contradictory and incredible." The Times, commenting on this tiial, says :—'‘ It is well to pass over this story of brutish profligacy disclosed in the ease withoat much comment. We feel, indeed, that it is incurring no small responsibility to do more than refer to the passionless nastiness, worthy of Yahoos, which has been the subject of inquiry. Silence in the circumstsnees is best. It is the miserable close of a public career et a statesman whohas performA considerable public services, who possessed many qualifications for the conduct of affairs, and who, while the friend of democratic movements, was saved by his knowledge from espousing crude, visionary schemes. He has published a letter in which he says, 'as far as public Ifs goes, I have no option but to accept the verdict;' and in the natural course of things his name will be struck off the list of Privy Councillors, and he will pass for ever oat al sight of the world in which he has played so conspicu- ous a part. But the public aspect of the case cannot be lest eight of—the letter addressed by Sir Charles to his former constituents forbids this. If the jury be right in their view of the evidence, there has been no ordinary perjury; it has been deliberate, systematic, and renewed; it is even possible that there has been subornation of perjury and conspiracy on a seals rarely witnessed." In the Divorce Court, on Thursday morning, before Sir James Hannen, Mr. Inderwick made an application on behalf of Mr. Crawford for the costs of the shorthand notes on the occasion of both trials. The learned counsel, upon the President hesitating, intimated that he would be satisfied with those incurred in the first trial, and to this his lordship assented.

SHOCKING FATALITY ON PRESCOT TRAMWAY. Considerable excitement was occasioned in Prescot and St. Helens during the early part of the week by the an- nouncement that at about a quarter-past twelve on Sunday morning the dead body of an unknown man was found upon the tramline. midway between Prescot and St. Helens. The head and left arm were nearly severed tram the body, the man apparently having been run over by the car which leaves St. Helens at eleven o'clock on Saturday night. Por- tions of the man's skull and brains were found on the wheel, and a piece of the car brake was found close to de- ceased. The body was removed to the Angel Inn, Eccles- ton-lane end, near Prescot, to await identification and the inquest. The body was apparently that of a tramp, and only 3d in money, a piece of soap, and a little bread and salt were found upon him. Deceased seemed about 40 years of age, sft. 41n. high, and had long dark brown hair and moustache with beard of about a fortnight's growth, and hazel eyes. He was dressed in a pepper-and-salt reefer jacket, with wool check lining, vest of the same material, moleskin trousers with metal buttons, on which were the words" J. Miller, Blackland ;" red and black Scotch plaid sad, elastic braces, two shirts, blue socks, strong lace-up boots plated at heel and toe, and a two-peaked cap. Mr. Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest on the body of the deceased at the Angel Inn, Eccleston-lane-ende, near Prescot, on Tuesday morning. The body of the deceased, still un- identified, was found to have been shockingly mutilated. Mr. .1. 0. Swift represented the St. Helens and District Tramway Cempany.--Thomas Appleton stated that he lived at 38, Market-place, Prescot. About nine o'clock on Satur- day night he was in the King's Arms Hotel. Deceased was there, and asked him for a copper. Witness gave him a penny and a pint of beer, and the man seemed so pleased that he gave him an old pocket-knife, and askrd him to keep it for his sake. Deceased had previously had some drink. Witness last saw him alive outside the King's Arms. On Sunday afternoon he went to see the body of a man who had been killed, and identified it as the man whom he had seen in the King's Arms. Deceased had stated that he had walked from Edinburgh in four days.— Mr. William Kitchen, houseand estate agent, Cropper's-hill, St. Helens, stated that he was driving from Liverpool about midnight on Saturday when his horse shied at something on the road. Witness got out and saw deceased. His head was on the tram line, and it appeared as if a wheel had gone over the back of his neck and across his jaw, which was laid completely open. His left hand was nearly severed from the arm. Witness gave information to the police. He saw a broken brake about two yards from the deceased on the Prescot side, and a cap about two yards on the St. Helens side of the deceased. It was a very dark night, and witness would not have seen the man If his mare bad not ehied.—Police Constable Millington stated that he found deceased in the position described by Mr. Kitchen, and re- moved the body to the Angel Inn. On deceased were found 3d in money, a broken comb, a piece of soap, a broken pipe, and some matches. The officer then described the appear- ance of the man. Deceased had apparently been run over by the car, as a portion of the man's brain was found on the hind wheel. From the position of the man witness concluded that he had put himself on the rails. Other vehicles passed along the road.—The Coroner remarked that they mast not saw that deceased put himself there wilfully, because they had no evidence to that effect. He might have laid himself down without thinking there was any Immediate danger there.—Alfred Large, connuctor of No. 2 car, which left St. Helens at 11-5 on Saturday night, said he was both driver and conductor from the Waterworks. It was an unusual thing, but the driver wanted to go back home. He did not know whether it was against the rules of the company. There were 13 cr 14 passengers on the car. A man named Holdcroft turned himself into amateur conductor. They proceeded slowly dawn School-brow with the brake on. He neither heard nor felt anything to lead him to the belief that he had run over a man. Nobody was with him on the driving platform, so that his attention was not distracted. There was only one wheelguard, and it was on the opposite side to that on which deceased was found. None of the passengers felt any unusual jerk.—Mr. William Goldsworth, jun., said he was a passenger by the car, and there was nothing unusual in the journey. He added that the last witness was perfectly sober and capable, and understood the driving.—Mrs. Elizabeth Swift said she was a passenger, and she felt a shock as if going over a stone, hut it was nothing extraordinary.—The Coroner said he did not see, in this case, that there was any point of law to direct the jury upon; it was simply a question of fact.— The jury then returned a verdict that the man was killed on the road, but there was no evidence to show how be came by his death. The jury recommended that the Tramways Company should place a safe guard on the front of each wheel of their cars.

William Carruthers, a wheel tester, was killed at Locker- bie Station, on Thursday morning. The funeral of the late Hobart Pasha took place at Con- stantinople on Saturday with great pomp, a large crows being present at the ceremony.

OLD CHESTER. "The English Illustrated Magazine" for August tpubliehed by Messrs. Macmillan and Co.) contains a capital paper on" Old Chester." it is by Mr. Mired Rimmer, and as it shows a close acquaintance with all the " ins and outs of the city, it will be read with special interest. The illustrations are from drawings by Mr. H. Railton, and as they are execu- ted in this clever artist's best style, it is a matter of course to say that they are charming. Chester affords ample scope for the pencil of the artist ; and Mr. Railton has as nice a faculty for selection as he has for execution. The frontispiece of the magazine is a fine engrav- ing of a fine "study of a head" from a drawing by I C. Perugine. "In Leicester Fields," a scholarly ! paper by Mr. Austin Dobson. is well illustrated, and we have more of the delightful illustrations by Mr. 1 Hugh Thompson of "Sir Roger de Coverley." We give a few extracts from the article on "Old j Chester : After passing Bishop Lloyd's we come to the 'Yacht Inn," a fine gabled hostelrie opposite to the I great quadrangle where the cheese fairs are held every month. There it was that Dean Swift stayed on his road to Dublin, and he invited the dignitaries of the, Cathedral to have supper with him, but they declined, so he wrote with a diamond ring on a pane of glees in ' the window : "Mouldy without—rotten within. The church and its clergy are all near akin." ' and this inscription remained for many years. Between the "Yacht Inn and Bishop Lloyd's house is a very beautiful example of black and white 1 architecture, called the "Custom House Inn," the I exterior of which seems not to have been altered or ' "restored,' and oppasite this is a fine old mansion connected with which which there is a story so dra- matic, that it would require no embellishing to convert it into a sensational three volume novel. At one time Chester, like other county towns, con- wined the town houses of the principal county fami- lies, who retired here for the" season." London was a pilgrimage to reach, and even to the end of the last century, the society was exclusiveness itself. Mer- chants and bankers were hardly admitted, even slave- owners, who were considered, perhaps, to follow the most respectable branch of business, could only with difficulty gain admittance. Into the middle of this exclusive region, Mr. Joshua Horton, a gentleman from London, was freely admitted with his family. He occupied the house spoken of, and rented a county seat called Cotton Hook, four miles from Chester, for three lives. His hospitalities were great, and indeed it became quite a privilege to have the eritrie of his mansion, though he was courtesy itself to all corners. There were many surmises as to who the stranger might be, but his prompt payments and affluence, and his dis- tinguished bearing pointed him out to be someone superior, and surmise even went so far as to gay that he belonged to the ill-starred family of Stuart; and his money came from France. Nis next door neighbour was Alderman Mainwar- ing, the head of a great Cheshire family, and at the time about to be alluded to, the city was full of the aristocracy of the county. The Egertons, and Leighs, and Wilbrahams, and Cholmondleye, and many others, had houses there, and these were occupied by the families. One night in the early part of the year iaoo, there had been the usual festivities, and torch- men and sedan-chairmen were conveying the revellers home, when a curious light was seen in Mr. Horton's house. A cry of fire was raised, and the volunteers to help were astonished to find the door barricaded; and they heard people moving inside. An entrance was forced, and there was a great scramble to escape; everyone did except Mr. Horton, who turned out to be the chief of a desperate gang of comer's. The cru- cibles were there full of metal, and one which had upset caused the conflagration. Dies and everything 1 were found. On the Bth April, x7OO, Chief-Justioe Jekyll opened a special aseize in Chester to try this late addition to the ranks of the county aristocrats. He was, of course, found guilty and condemned to death. Some legal points were, however, raised in his behalf, and these were referred to London ; and taking advantage of the delay he seems to have man- aged to make his peace with the sheriff who doubt- less had often enjoyed his hospitality—for his career extended over some three or four years—and he made his escape, for which the sheriff WAS heavily fined. This worthy must have made friends when be had the opportunity, for he lived and died in obscur- ity, and was never called on to expiate his crimes. The next illustration takes us to Bridge-street, which in strict parlance should be called Southgate- street, as it leads us to the south gate of the ancient city, but the circumstance of its being the road to the bridge which spanned the Dee overcame its more ob- vitras appellation. There are many fine remains here, and the shops are in numbers of instances built over splendidly groined and arched crypts, of which no history is preserved; some of these at the upper end 'of the street are eonnected with similar ones in Water- gate-street. They are not exposed to view, but may be seen in most oases by a request being made to the shopkeeper under whose premises they are. At the top of Bridge-street on the left-band side is a fine old gabled house, on the front of which some very good carved work was recently exposed that had been covered up with plaster, and it is in excellent preservation. Unhappily the city fathers are moving for the demolition of this ancient pile, to widen the street, though indeed it has never been encumbered with too much traffic since it was a street A little -lower down on the game side is all that remains of the old "Blue Posts" Inn, about which there is another legend of undoubted authenticity, though it takes us farther back than either of the others, but docu- ments are yet extant that attest to its accuracy. In 1558—the last year of the reign of Queen Mary —Dr. Henry Cole, the Dean of St. Paurs. was sent to Chester on a special commission from the Queen to prosecute the heretics of Ireland who were beginning to increase alarmingly. This hostelrie was then kept by a Mrs Mottershead„ a singular name that yet sur- vives in the street. The Mayor of Chester called at the inn to pay his respects to the Dean, and Mrs llottershead overheard the Dean to say exultingly that he would carry that which would " lash all the heretics in Ireland," and then he took out a leather box and showed it exultingly to his worship. Now the landlady had a brother in Dublin, and anxious for his safety she took occasion during the night to ab- stract the commission from the leather box, and sub- stitute a pack of cards tied together by a threid, with 'the knave of clubs uppermost. On his arrival at Dublin he.presented his box to the Lord Deputy and the Privy Council, who were surprised to find such an authority, and at once dismissed him. He returned to London to retrieve his loss, but on his arrival he learned that his Royal Mistress was dead, and Eliza- beth granted Mrs Mottershead a pension of forty pounds a year for the part she had taken in the tran- saction, a sum that would at least represent Xsoo of our money. The building which is called the " Fel- con Inn" is directly opposite to the hostelrie where the adventure narrated occurred. There was another inn called the "Falcon" in Northgate, which was the scene of several singular episodes. About the year 1720 a man came from London and lodged here, he had a very large 811711 of money with him which he had robbed from a bank, where he was employed as a clerk. And one night he heard the constables come upstairs and try to enter his room; this of course was fastened on the inside, and he found time to make away with his plunder by throw- ing it out of the window into the pad. Be was taken to London, but nothing could be proved again-t him, so he was acquitted, though he was afterwards arrested for some other offence and executed. One Mr. Jarvis had a small loom and a yard ad- joining the "Falcon." and up to that time he was never in affluent circumstances, but he appropriated the money, and laid it out to such advantage that he was soon able to purchase a large estate at Moiling- ton, a beautiful country place three miles from Ches- ter, and here he built himself a fine house. He became mayor of the city, when this offiee was con - sidered to confer great honour, and was even pricked for the higher honour of the shrievalty of the eounty, but he died before the appointment was con- firmed. Below the Falcon are remains of many black and white houses, and some very fine old mansions that were formerly the abodes of the aristocracy of Che- shire.

Early on Wednesday morning a fire broke out in a house in North Shields in which a number of persons were sleep- ing, and before it could be extinguished a blind woman named Alice Allen, aged 39, was burned to death. Twe other women were rescued from the roof of the building. The action against the High Sherif of Carnarvonshire by Colonel Platt, late Conservative candidate for Carnarvon- shire, to enforce a penalty of £lOO for failing to carry out the provisions of the Ballot Act, WAS concluded at Chester Assizes on Wednesday, before Mr. Justice Matthews, when the jury returned a verdict for the defendant. DESTROYING A TOLL HOUSE. - An extraordinare scene was witnessed at Cardiff on Monday night, when a large body of workmen, armed with battering-rams, attacked a toll-gate erected upon a bridge, hitherto free, approaching the docks. The gates were thrown into the river, amid lend cheering. The mob then attacked and destroyed the col- lector's hut, the collector escaping with his cash-box. A policeman was struck by a stone on tke face, and sustained a nasty wound. A number of the police present were powerless to prevent mischief. The toll of id. per head was imposed by the Taff Vale Railway Company.

div.head: ANOTHER THUNDERSTORM .-GREAT
div.p: ANOTHER THUNDERSTORM .-GREAT
.DAMAGE.

On Sunday night, a great rainfall occasioned much destruction of property at Park Bridge, about two miles from Ashton-under Lyne. Here is dituated a doubling mill, worked by Messrs. Herbert Briggs and Co., of Manchester, and owned by Mrs. Hannah Lees and Sons, of Park Bridge. The mill stands at the confluence of the Sheepwashes Brook and the river Medlock, and the brook passes under one end of the mill by means of a large stone culvert. The stock thus carried away or buried in the room is valued at £3,900, exclusive of the damage to the buildings, which must be very heavy. About three miled lower down the Medlock, at Daisy Nook, anew bridge, just erected, has been much damaged. The storm visited Oldham on Sunday night with unex- ampled severity. An enormous azwunt of damage was done in all parts of the borough, but particularly at Mumps, which is the converging point of the drainage for a consider- able area. There the cellars and the shops were flooded, and the highway was for a time rendered impassab:e. A. signal box on the railway at Mumps was washed down, mad the traffic impeded by the great volume of water, which converted the track into a river. The trains to Roy'ort from Oldham could not rnn, oeing to the lines being blocked by wreckage, and traffic between Oldham and Middleton Junction was stopped for the same rea-on. The tramway services were also suspended. A thunderstorm of extraordinary violence broke over Newton Heath and Failsworth on Sunday evening, and eon- tinned almost without intermission for two boors. Daring the height of the storm the embankment of a reservoir be- longing to Messrs. Crabtree and Sons, at the Spring Valley Dvovorks, gave way, and the water thus released rushed into the valley with great velocity. Fortunately, however, no serious damage was done. Daring the past few days a series of thunderstorms have occurred in East Kent, and various incidents are reported. Farm buildings at Herne, near Canterbury, were set on fire by the lightning, and damage done to the amount of £250. At Moxtoc, the wife of a retired Dover tradesman, while standing at the door of her house, was renth!red icsensible by a blinding flash, and continued so for several hours. Sunday night's storm wrought considerable damage to property in Leeds. Dwelling-houses and shop have been flooled. and public as well as private property hal' suffered severely. In Knottingley, Featherstone, and Ferrvbridge, and lower parts of Pontefiact, houses were flooded op to the fireplaces, and poultry drowned in numerous cases. Many roads were mpasaable for a time.

As in water steel is better than gold for use, so wisdom is better than wealth. The chief business of a wise matt is to distinguish what is good and to shun what is other- wise. Our powers are all limited, and their best effi- ciency is never secured by straining them to the utmost. always to leave a margin, a reserved force of strength or means, is a valuable rule of life. A SINGULAR INTERPIALLDEIt CLQIc.—AI St. elens County Court, en Wednesday, before his Honour Judge, Thompson, Margaret Duncan-Patterson and her daguhter Margaret Duncan, of Allerton-road, Woolron, sought to re- cover the furniture dietraintd by Solomon Auerbach, money lender, Liverpool, the execution creditor, in respect to a debt adjudged by the Liverpool Court of Passage to be owing by George Patterson, the debtor.—Mr. H. L. Riley appeared on behalf of the execution creditor, and explained that his &bet in the original action in the Court et ravage for the sum of £l5 loan, got judgment for that amount,with costs £7 is 6d. Mrs. Patt-reon alleged that the formture seized belonged to her and her daughter, excepting a book- case, some books, and a few pictures. The furniture was bequeathed to her by eer aunt, of Edin- burgh, under a will, in 1872. —ln reply to Mr. Riley, the complainant said she was never lawfully married to Mr. Patterson. She adopted his name by mutual arrangement —The Judge: Don't you consider yourself as Patterson's wife ?—Witness : I am not lawtully married to Mr. Patterson.—The Jedge : There is no mention made in the will of your daughter.—Witness : It was my aunt's wish that she should get some of the things —The Judge: nat goes for nothing. All the things were left to you —Mr. Riley : Is your daughter the child of Patterson? —Witness: —Mr. Riley: You commenced to live with this man in Scotland ?—Witness : Yee. —Mr. Riley : Don't you know that according to Scotch law that is equivalent to marriage ? itness : I did not know it.— Mr. Riley : Has Mr. Patterson never bought any goods ? Witness: He never bought a stick.—Mr. Riley put in an invoice, which showed that Mr. Patterson had purcha-Pd a chiffonnier knd soma other furniture from a Livrrpool tradesman.—Witness said she had not heard anything about such a purchase. She did not remember Mr. Anerb,ch coming to their house to see Mr. Patterson regarding his getting a loan ef £l5, but she remembered taking him through every room and showing him the beautiful furni- ture.—Mr. Riley : Was not your obi-ct in doing that to let Mr. Auerbach see that Mr. Patterson was a sut stantial man ?—Witness : N&—His Honour said he could make no order. He could rot interfere upon such evidenc,. woman first claimed as the wife of Patterson, and then said she was not his wife. He would dismiss the claim.

LORD SALISBURY has accepted the re- sponsibility of forming, a Government, but evidently not without some misgiving. He is fully conscious, in the peculiar circumstances of the situation, that though he is in office he will not be in power. He would have liked to have Lord HARTINGTON with him in the Cabinet; indeed, so anxious was the leader of the Tory party to.induce the member for 'Rossendale to break with the Liberals that he went the length of offering either to serve under him, or stand aside and` allow the Unionist Liberals to try their hands at govern- ing the country. But this was not to be; Lord HARTINGTON has resisted the tempta- tion, a fact which is greatly to hisAordship's ;credit, and one which should not be lost sight of in the future in any complication& which may arise. It was to be expected' that, after offering so much, Lord SA uSI3uRY would - 'seek something in return; and he was cer- tainly entitled to ask Lord •HARTINGTON give a promise, however conditional,,of sup- port to a Conservative Administration. That pledge Lord HARTINGTON has given,,but it .does not go beyond an engagement to sup- port the policy of the new Government upon Irish affairs, and in so far as it tends, in his. view,, in the direction of the• unity of the. Empire. The tams, it will be seen, are very general, and do not bind the member for Rossendale to anything outside the Irish question; while even as to that it is not im- probable that the understanding will come to an end as soon as the Tories attempt to carry out a policy of their own. It is one thing for the Dissentient Liberals to. agree with the Tories in opposing Mr. GLAMSTONZ'S scheme of Home Rule; it may be quite another when they are asked to support a measure brought in by Tory Administration. There is to be no Coercion just yet; that seems to be determined .on. Lord SALIS— BURY met his followers at the Carlton Club on Tuesday, and intimated his in- tention to, proceed with Supply, and leave the Irish question, over "until the early part of aext year, when. the Government would be in a position to state their views on that important subject." What is this but a confession that the Conservative Government are abont to meet the new House of Com- mons without anything to propose in the shape of a policy? What, it is pertinent to ask, has become of the policy of the 26th of January—" the policy of suppressing the National League ? If it was the right course to take six months ago, how co.mes it that it is not the right course to take now? Perhaps. the Tories will tell us that with a Liberal Government in power—with Lord ABERDEEIi as Lord Lieutenant and Mr. JOHN Moßuir as Irish Secretary—the condition of Ireland has. so greatly improved that it is not neces- sary to propose a resort to coercive measures. In that case it would seem that they will begin, as they have begun heretofore, by reaping where they have not sown; and it will therefore be especially interesting for Liberals to see what becomes of the crop- The Tories have a way of getting rid of a surplus of political as of other capital which is peculiarly their own. It is significant that Colonel TorrENHAm, on behalf of the Ulster members, asked Lord SALISBURY at tbe meeting, what measures would be proposed for the protection of life and property Ireland before the Government brought filo any bill dealing with Vag Wall questiol3.

The Ulster men want the reward of victory; they want the National League to be sup- pressed. But Lord SALISBURY is in no hurry to commit himself ; he is not prepared to say anything "at this particular moment." How can he return to Coercion when he knows , that the Dissentient Liberals would over- throw him if he were to propose such a thing? It is true that he is turning his back upon himself, and that the evasive answer which was given to , by any means Colonel TOTTENHAM is not content with the suggested twenty years of resolute government and final repeal of coercive laws. But Lord SALISBURY does not pride himself on his consistency; as he himself once said, he has been brought up in a different school from such politicians as Mr. , GLADSTONE. The Orangemen have served his turn; they must be content to wait; they are not the important people they were last year, for they do not command so many votes as the Liberal Dissentients. And Ire- land as a whole must wait too,—if she will. Mr. GLADSTONE was called upon whilst Par- liament was sitting to formulate his policy, and the Tories were clamorous until he laid his Home Rule Bill upon the table. Lord SALISBURY has had the advantage of the six months' interval whilst the Liberals were in office to decide what he would do, if again called upon to form an Administration; and, further than that, he has had the benefit of that appeal to the country which he so much desired. And yet he is unprepared; he is 1 SALISBURY the Unready. He asks the people of Ireland to wait until "next year ; " and meantime he will see if he can lick some- thing into shape which will please the 'Orangemen, bamboozle the Nationalists, and satisfy Lord HARTINGTON and Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN I

THE failure in floating the Manchester Ship Canal Scheme has alike astonished and disappointed the people of this district. They do not seem to have been in the least pre- pared for such a check, and were therefore incredulous when the first rumours reached them. There have doubtless been some sinister influences at work; but the main consideration is that the investing public have not, as yet, confidence in the scheme as a 'financial undertaking. Some of the London organs of opinion urge that a much better start would have been made if those who are •• immediately interested in the making of the Canal had backed their opinion in a more substantial fashion. But as to this it should be remarked that nearly three quarters of a million was subscribed in advance; and that as to what we may call investment on the part of the people at large, sufficient time had not been given for a knowledge of the situation to reach them. Take the case of weekly papers, such as our own series. No Opportunity was afforded for us to bring before our readers the fact even that applica- tions for shares could be made; the four days fixed by the prospectus came and went during the interval between one issue of the papers and another. If the inhabitants of this dis- trict are to be called upon to subscribe, the prospectus must be seen in the weekly papers. and people must have time to think and talk the matter over. It is not to be done by a four-days rush, and we cannot but think that a great mistake has been made in trying to Carry the thing by storm. As a matter of fact, the general public were to a great extent in ignorance as to the real significance of the statement that the scheme was to be floated for one per cent. by Messrs. ROTHSCHILD and SONS. It was commonly thought it meant that Messrs. ROTHSCHILD would "find the money" if there was any difficulty; and there can be no question that many who would have felt bound to risk something in supporting the scheme have done nothing in the way of taking up shares • because they thought there was nothing to be done. With regard to the hostile com- binations on the Stock Exchange, it is stated that there was not sufficient time to overcome the opposition in the four days set apart for the share lists remaining open. Granted, but does this not suggest a want of knowledge or foresight? Can it be that Messrs. ROTHS- 'CHILD. powerful factors as they are in dealing with foreign loans' are lacking in the requi- site qualifications for floating such a project as that of the Manchester Ship Canal? Their name is evidently not one to conjure with; they are powerful, but they are not so power- ful as they were supposed to be on the Eng- lish Stock Exchange. But it will be asked— what is to be done? Is the scheme to be abandoned? It would be an ignominious 'collapse if no further steps were taken. The directors have a clear twelve months before them—they have till August, 1887, to raise the money—and everything that is required may yet be done, if the promoters continue to exercise the energy and perseverance they have hitherto displayed. They are deserving of sympathy and support in the misfortune which has overtaken them;' and if they toil and faint not they may yet see the fruit of their labours in a S.hip Canal between Man- chester and-Liverpool.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

A circular letter of thanks which Sir George Errington has issued to the electors shows that he is in good heart. He has faith in the -masses, and, as they have faith in him, he may yet win a victory in the Newton Division.

The rain which was wanted has come— something too much of it in some parts of the country—and the crops, taking them all ,round, are likely to be heavy. But as Giles says-4g When crops is heavy prices is light." Man never is, but alway to be, blest.

Lord Salisbury does not seem to know what to do with Sir Richard Cross now that his post—that of Home Secretary—has been ;given to Mr. H. Matthews. "The Times" suggests that he should be shelved as a. 'Cabinet Minister, and consoled with a peer- age.

Mr. Robert Verdin seems to be taking to his new duties as a member of Parliament. He opened a bazaar at Weston Point on Wednes- day, and on Monday addressed a meeting at Northwich. It is satisfactory to see that he reminded the audience that he is a Liberal, although he is opposed to Home Rule.

Another attempt is to be made to come to terms with the Warrington Waterworks Company for the purchase, by the Corpora- tion, of their undertaking. It is to be hoped that this time it will be successful, as, indeed, it must be, if the representatives of the Com- pany are not too anxious to drive a hard bargain. St. Helens is peculiarly associated with petty frauds on the Railway Company. A Town Councillor has this week been fined 22 and costs for attempting to defraud the rail- ay authoritiesof fourpence, Can it bethat the

Junction affords special temptation to go wrong? Or is it something in th..; air? There must be a cause. It is stated that the visits of the Indian and Colonial representatives and the Marquis Tseng and suite to Leeds have cost the Cor- poration [1,500. Why do Corporations spend money in this way? It is not fair to the ratepayers; and is not fair to the visitors, whose object is best attained when they see things just as they are. , , • • „ .

Whilst the factory girls of Glasgow are out on strike igainst a proposed reduction of is. 6d. per week in wages, the weavers of East Lancashire are commencing an agitation for an advance. It is pretty well known that the cotton manufacturers have had a "good time" since Christmas; and it is not un- natural that the operatives should now want to taste the sweets.

Elizabeth Tither, of St. Helens, has a large acquaintance with the" bar" and the 'bench." On Saturday she was brought before the mag- istrates for an offence committed on the pre- vious night. It was her toBth appearance, and she was committed to prison for fourteen days. It would seem that it is much easier to convict Elizabeth than to convince her that it is time to mend her ways. .. ,

The Health Committee of the St. Helens Corporation insist that chimneys for lame works shall be 150 feet high. They have just decided against a proposal to erect one of 120 feet. When will the Corporation of Warrington so learn their duty, and do ii? As things go, if there is no change, the chil- dren of the third and fourth generation will, for the sins of their fathers, be taken for quadroons—they will be so much darker from the taint of "Black Jacks."

The appointment of Lord Randolph Churchill to be leader of the Tors, party in the House of Commons is the Apotheosis of Impudence. Lord Salisbury does indeed "stoop to conquer," and he may not conquer after all. " Great is cheek," but it is not everything.

Sir Stafford Northcote was elbowed out of the House of Commons because he was con- sidered too weak for the leadership; but he is now considered strong enough as Lord Iddesleigh to be Secretary for Foreign Af- fairs. Consistency is not, however, the boast of the Tories, and having done this we shall doubtless hear something next about "a spirited foreign policy."

Sir Michael Hicks-Beach is a failure; so he is told to—"go to Ireland," to be out of Lord Randolph's way. He, too, is pushed off his pedestal as leader in the Commons, but no- body feels sorry for him, because he meanly joined in the intrigue which led to the down- fall of the gentle Sir Stafford." All this comes of nursing Lord R. Churchill. As Shakespere has it— _
The hedge sparrow fed the cuckoo so long, That it had its head bit off by its young.

i History will repeat itself. The following s an extract from Wyon's "History of Great Britain during the reign of Queen Anne ": "It was well known that the leading spirit in the Council had been for some time past a younger brother of Marlborough, Admiral George Churchill. The mental constitution of this man was the opposite of that of his illustrious relative. He was a Tory of the extreme school, virulent, domineering, and foolish. His tattling propensities, his love of brag- ging, his insane love of insulting political oppo- nents, and the offence which this array of qualities gave to the Whigs, rendered him a perpetual thorn in Marlborough's side." Lord Randolph Churchill is also "a younger brother," and he would seem to have in- herited all the bad blood of that younger brother who was an Admiral.

Two little boys at Sutton have been show- ing themselves quite big in the way of mis- chief. They released, in their play, a number of railway waggons that were " scotched " on an incline. It was all done for the fun of the thing; but the result was that the wag- gons got beyond control, and four of them were smashed. Being of tender years— seven and ten years of age—they were let off with a fine of 205 each and six strokes of the birch rod. Let boys beware; another such offence will be followed by other and heavier punishment. Sir Edward Watkin would make it appear that the Railway Company with which he is connected has done nothing in opposition to the Ship Canal project; but he will not be able to say that his speech is not in oppo- sition. It goes tooth and nail against the scheme. Sir Edward has a plan of his own. He would begin by cutting across the Birken- head peninsula. He would first remake the approach to Liverpool; and, in this way, Manchester would get attended to, say, a hundred years hence,

• HALFPENNY STAMPS FOR RECEIPTS.—In reply to a correspondent, Mr. W. 11. Cousins, of the Inland revenue Department, has written :—" I am directed by the Board of Inland Revenue to inform you that under the provisions of the Act 45 and 46 Vic., cap. 72, sec. 13, two halfpenny postage stamps may be used to denote the duty of one penny on a receipt. lam tb add that the issue of a new halfpenny stamp, bearing the words Postage and Revenue 'is in contemplation." SIR GEORGE ERRINGTON AND THE NEWTON DlVl- sioN.—Sir George Errington, the late Liberal can- didate for the Newton Division in opposition to Sir Richard Crosi, has issued a circular letter thanking the Liberal workers in the division for their servi:es during the last election. Despite the fact, he says, that the contest was entered upon at short notice, it was conducted in a manner creditable to all con- cerned. He feels sure that in a future contest a great triumph will be achieved for the Liberal cause in this division. RURI-DECANAL CONFERENCE.—On Tuesday the annual conference of the clergy and lay representa- tives of the rural deanery of Frodsham was held at Northwich, Canon Greenall, of Grappenhall, presid- ing. There was a large attendance.—In opening the proceedings, the Rev. Canon referred to the two great political convulsions which had taken place since the last meeting. As regards the last he was glad that patriotism had prevailed over party politics, and prevented the disruption of the United Kingdom. (Applause.) At the previous election the burning question was the danger to the church. Their enemies had said that church-people had been too susceptible and suspicious; but he was con- vinced that it would be most unwise to lose sight of the question of church defence. Referring to the subject of parochiol councils, he expressed the hope that such a bill as was introduced into the late Par- liament would never be passed. Ile advised that the number of sidesmen should be increased in each parish, and that the clergyman, churchwardens, and sidesmen should form a council, having the func- tions which it was proposed to assign to the new councils.—ln answer to Canon Blogg, Canon Dodd (Stretton) said that Lord Brabazon was trying to form a Young Men's Friendly Society. The success of the Girl's Friendly Society was mainly due to the interest taken in the members by ladies. If there were gentlemen ready to take the same interest in the boys as the ladies took in the girls, he had no doubt the new society would be successful.—lt was decided, after some further consideration, to refer the matter to the Diocesan Conference.—A discus- sion on Free Education having taken place, Canon Dodd, in a brief paper, invited statements as to the result of dividing the morning services in country parishes.—This concluded the business.

CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY.—A meeting was held in the National Schools, Farnworth, on Tueeday evening, vbe i an address was given by the Rev. J. Hirst, Diocesan Secretary. About 140 persons were present. RUNCORN STARR-BOWEETT BUILDING SOCIETY.—This week the 31st appropriation in connection with the first society took place, with the result that Mr. Thomas Dean, of Bracklev-street, Runcorn, is entitled to the use of £4OO for 12 years, free of interest. RUNCORN PARISH Cnuncn Cnota TRIP. This choir had their second annual trip on Saturday last, when a most pleasant and enjoyable day was spent at Pen maenmawr and Conway. On Weanesday the younger members of the choir were given a trip to Southport. PIC-NIC TO KNOWSLEY.—On Saturday last, teachers and friends, about 50 in number, belonging the Widnes Wes- leyan Sunday School had a plc-nic in Knowsley Park. After a walk through the gardens and pleasure grounds, the company sat down to an excellent tea provided by Mr. S. H. Amer, of Eccleston, St. Anues. UTTERING COUNTERFEIT COIN AT WIDNES.—At Liver- pool Assizes on Wednesday, John Williams, aged 17 years, carter, was found guilty of having, at Widnes, oa the sth July, unlawfully and knowingly uttered two counterfeit half-crowns. Prisoner had other similar coins in his pos- session when arrested. Mr. Lumb prosecuted, and Mr. Seger appeared for the prisoner, who was sentenced to three months' imprisonment. WIDNES POLICE COURT.—Yesterday, before Mr. John Brock, John Rogers, of no fixed residenee, was sent to gaol for seven days for begging in Ross-street on the previous day For being drunk and disorderly, and wilfully damaging the uniform of P.C. Middleton, a man named Sidney Kirk was fined 104 and costs, and ordered to pay the amount of damage, 3s. On Tuesday Patrick Murray was sentenced to seven days' hard labour for begging. A CONFIRMED THIEF AT RUNCCRN.—WiIIiaM Milling- ton, a boatman, was brought before Mr. Brundrit at the Runcorn Police Court on Thursday charged with stealing two boat hooks, the property of Mr. Richard Abel. On the 20th July the prisoner was loading his boat with oil casks alongside the premises where the boat hooks were. The boat hooks were substqaently missed, and on Wednesday one of them was found on board his boat by Inspector Millington. The prisoner having been previously convicted, was committed to the sessions for trial, bail being ac-

cented. THE RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS' ACCOUNTS. -- A state- ment of the accounts of the Runcorn Board of Improve- ment Commissioners will be found in our advertising columns. The total revenue amounts to £5,391 lie 91, which sum includes £4,820 19s 8d from the general district rate. The expenditure amounts to £5,699 is 4d. The largest item is £1.007 4s 4d for scavenging, the next in order being £B5O 14s 10d, put down for legal and Parlia- mentary expenses. Public lighting has cost £7lO us 2d, and £542 has been spent in salaries. The Public Library

cost .£193 6s Bd. MILITARY FUNERAL AT RUNCORN.—The funeral of James Webb, a private of the El Company of the Prince of Wales Volunteers, South Lancashire Regiment, took place at Wid- nes on Satarday, with military honours. The body was followed to the grave by 40 members of the corps, including a firing party of 12, and the Widnes Parish Cnurch band played the Dead March in " Saul." The coffin, covered with the Union Jack and a number of beautiful wreaths, was borne to the grave on the shoulders of four of the dcceased's comrades, and three volleys were tired. The Rev. A. P. Hamilton Wilson was the officiating clergyman. DOGS AT LARGE.—RaIph Tickle, of Sutton, was brought before the Runcorn magistrates on Monday, charged with allowing his dog to be at large, in contravention of an order made by the justices.—P.C. Fryer proved the case, and stated that the dog in question was the one that caused the order to be made.—The defendant contended that as the dog was on his premises it was under his personal centrol.—Ele was fined Is and costs, 103 6d.—Frederick Blythe, of Run- oorn, was summoned on a similar charge, which was proved by P.S. Cooper. Defendant was fined Is and costs, 108 6d. For a like offence, Alfred Jones, of Runcorn, was, on the evidence of P.C. Smith, fined Is and costs. Thomas Robin- son pleaded guilty to a similar charge, and he was fined is and emits, 9s 68, on the evidence of P.S. Cooper. ODDFELLOWS' FESTIVITIES AT HALE. —ln miserable weather the annual festival in connection with the Oddfel- lows' Club, Hale, was held on Monday. Dressed in their regalia, the members of the dub paraded the lanes of the village in the morning, being headed by the Ditton Brass Band, and afterwards they proceeded to the church, whore service was held and a sermon preached by the Rev. Mr. Steward, rector of the village. Dinner was then partaken of at the Childe of Hale Hotel, which had been prepared by Mr. T. Rowe, the manager, and was done ample justice to. After dinner speeches were delivered, when the party ad-1 journed to the greet), where dancing was indulged in for some time to the strains of the Ditton Brass Band. On the' green were also a number of roundabouts, shooting galleries, Aunt Sallies, and the other accessories that are to be found in a fair, which had been provided for the delectation of the juvenile population of the village. A HOAX UPON LENVIs'S AT LIVERPOOL. A joke has been played off at the expense of Messrs. Lewis's, clothiers, Liverpool, by some person who has adveitised in the news- papers that a suit of clothes would be given to each person sending a parcel containing a thousand cherrystones. Scores of people have searched high and low for cherrystones in order to gain the suit of clothes, but we regret to say that their industry will not be rewarded In the manner indicated in the advertisement. The following is a copy of a letter received by Mr. W. E. Howard, 111, Church-street, Run- corn, who had forwarded the necessary number of cherry- stones:—" Liverpool, July 23rd. We have received your parcel of cherrystones, which are of no use to us. If you have the paper in which this advertisement appeared we shall be much obliged if you will send it to us. We have never advertised for cherrystones, and should like to find out who has, as we haye received a large number of par- cels." Larmos BAND OF HOPE.—The third annual excursion of the above society took place on Saturday. The society was organised in the year 1882, under the rules of the Wesleyan Methodist Conference. Its members now number 250. On I Saturday 216 of them were conveyed to Mersey View, Overton, by horses and lorries kindly lent by the following gentlemen :—Messrs. Joseph Baguley, William Nixon, John Bagulev, John Ccoke,loseph Astbury, Richard Nixon, John Ackerley, and John Booth. Vie drivers had spent mach pains in dressing their horses, while the officers and friends of the society bad profusely and tastefully decorated the lorries with evergreens, flowers, and mottoes. On their ar- rival at Overton Hills the clouds had dispersed, giving place to a bright and bracing atmosphere. The children sat down to a free tea, provided out of the funds of the society. The adult members and friends (about 65) were conveyed by ve- hicles supplied by Mr. Peck, of Runcorn. After enjoying the emery and inch:dying in games, the return journey was made, the party arriviving at Halton, at 8-45, with an abun- dant evidence from the "Hurrahs" of the children, and the hilarity of the friends, that they had spent a most enjoy- able afternoon. FASHIONABLE MARRIAGE AT WIDNES. - A marriage which excited considerable interest in the neighbourhood was solemnised at St. Bede's Roman Catholic Chapel, Appleton. on Thursday morning. Mr. J. H. Forster, of Earlestown, son of Mr. Thomas Forster, of Birkdale, for- merly of Earlestown, was the bridegroom, and the bride was Miss Mary Tracey, eldest stepdaughter of Mr. John E. Johnson, Simms Cross, Widnes. The ceremony was wit- nessed by a large congregation. lhe bride was attired in a dress of white silk, her brow being wreathed with orange blossoms. A gold bracelet and gold earrings, the gifts of the bridegroom, formed part of her adornments. Five brides- maids (Miss Hannah Tracey, Miss Moran, Miss Leather- barrow, Miss Lily Leatberbarrow, and Miss Flora Johnson) attired in cream-coloured dresses, carried the train of the bride, who entered the chapel leaning on the arm of her father. Dr. McCambridge acted as best man, and amongst the friends present were Dr. Mangan, of Runcorn ' • Mr. and Mrs Morrison, Mr. and Mrs A Tracey, and Mrs Leatherbarrew. The Rev. Father Finegan performed the ceremony. Up- wards of sixty sat down to the breakfast provided, and in the afternoon the newly-married pair departed for North Wales, where they spend the honeymoon. The presents were numerous and costly. ASSAULT ON A WOMAN AT RUNCORN.-At Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday, before Mr. Brundrit, Wm. and John Joinson, quarrymen, were charged with indecently assault- ing Mary Perry, who lives with her husband in the Hol- loway, Runcorn.—About nine o'clock on Monday evening, Mrs. Perry passed the prisoners in the Holloway as she was on her way home. The prisoners followed her, and John put his arm round her neck and committed the assault complained of. She said, "Yen dare to insult me! lam a - married woman, and you will find it out if you are going that way." The prisoner released her, and farther along the road William seized her by the collar, and said several times, "What do yen say?" accompanying his words by blows on the face. Blood flowed from her nose and month, and one of her teeth was loosened. A girl named Annie Holland, who was with her, screamed, and the prisoner ran away, Thomas Schofield and Thomas Huxworth being in pursuit. They were subsequently apprehended by P.C. Dale.—The prisoners contended that they were at Weston Point at the time of the assault, and called John Match, a quarry man, to prove this.—The prisoner John was com- mitted for trial, and William was discharged.—Superinten • dent Hollingsworth caused William, however, to be at once arrested on a charge of common assault, and on Thursday morning he was brought before Messrs. John Brundrit and James Handley and Captain Hazleburst, and sentenced to n two months' hard !about.

CATHOLIC ACADEMY OF ST. PAULINUS, CATTERICK, YoßKsinn..E.—lt appears from the list just pub- lished of successful candidates at the Kensington Local Examinations held in June last, that thirty- three pupils were sent from this school, and all passed. Six passed in the higher division, of whom two obtained honours of the first class and two of the second. One was specially commended for Latin, and got full marks for French. Five obtained marks of distinction for arithmetic, and four in algebra and euclid. At the Government Science , and Art Examinations held in May and June, twenty-one candidates from this school passed. Four passed in mathematics, one in the first class. One passed in theoretical mechanics, ten in magnetism and electricity, one in the first •class ; two in the principles of agriculture, both in the first class; and four in the second grade drawing. The following remarks were appended to the examiners' report of the. Kensington examination :—" Writing specially commended. Arithmetic most excellent. The whole work is excellent, and reflects the highest possible credit on principal and teachers. One of the best schools brought under the society's notice."

P.S. Lowndes and P.S. Nield deposed to finding Moore's hat in the granary when they arrested the prisoners. Dr. Carruthers stated that he had examined Barker and Moore. The former was suffering from a punctured wound in the thigh, and the latter from a wound on the forehead an inch and a half in length, which laid bare the bone. There was a similar wound of the same size on the right side of the head, and a third of a similar character lay on the back .of the head. There were also five other smaller wounds, be- sides several bruises about the body. Moores had since been suffering from shock atd loss of blood. The magistrate discharged Dennis and Thomas Farrell. The rest on being charged made statements to the effect that they were set upon first by some men in Halton-road, and only acted in self-dtfence. They denied having seen anything of Moores
The four men in custody were committed far trial at the Chester Assizes.

The prisoners were tried at Chester Assizes on Thursday. Mr. Burke Wood prosecuted and Mr. Marshall defended the prisoners. The prisoners were formally acquitted of the charge of feloniously wounding Richard Moores. and were then indicted for unlawfully wounding Barker and Powell. The case for the defence was that the prisoners were set upon by the prosecutors and others, who said, " We'll give them H-,me Rule."—The evidence of Mr. Taylor,the deputy-governor of Knntsford prison, showed that Henry Farrell bad a severe knife wound in his hand, and his state- ment to Mr. Taylor was that someone set on him with a belt, that he held up his hand to defend himself, and that his assailant stabbed him in the hand with a knife. There was a strong probability that the knife was used by Powell. —The jury acquitted Michael and Henry Farrell, and found the other two guilty of common assanit.—His Lordship said the prisoners had undoubtedly had great provocation, but they must be more peaceable in future. They would be discharged on entering into their own recognizances in the sum of £lO to come up for judgment if again called upon. Both bound themselves over, and the four prisoners were discharged.
