div.head: WARRINGTON CHAMBER OF • COMMERCE.
div.p: WARRINGTON CHAMBER OF • COMMERCE.

A general meeting of this Chamber was held at Bewsey Chambers, Bewsey-street, on Thursday morn- ing. Mr. John Fairclough, in the absence of Mr. F. Monks, the president, took the chair, and there were also present Messrs. T. Jolley and C. Broadbent, and J. Davies end J. L. Tunstall (hon secretaries). CORRESPONDENCE—The CHAIRMAN read letters (1) from the Leith Chamber of Commerce, on the currency question ; (2) from the South of Scotland Chamber of Commerce, in reference to the 53rd clause of the Facture and Workshops Act, 1878, concerning the employment of young persons and children in non-textile factories; (3) from the office of the Agent-General of South Australia, London, enclosing a prospectus of the forthcoming Adelaide Exhibition to com- memorate the completion of her Majesty's jubilee, and the fiftieth year of the colony of South Australia. The third letter asked if the Chamber would have the goodness to take such steps as might seem expedient to make the exhibition known amongst such of the residents of the district as were likely to utilize the opportunity of exhibiting.—On the pro- position of Mr. DAVIES, seconded by Mr. JOLLEY, it was decided that a suitable circular be sent to manufacturers and others, and especially to those who are exhibiting at the Liverpool Exhibition, calling attention to the subject. )31-morrstusx.—A short discussion teok place on the subject of bi-metallism, but no resolution was passed. In the course of the discussion, Mr. DAVIES said that he rthosght there would be an increase of trade and prosperity !for a time if they had bi-metallism. He based his argu- ment on the principle that when there was an influx of gold in 1851 and 1852, from Australia and other places, there was an immediate increase of trade, because there was plenty of money. He was not, however, quite satisfied as to whether that prosperity would continue.—Mr. J. L. TUNSTALL thought the prosperity would be permanent, because there would be a much greater production of metal used for cainage.—Mr. DAVIES said that so long as there was a scarcity of gold there must be bad trade.—Mr. Ttrer- STALL Add the silver to the gold, and it must increase trade.—Mr. BaosDßErrr said the question was now occu- pying the serious attention of persons who were op- posed to it years ago. It was considered an im- portant question, and one which was occupying the att.ntion of the mercantile classes especially. There might be prosperity both with high and low prices; but what was wanted was stability of prices. As Mr. Davies had said, when there was a sudden discovery of gold in Aus- tralia it was the means of increasing prices, and there was a degree of prosperity. New they had the reverse of that state of things, and the value of gold was diminished by one half, and along with that they had some of the great commercial Empires of Europe adopting the geld standard instead of the silver standard, so that that mast necessarily 'ower the prices all round._ The question was, Where was _ _

It to step? If they had the gold production diminished and a larger number of the civilized nations using the gold, there would be a decrease constantly going on, and a con- stant shrinking in value.—After a few more remarks had been made the discussion terminated. THE CONGRESS OT CHAMBERS.—Mr. C. BROADBENT gave to the meeting a tew particulars of his visit as a delegate to the Congress of Chambers of Commerce recently held ha London. The Congress, he said, was of a very interesting character, and it was largely attended by representatives from the colonies and from India. Referring to emigration, Mr. Broadbent said that the opinion appeared to be that- there was a large field for it, but that if the colonies pro- vided land England should send some of its superabundant capital. It was no use sending out men who would imme- diately congregate in the towns. They should have suffi- cient capital to enable them to get into the country. Mr. Broadbent also spoke highly of the manner in which the delegates bad been entertained by the London Chamber, and it was resolved that a vote of thanks be passed to that Chamber. This was all the business.

William Match, labourer, was found in his house in Old Aberdeen, on Monday, with his throat cut. The body was discovered doubled up in a chest, and the circumstances point to the supposition that the deceased met his death by foul play. The statement that Mrs. Britland, the woman now lying in Strangeways Gaol under sentence of death, has made a confession is denied. She has made a statement, which has been sent to the Home Office, but its nature is not divulged. RICSPITE OF A MURDERSR.—The governor of Dorchester Gaol, on Tuesday, received an intimation that a re- spite had been granted to John Gerrard King, who was lying under sentence of death for the murder of Alderman- Hamilton, at Poole.

NOTES BY THE WAY.

It was not to be expected, after the loss of so much play in the match, Yorkshire y. Australians. at Huddersfield on Thursday and Friday, that the contest would be brought to a definite issue, and on Saturday it ended in a draw. The Yorkshiremen, however, had the satisfaction of compelling their formidable antagonists to follow on, and possessed a great advantage at the ftish, as the Colonists, with a wicket down is the second innings, were still 6.5 runs in arrears.

There was a full day's cricket at Sheffield on Wednesday, but the loss of play through rain en Menday could not be made up, and when time WAS called the match between Yorkshire and Gloucestershire had to be left drawn,Glouces- tershire with half their wickets down, wanting 148 runs to win. The chances were them distinctly in favour of York- shire. but it must be remembered that amongst the Glouces- tershire wickets still to fall were those ef W. G. Grace and Brain. At Nottingham, on Satnrday, Attewell accomplished a remarkable bowling performance against Sussex. When the Notts side went en in a minority of 88, Attewell bowled right through the innings. and in the course of 39 overs. 23 of which were maidens, he took 9 of the 10 wickets at a cost of 23 runs, Notts winning the match by an innings with 15 runs to spare. The cricket at Stoke-on-Trent on Wednesday went all in favour of the Australians, who were robbed of an easy vic- tory by time alone. In order to allow the Colonists to catch an early train to London, where they were to meet Surrey on Thursday, it had boen arranred that stumps should be drawn at a quarter to six, and when the last wicket fell at half-past five in the Englishmen's second innings only 20 runs were wanted to win; but bearing in mind the usual quarter of an hour's interval the Colonists did not go in again, so the watch was left drawn greatly in their favour.

England and Australia have now played seven matches and the mother country has won four, lost one, and two have been drawn. The first of the series, the memorable match at the Oval in 1880, was distinguished by Dr. W. G. Grace scoring 152 in the first innings of England, which ran up the formidable total of 420. Mr. Murdoch, the Aus- tralian captain, after being dismissed for a nought in the first innings of 140, made amends by carrying his bat right through the second innings, scoring 153 not out, and bring- ing up the innings to 327. The Englishmen ultimately won ay five wickets. The match in 1882 will be best known for the small scores made and the close finish. The Austra- lians, who won by seven runs, scored 63 and 122, and Eng- land 101 and 66. In this match also Mr. SpDfforth achieved his remarkable feat of taking 14 wickets at an average of not quite seven runs per wicket, namely, seven for 46 runs in the first innings, and seven for 44 runs in the second innings. The fourth Australian team in 1884 played three matches against England, two of which are notable for the heavy scoring. In the first of the three, played at Lords, Mr. A. G. Steele was the hero of an innings of 148, the total English score being 379, and the Australians being defeated by an innings and five runs. In the second Australian in- nings Ulyett took seven wickets for 36 runs. The second match of the year, at Manchester, produced nothing sensa- tional, and was drawn. The Australians made the enor- mous score of 551, and were indebted to Mr. Murdoch for 211, Mr. M'Donnell 103, and Mr. Scott (captain of the pre- sent team) 102. The Englishmen scored 346, Mr. Walter Reid contributing 117, and Scotton, the Notts professional, 90. When the match was drawn the English team had lost two wickets for 85 runs, the match thus producing the won- derful aggregate of 982 runs for the fall of 22 wickets. As will be remembered, the match at Old Trafford this year was won by England by four wickets. There is only one other England v. Australia match to be played this year, and that is at the Oval next month.
The I ancashire and Gloucestershire match shared a fate similar to many others last week, viz., a draw owing to the weather. The first day's play was abort, only proceeding

until 143 bad been put on by the borne team for seven wickets. On Friday just sufficient time was stolen to nem- plete the innings. Watson making 24 and Robinson 17. On Saturday the Gloucestershire nen were handicapped, as the heavy rain had told on the wicket.

TERRIBLE TRAGEDY IN PENZANCE. FOUR PERSONS KILLED. About half-past one on Wednesday afternoon a shocking crime was enacted at Penzance by a man named James Hawke, who shot his sister, her hus- band, and the wife of a neighbour, and to complete the tragedy shot himself. A Penzance correspondent supplies the following details :--The murderer was the son of a shoemaker, and was fifty-two years of age. He had passed many years in Australia, where he attained some success in the wool trade, and returned to this 11 country about the end of last year. He had latterly visited Bristol, and came back to Penzance six weeks ago. He was of a quiet and sociable disposi- tion. His sister Mary was many years his junior, and her husband, Charles Wren, shoemaker, was the son of Mr. John Wren, printer. They all lived to- gether in Marine-place. The ether victim, Mrs. Gerrard, was the wife of a watchmaker in the town. Hawke had been in conversation with several young men at the bottom of Queen-street, and on going to his house one of the young men who had occasion to go to the same court followed him. De- ceased went in, and in a few moments afterwards shot the sister and then the husband; eoming out to the door he followed and shot Mrs. Gerrard in the side. All three expired almost immediately. The young man previously referred to spoke to ' him, when he put up his hand and said, "Stand back." Placing the muzzle of the revolver under his ear: he fired, and fell dead in the doorway. The house is situated in a tolerably spacious courtyard behind the Queen's Hotel. The stone steps inside ,the little garden gate were stained with blood, and , inside the house the kitchen floor was also ailuilarly , marked, and the entrance into the small back yard was also stained with blood. The murderer and his victims were discovered stretched on the floor side by side in a large pool of blood. Wren was shot in the right breast, The murderer lay next to him. He is a short, thick-set man, dressed entirely in blue Adams b Green Green l4 serge. The faces of all wore a peaceful expression. G. Connolly b 'Davies b Green ....... o Mrs. Wren had evidently been shot near the mouth, Taylor b corner 0. Connolly run out Phillipa lbw. b Green 5 2 Eterrard's body lay to the right of the others. She Kaight not out Floyd e Burgeas b Oolier o had been struck in the back as she attempted to es- ilyoo6k b Colller o cape, and had evidently died at once. IRowarth c Bennett b Green 3 Superintendent Nicholas, with a sergeant and two ,BAldwin b Green constables, was soon on the spot, and Drs. Grenfell, Hooking, and others were promptly in attendance, but no sign of life was visible in any of the victims. The murderer had been ping about in the morning conversing with friends, but nothing unusual was noticed in his manner or appearance. There is no motive known which can explain the frightful
tragedy. Mr. and Mrs. Wren leave seven and Mrs. Gerard six children.

div.head: SERIOUS DAMAGE ON THE RAILWAY.
div.p: SERIOUS DAMAGE ON THE RAILWAY.
EXTRA.ORDINARY CONDUCT OF LADS.

At St. Helens Town Hall, on Monday, before Mr. W. Blinkhorn and Alderman J. Harrison, two lads, named John Makin, seven years of age, and Samuel ; Dim, 10 years of age, both residing in Mill-row, Sutton, were summoned by the London and North- , Western Railway Company for "turning and mov- ing the brakes upon certain trucks, with intent to upset and destroy the said trucks." Mr. Preston (Liverpool) appeared on behalf of the company. The defendants appeared in oourt, but were not profcs- sionally represented. Mr. Preston said the proceedings were taken under the "Malicious Damage to Property Act," and stated that though the defendants were but of tender years. unfortu- nately very great events happened from little circumstances. The evidence would show that a most dangerous act had been committed. On the 19th July 15 waggons were placed on a siding near Messrs. Pllkingtons' works, and were " scotched " by the brakes, and remained there until the afternoon of the following day when the two lads were seen at the waggons, one jumping on the handles of the brakes while the other pulled the " pins " eut. The wag- gons being on an ir,oline began to move, and the defendants tried to stop the waggons by pulling at them, but they did not succeed in stopping them. The train of waggons, whilst on the move, gradually gathered speed, and run on towards St. Helens. where they would have got on to the main passenger line but a pointsman near Messrs. Menzies siding observed them coming sad turned them into a siding near Messrs. Nuttall'a works. A stop-block was carried away by the force of the waggons, which dashed against the warehouse of Messrs. Nuttall, where a window was smashed and the bricks damaged. The waggons were also damaged, four being thrown off the line and the buffers smashed. A shunting engine happened to be oft the same Line and saw the waggons coming, and the driver put on speed and proceeded rapidly in front in order to prevent them colliding with the engine. He (Mr. Preston) thought the case called for a severe punishment. —Railway Detec- tive James Henry Perkins said he had spokes to the defend- ants about it, and they acknowledged having been playing with the waggons and pulled the" pies" out.—Robert Bar- net, employed at Messrs. Pilkington's Ravennead Colliery, deposed that the pwaggons were is the siding, and ! spoke to the damage occasioned by the waggons running 1 into the siding near Messrs. Nuttall's works.—Joseph Hew- itt, a pointsman in the employ of the London and North- Western Railway Company, said he was stationed near Messrs. Menzies siding. He saw the waggons running down the incline and he had them turned into a "stop- block," which was smashed, and the waggons ran against the warehouse adjoining. Four of the waggons were smashed, and other damage was done.—John Robert Shaw and Thomas Wilcock, lads, proved that they had seen the defendants playing with the waggons —Mr. J. 0. Swift (solicitor) said he had been instructed to prosecute the same boys on behalf of the St. Helens Collieries Company, for doing damage to the amount of over £l6 to another waggon, but after the case just heard, he did not propose to take any further proceedings against them.—The Chair- man (Mr. Blinkhorn) said: This is a very serious case, and but for the extreme youth of the boys we should have visi- ted it much more seriously than we shall do. As it is we shall fine them each £1 and costs, and they will each have six strokes with a birch rod.

John Hall (12), Thomas Hall (12), Robert McComus (11), James Stirrup (14), and Arthur Cully (14) were then charged with moving and directing railway points with in- tent to upset and destroy certain trucks, on the 4th inst.— Mr. Preston, who again prosecuted, stated that a waggon loaded with salt petre kad been placed on the siding near Messrs. Lockwood and Leith's Ravenhead branch, protected by" catch" points. On the afternoon of Sunday, the 4th inst., some lads got on the siding. pushed the waggon down the single line leading to the main branch, and one of the lads held open the catch points, so as enable the waggon to pass through. When the waggon got on Ravenhead line the lads jumped on it and rode some distance, and they then let the waggon take its course. It went down the incline at a terrific pace, going through a pair of points which were damaged and doing damage also to the signal there, while it knocked a crossing gate down and finally came to a stand by rushing into a coal waggon and knocking it off the line. —Detective Perkins gave evidence as to the lads acknow- ledging their guilt, and corroborated the statement of Mr. Preston as to the damage done.—William Cross mad Henry Meadows (lads) gave evidence that the defendants had com- mitted the offence, and the Bench fined John Hall, Thomas Hall, and McComus £1 and costs, and ordered them to re- ceive six strokes each with the birch rod, and Stirrup and Cully were each fined 30s and costs.

It is believed that there will be no conflict between the Tiree crofters and the Government "expedition," the ac- knowledged leaders of the people having counselled consti- tutional procedure for the future. A box, which was left at a house in Great Oambridge- street, Hackney-road, London, by a railway carrier, on Wed- nesday evening, was found to contain the body of a child which had evidently been murdered. The third and fourth will be divided by Taubenhaus and Gnnsberg Samsun CHAMPAGNES.—To champagne drinkers it has long been a mystery why this wine should command prices which are almost prohibitive. The question is all the more important as champagne has secured a position in in oar social requirements front which no other variety of wine seems likely to displace it. If a child is to be christened, a daughter mar- ried, or a friendly entertainment is to be given, the supply- ing of champagne to the guests is almost de rigeur. it is true that ene of the conditions of a Cinderella dance is often understood to• be early hours and no champagne, but many a hostess knows to her sorrow how difficult it is to infuse life into her gatherings under such conditions. Messrs. W. and A. Gilbev have however by their enterprise stepped , in to help our hostess in her difficulty, and offer at 2s. 61 a bottle their "Castle Gold Foil" Saumur Champagne, which, in addition to being as pure, wholesome, and ex- hilarating as the most expensive brands, can be nbtained at that price anywhere in the United Kh3gdona.—The Morning Post, July 27th, 1856.

THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.

A full meeting of the directors of the Manchester Ship Canal was held at the offices of the company, in Manchester, on Tuesday afternoon, when the position of affairs WAS discussed at length, the di-1 rectors expressing a determination to persevere with the project. Fresh steps will be taken to raise the required capital, but the plan to be adopted was not decided upon. As soon as the course to be pur- sued has met with the approval of the directors, it , will be made public as early as possible. , SIR EDWARD WATKIN ON THE SCHEME. At the half-yearly meeting of the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway Company, at the London-road Station, Manchester, on Wednesday, Sir Edward Watkin said that, as their company had been included in other railway companies by pla- cards on the walls as inimical to the Ship Canal project, and having done all they could to defeat it, he might state that he had nothing to do with any other assembly of shareholders except the Manches- ter, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway Company, and he was sure they would agree with him when he stated that they had done nothing in opposition to the Ship Canal project except to get pro- tection for the works which they had erec- ted and which would be affected by the Ship Canal. He was strongly in favour of improved water communication between Manchester and Liverpool. (Hear,hear.) Hebelieved, ; however, that the present canal project had been badly designed, and did not carry out two essential points which, in his opinion, should attach to a ship canal. One was that the canal should be without locks, and the other was that the entrance from the sea to Liverpool should have been improved as a precedent to any other increased water communica- tion between the two cities. ' When they considered that Lancashire, Cheshire, Derbyshire, Yorkshire, and the other districts which depended so largely on the height of the bar below the river at Liverpool, which at certain periods of the tide was only Bft. below the surface—when they considered that, it would be seen that the first thing to be done would be to improve the entrance to the port. Many schemes had been suggested for reducing the bar either by ' dredging or training walls, and so forth; and another, which he thought was the best plan, was to make a cut across the Birkenhead peninsula into deep water, and make a second entrance for the sea to Liverpool, by which they would then be able to get over any diffi- culty that might arise with regard to the present bar at Liverpool. (Hear, hear.) He thought the Manchester Ship Canal had been a great delusion. He thought it was about the worst engineering , piece of business that he remembered having come 1 ' across in his 40 years' experience. The way the 1 public had been deceived in money matters deser-1 , Ted very severe reprobation. (Near, hear.) They, had been told—he believed it was by Mr. Daniel 1 Adamson—that Messrs. Rothschild would find the capital at 1 per cent. interest. It now appeared, ! that all Messrs. Rothschild would do was to charge I per cent. on any money they might collect. It had been a failure, and he believed it would be a failure if the present works were carried out, for the canal might perhaps close the bar at Liverpool. They must remember they had the rivers Irk, Irwell, and Mersey with their silt and sand, which must go somewhere, and where would it go 1' It would go I down the river and settle on the bar, and that might lead to the ruin of the port. He thought the , Ship Canal, as at present projected, was a gigantic mistake. The public had been deceived. He thought, however, that it was incumbent on the commer- cial populations of this quarter of the kingdom to improve the bar at Liverpool, or open another en- trance to the port, so that they would be less depen- dent on the present bar. He should not have made any reference to the Ship Canal except that, as rail- way shareholders, and having been accused of hav- ing opposed the Ship Canal project, he thought it necessary to make those remarks.

• LIVERPOOL ASSIZER.—In charging the grand jury at the Liverpool Assizes on Wednesday Mr. Justice Smith congra- tulated them en the lightness Of the calendar considering the population. There were no cases of murder, and only two of manslaughter. There were 20 cases arising out of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, and but for the passing of the Act, the number of such cases would have been re- duced by 17 or 18 at least. SAD SEOI7PL TO ATTEMPTED FRATRICIDIL—The body of Benj. Johnson, of Shaw View, Flixton, was found about a hundred yards from Flixton Railway Station early on Tues- day morning. Johnson, who was convicted at the last Win- ter Assizes of shooting at his father, mother, and brother, and sentenced to six months' imprisonment for the offence, came out of prison on Saturday. His father left him in the house at six o'clock that morning, at twenty minutes past seven he was found at the spot stated quite dead, death having been caused by a guide rod entering the skull. The previous train was the 6-35 from Flixton to Manchester. The act was an evidently premeditated one, for the man had taken off his coat, hat, kc., folded them up, and left them near.

TERRIBLE ATTwarm) MURDER BY A Lusanc.—On Thursday, at Whitehaven. Alexander Murray was brought up in custody charged with attempting to murder Lillian Murray, his wife, by cutting her throat. Mrs. Murray, who was in a weak state, gave evidence that last week her hus- band was in a desponding state, and she concealed a razor from him. On Saturday be obtained possession of the razor, told his wife to say her prayers, and a desperate struggle took place between husband and wife, in which her throat was cut, and she was otherwise severely injured. Some men broke into the room, and pulled Murray away, bound him with cords, and he was taken into custody. Dr. Lamb said the prisoner was insane, and suffered from melancholy. He was committed for trial at the assizes.

THE BRITISH TEMPERANCE LEAGUE—The fifty-second annual conference of the British Temperance League, which is the oldest temperance organisation in the world, was opened in Burnley, on Taesday. Mr. James Barlow, J.P., Bolton, president, occupied the chair. The annual report reviewed the temperance work which had been carried on during the past year, and rejoiced in the evident progress of teetotalism in all ranks of the people. Delegates were present from about 130 societies in different parts of the country, who submitted reports of the work being done by the societies they represented. The balance sheet showed a deficit of £52. Mr. Barlow was re-elected president, Mr. S. Thorpe. of Sheffield, treasurer; and Mr. Clegg, of Sheffield, secretary. In the evening a public meeting was addressed by Mr. Thomas Watson, M.P. Rochdale; Mr. J. H. Raper, London; and others. On Wednesday the Executive were re-elected with the exception of Mr. Watson, M.P., of Rochdale, who was replaced by Mr. James Duckworth, of the same town. The conference also recognised with great satisfaction the election of SD many valuable and earnest temperance reformers to Parliament.
A VOYAGE TO TASMANIA. LETTER FROM A WARRINGTON MAN.

The following is a copy of a letter which has been received by Mr. James Roberts, of 16, Hop- wood-street, Warrington, from his son, Mr. George Roberts, who was formerly a photographer in Warrington, and is now residing at Hobart, Tas- mania :

I left home, or rather Gravesend, on the 9th October, about nine o'clock. We had fine weather until night came, and then the sea rolled us about till we reached Plymouth at 11-30 on the 10th. We left there at three o'clock in the afternoon, and had fine weather until we got near to the bay of Biscay, when my troubles began in fine style. All were sick on board. On the night of the 11th it was very rough, and while I was feeding baby, George slipped away from my side, and I thought he had gone on deck. It was very rough and dark, but as soon as I missed him I took the child and laid it by, and was up on deck in a crack, in spite of the rolling. I went into every nook and corner about the ship striking matches, as I could not get a lantern, and I had been all over the ship three times when I saw an officer, and he ordered a lantern to be got at once, when we found George asleep behind the mast on a form in the cabin. I will leave you to guess my feelings, as they will be easier felt than described. Monday, 12th,. weather fine, sea choppy. Just as we were getting through the bay I thought my work would be eased a little, as they were all get- ting over their sickness, and had the children out washed and dressed, except baby, which Annie was going to wash, and, contrary to orders, she would go for water. Then, to add to my troubles, a sea came and washed against the galley, and they carried her in helpless. I got the doctor to her, and he found', her shoulder to be broken. It was bandaged up, and we were told she would have to stay in bed for a fortnight, so I will leave you to guess what a pickle I was in. At the same time they just brought Hamlet in bleeding like a pig. He had fell against a door. Tuesday, 13th, up at 4-30; got all the children washed and dressed ready for breakfast, which was at seven o'clock; things washed up and myself straightened up and on deck about an hour, when I was told the doctor wanted me. I went, and found he wanted to vaccinate the baby. I can tell you I did not like it, but I thought I had better submit. In fact, I was informed by the steward that they would not let me land them unless the doctor had filled up the certificate to tha': effect, so I got it done without a murmur. Annie a little better; nothing more to-day only sailing over miles of water with fine sunshine, which you know I enjoyed very much. Thursday we reached Ten- eriffe about three in the afternoon. This we had a fine view of, as we sailed round a part of it. We coaled here, and nearly all the male passengers went ashore. It was quite a treat, as we dropped anchor, to see the Spaniards swarm round the ship bringing for sale a great quantity of fruit, wine, birds, and other things. I went on shore. Here the streets are very narrow, paved with sharp stones about the size of pota- toes. The houses reminded me of Ostend un- til we got nearer them. The shops having no win- dows of glass, but simply an opening left, and the same for a doorway, it was like going into a cellar. We left Teneriffe about 11-30 p.m. We have now 15 days' sail to the Cape—fancy 15 days ploughing through the waves—nothing to see only now and then a ship at a distance. The weather is beauti- ful, but getting very hot as we are nearing the line. I saw the lightening last night and it is a sight I shall not forgot; up late and up early washing shirts and other things. Still I may say lam en- Ijoying myself well under the circumstances. On Sunday up rather late, but got my work done in time for service, which Nellie and I attended. This being about the first fins Sunday it brought all the pious people out—as there was service in the 2nd saloon and all parts of the ship—preaching their different doctrines. In the evening there was ser- vice held in the 3rd cabin, in which the male sec- tion of let and 2nd classes took part. I may say that during this service there was an accident took place which changed the looks of those that hap- pened to be outside. Here the 3rd and 2nd and a part of the Ist classes being all at the stern of the ship it was packed with people singing. The re- mainder of the females from the 2nd saloon were quite in a panic, as after the noise had stopped they came running up, and I can tell you they had some very funny faces, as all the males .had left them to go preaching and to listen, and they were frightened to begin with. There was , a slight knocking which increased to a loud thumping, and then a tremendous crash, and at the same time the

ship trembled and lifted up as though she had been shot out of the water, and the head engineer jumped off the bridge and ran aft. I went after him to see what was the matter, when I was told that a screw or bolt had given way. The news soon went round, and by this time the captain had got down and the ship was stopped, when they found that a blade of the propellor had broken. Being very dark they did not know what was the matter, but they started the ship again slow and she went with a -very funny motion, going along and up and down at the same time. Next morning they found out that the propellor had lost one blade entirely, and that was what had caused the funny motion to the boat. As this day, Monday, turned out fine, we got up athletic sports. We had running, walking, wheel-barrow race, and jumping—long, high, and run jumps, obstacle race, and tug of war. After the sports came the concert, in which the Ist and 2nd joined. The captain took the chair. We had the deck covered with awning, and well lighted, and bunting displayed, and some good singing took place from both Ist and 2nd, but our team took the palm, and great praise was given to them; wound up at 11-30. This was a most en- joyable day for all, as the children came in for their share, as they had races for cakes and sweets. On Monday we arrived at the Cape about 3-30 in the afternoon. We went ashore Just to see what sort of a place it was, and were quite taken up with the appearance of it, for it is a beautiful place. As we enter the table bay we have a fine view of the city, in front the table mountain, and on the left and right we have its surroundings of broken jagged smaller mountains, which are lovely to look upon. The houSes are nice and clean look- ing; the roads are not paved, but the foot- paths are bricked, rising up with a step or two, or three, according as the road rises. Next day I went to a place called Wynnturgh, where they grow grapes on a large scale. Here are some splendid walks. On either side of the roads there are some splendid trees with lovely foliage. From this place I went to Constance, a very large estate of a Dutch family; and this was more lovely than all, as there was a lot of niggers to keep the place in order, in fact it was really i farmed n a proper, systematic style. Here I was taken into the wine stores and allowed to taste the different samples just as if I was a large buyer, as each wine was brought on a tray by a black, who was ordered to go round with us. After that we were taken out on the plantations where the vines grow. They are never allowed to grow more than two feet high, but bushy. There are acres of them just beginning to form the berry. Then we were taken round and shown the different kinds of fruit. I forget the names, but I did not forget to taste them all. We walked round the woods and saw ' lots of doves flying wild, and other birds of most beautiful plumage. We left Capetown Friday, November 7, at 6-30, with fine weather. Having referred to several minor incidents of the voyage the letter proceeds: Nothing eventful took place until Tuesday when we began to sight land. Then all were out with their glasses, but nothing could be properly discerned until the next morning. Then came something worth all the suffering, and once seen will never be forgotten. Well, I cannot des- cribe it, but will give you some idea. As we pass the Tamer heads it is a lovely sight along the shore. From this point it is very mountainous, and I see by the aid of the glasses that it is nearly all stone, rising a great height in some places, and at the top of these rocks the trees seem to be planted as thick as pins on a sheet and as regular; and the bay is filled with sea birds--swan, duck, diver, goose, and sea-hawk—which add much to the beauty. Pas- sing on to Storm Bay we have both sides alike, and looking first on one side and then the other as we go in the sight increases in splendour. When enter- ing the Derwent and Conse, in view of the city, it crowns all and is well worth the whole Df the journey to see. We dropped anchor here and those for other ports were left gazing, wishing they were stopping here too. The storm abated, we were taken ashore in a small steamer, went and got lodgings; went back, got my luggage, saw that landed right and had a walk through the city.

FITE CHILDREN BURNT TO DEATH.-At Halateao, Kent, on Saturday morning, thrae children, belonging to fruit pickers in the employ of Mr. Bath, were left alone for a abort time in a tent erected upon Mr. Bath's ground, when the canvas caught fire, and the three children were burnt to death. Their injuries were of a terrible nature. The ages of them are respectively four years, two years. and six months. A fire, on Sunday, at Southport, caused the death of two children and great destruction of property.

div.head: EARLESTOWN.
div.p: EARLESTOWN.

LIMIRAL Proanc. A party of members of th. Earlestown and District Liberal Club had a picnic to Lymtn on Thursday afternoon. They assembled at th• club shortly after noon, and started for their destination In a conveyance about two o'clock. THH PREBRNTATION TO Ma. WiLuemsoN.—The tecti raonial to Mr. W. Williamson, on his retirement from the , management of the 'Vulcan Foundry, after 41 years' service will be made this (Saturday) afternoon. The gifts comprise , paintings of himself and wife, aud a handsome timepiece with a suitable inscription. The articles have been on view in the window of Mr. Taylor's shop, 12, Queen-street, Earlestown, during the week, and have attracted many fa• vourable comments.

INDEPENDENT DIIITHODUT9.—SpeciaI sermons in con- nection with the Independent Methodist Connexion were preached in the Mission Room, Bridge-street, on Sunday. The preacher, both morning and evening, was Mr. J. Knowles, of Lymm. Appropriate hymns were selected for the occasion, and a number of friends took part in the musical portion of the service. The collections were in aid of the Sunday school funds, and a satisfactory amount was realised. The mission is stated to lie making steady pro- gress.

- CROW-LANB CONORBGATIONAL STJNDAY SCHOOLB.—OR Saturday morning the teachers and elder scholars of these schools, to the nnmber of 50, had a picnic to the Inter- national Exhibition, Liverpool. The party, under the guidance of Mr. B. B. Glover and Mr. F. J. Holmes, left Earlestown at nine o'clock. On arrival at Liverpool several proceeded direct to the Exhibition, whilst others paid a visit ,to the Cheshire side of the river, visiting the Exhibition later in the day. Tea was partaken of ia the school of cookery, and after a most enjoyable day the party returned home, reaching Earlestown at 10-30 p.m. GOOD TEMPLARY.—The weekly session of the Hope of Earlentown Lodge of Good Tempters was held on Monday evening, when there was a very large attendance. The chair was occupied by Bro. J. Macdonald, w.c.r. The principal business was the completion of arrangements for taking part in the united temperance demonstration at Earlestown, and the evening's programme, which was" Ex- perience meeting—short addresses,' Why lam a Good Tem- plar.' " In accordance with the programme appropriate addresses were given by Bros. J. Macdonald, W.C.T., Wil- Um Jameson, John Taylor, C. E. Newman, and G. Clarke, and Sister Mrs. Whitty. Rairmaz EXTBNSION AT GOLBORNB. The London and Nerth-Western Railway Company have just let a con- tract for important extensions at Golborne. The work con- sists in cutting a new double line of rails for Golborne Junction to Bamfurlong, near Wigan, to facilitate the ex- tensive traffic from Wigan to the south. The extension will necessitate the erection of a number of large bridges, lan underground railway for Messrs. Evans's colliery, at Edge Green Colliery, to the canal, underground passages, ac. The work, which will commence at once, has to be completed in fifteen ant nths, and a large staff of hands will be engaged night and day. Mr. Braddock, Southport, is 1 the contractor.

LOCAL TEXPERANCE CHOIR. 9 AND THE LIVERPOOL Ex- HIBITIOX.—The temperance party of Liverpool and ant- rounding districts having arranged for a monster demons- tration at the Liverpool Exhibition on Saturday, August 28th, a feature will be concerts by two choirs, one com- prising one thousand children from the various juveoile temperance organisations of Liverpool, and the other formed of 500 adults selected from societies connected with the Lancashire and Cheshire Band of Hope Union, whose headquarters are at Manchester. The Earle's- town and District Band ef Hope and Temperance Union, as members of the Manchester organisation have been invited to form a section of the choir. Consequently, the local Union has taken the matter up, and the different societies connec- ted therewith have chosen the required number of their choristers to take part. The practising of the pieces to be sung at the demonstration has been ckenmenced in Earles- town during the present week. The contingent from Rifles- town will number about 60 members. THE STABBING AFFRAY AT Evarzt3Towie.--At the Liverpool Assizes, on Thursday, James Kelly (24). labourer. ef Crew-lane, Newton, wai indicted for having, at Newton- le-Willows, on the 3rd inst, wounded James Cavil, with a knife, with intent to do him grievous bodily harm. Mr. Cooper prosecuted, and Mr. t•wift defended. It appeared that on Saturday night, the 3rd iust, about a quarter to eleven o'clock, a man named English was going hems when Ihe was attacked by three or four men, of whom the pri- sonergwas one. English called out, and Cavil, hearing the cry and knowing the voice, went to English's assistance. A row ensued, and Kelly was seen to draw a knife and stab Cavil with it on the arm. He also made several blows at Cavil's head, one of which took effect and cut the scalp.— Prosecutor and his witnesses could not identify the prisoner as the man who inflicted the injuries, but said the man who attacked prosecutor was dressed in white clothes, as the prisoner was when apprehended.—Mr. Swift cross-examined prosecutor as to his sobriety on the night in question, and witness admitted that he had had a lot of di-Ink. Five or six pints, he said, would not put him on his head. (Laughter) He would have had twenty pints. (Renewed laughter.) H. could not give any reason why the prisoner attacked him—The jury found the prisoner guilty of un- lawful wounding, and he was sentenced to a month's hard labour,

div.head: CROWNING OF THE ROSE QUEEN AT WARGRAVE.
div.p: CROWNING OF THE ROSE QUEEN AT WARGRAVE.

On Thursday evening week an interesting ceremony was witnessed at Wargrave, which created a widespread and all absorbing interest in the neighbourhood. This consisted of the " erowning of the Rose Queen," attended by other pro- ceedings of an enjoyable and unusual natare. The event had been principally arranged by Mn. Norman and Mrs. Ha-neon (of the Victoria Inn), who received the assistance of other ladies residing in the vicinity, including 31!s. McMullen, Mrs. Henderson, Mrs. Williamson and Miss Sweetlove. Financial support and contributions were re- ceived from Mr. T. Molyneux, Market-street, Mr. John Dunn, fruiterer), and other friends. Unfortunately the weather in the carder part of the day was unfavourable and about noon a heavy shower fell. This interfered with the arrange. ciente to some extent. The children in the district were asked to assemble in the field opposite the Victoria lon, but the wet prevented this being carried out. They, however, met at the Victoria Inn, and were formed into processional order. The children were dressed in characteristic cos- tumes, representative of various trades, Lc. The Rosa Quen elect, Miss May Sweetlove, who, by a singular co- incidence, attained her seventh birthday on the day of her "coronation," was attired in costume of a cream colour, with a blue veil, and a wreath of roses, while in her hand she carried a beautiful bouquet of flowers. The maids of honour were. Misses Lillie Harrison, Rose Ellen Knox, Ethel Knox, and .Sissy Williamson. Miss Foulkes was representative of " Sleeping Beauty," while other parts in the programme were well taken by Miss Mary Ellen Williamson, Miss Eliz- abeth Ann Knox, Miss Ruth Norman, Miss Maggie Wil- liamson, tkc. Many of the children in the procession carried bunches and bouquets of flowers, and the procession, its charge of the ladies previously mentioned, moved along the road as far as Wargrave Church, where they retraced their steps. Owing to the wet grass the children were unable to enter the field, and the coronatien took place in front of the Victoria Inn, where amid a picturesque scene the ceremony was performed by Mies Lillie Harrison. The crown was a floral one of beautiful design, and was carried on a a cushion to the coronation chair, which had been covered with a pure white skin rug for the occasion. The coronation being over, the children, who numbered nearly 70, after- wards sat down to an excellent tea, which was served on tables erected in the road near the Victoria Inn. The " open-air tea party" was an unusually plea- sant part of the proceedings, and fortunately the I weather was fine during the rest of the evening. The tea tables were presided over by Mrs. Norman, Mrs. Harrison, Mrs. McMullen,Pirs.:Henderson, Mrs. Williamson, Miss Sweetlove, and other willing helpers. These, in com- pany with a number of friends, afterwards partook of tea while the chilnren were enjoying themselves in the large room of the Victoria Inn. The rain having cleared off, the children proceeded to the field near Warg-ave School, oppo- site the Victoria Inn, and here the evening was spent in various amusements. The elder portion of those present enjoyed themselves in dancing, which, after dusk, was con- tinued in the club room of the Victoria Inn. The day's proceedings have since been a topic of enviable talk in the neighbourhood, and one or two minor "coronations of Rose Queens" have taken place. On Wednesday night a 'coronation " took place at the Vulcan. It is stated that next year it is intended to have the " coronation " on a more general and extensive scale.
THE NEWTON COMMISSIONERS AND THE RATEPAYERS. -.AN/QUAL MEETING AND ELECTION.

The annual joint meeting of the Improvement Commis- sioners and the ratepayers of the township of Newton was held in the Town Hall, Newton, on Wednesday afternoon, when there was a very small attendance. The only persons present were Mr. Thomas Stone (commissioner), who pre- sided, Messrs. W. F. Gooch, J.P., T. J. Gillespie, J.P , J. W. Emmett, T. Forster, (commissioners), J. E. Woreley (law clerk), R. Brierley (surveyor), Joseph Barchall (Earlestown, one of the auditors of the Board's accounts), and Henry Houghton (assistant overseer).

div.head: _ RECENT ELECTION.
div.p: THE _ RECENT ELECTION.

The Chairman said : I think the first business to-day is for me to declare to you the result of the election. The no- tices were duly issued calling the attention of the ratepayers to the fact that the election would take place to day, and I received four nominations, .and the four nominations were those of the gentlemen who were retiring, namely, Messrs. W. F. Gooch, J. W. Emmett. B. B. Glover, and Thomas Forster. I received one other nomination—a gentleman who was nominated, but was not duly qualified to act as a Commisioner, and I apprised his nomi- nator of that fact, so that I have now only to announce that I hereby declare Messrs. William F. Gooch. James W. Emmett, Benjamin B. Glover, and Thomas Forster to be duly elected.—Mr. J. W. Emmett: I think on behalf of my- self I should be falling in my duty if I did not thank the ratepayers for re-electing me again. I have had the honour of being a commissioner now for something like 16 years, and it appears that they have confidence in me by re-elect- ing me, or allowing me to be re-elected. And therefore I thank them very much, and I shall take care, as I have done in the past, to try to merit their further confidence by doing my duty.—Mr. W. V. Gooch, J.P.: I thank you for the honour you have done in re-electing me, and the confidence , Yon have shown in so doing. I only hope that in the future f may retain your further confidence.—lt should be stated tLat Mr. Forster (who had also been re-elected) did not enter the room until a later period of the meeting.

WIT AND HUMOUR. How can a pig always build his own dwelling-place? ..-By tying a knot in his tail, which will be a "pig's tie" (pig-sty). When Fogg was asked regarding the latest additions to the English language, he said he would ask his wife; Ehe always had the last word. An Irishman, mourning his wife, tearfully exclaimed;: "Faith, an' she wos a good womark ; she always hit me the.soft end of the mop." An Irishman who had on a very ragged coat was asked of what stuff it was made. " Bedad, I don't know! said he. "But I think the most of it is made of fresh 44.2, M. Guibollard and his son Tote stopped in front of a statue of Joan of Arc. • " Papa," said the child, "who is that lady?" "That, my son, is one of our greatest men!" was the reply. Scene—Art-school. Mrs. Nouveau : " And is that large picture some of your work?" Pupil: "Mine? Oh, no, madam! That is one of the old masters." Mrs. Nouveau, in an undertone to her companion: "I don't like to hear a young man speak so disrespectfully of his teachers." "There is something in this little fellow I like," said an appreciative up-town visitor of a young hopeful he Was trotting on his knee. "Say, now," said the boy, "how did you know I had swallowed a shilling ?" An excellent old gentleman had a very strong desire to make a balloon ascent. "What!" said one of his friends. "At your age?" "Certainly, my friend," he replied. "It is solely for the purpose of accustoming imayself to quit this earth." "Robert, what did you do with the letter I left on my dask a little while ago ?" "I took it to the post.' " What ! Did you not see that it had no address ?" "Yes, sir; but I thought you didn't want me to know for whom it was intended." Little Harry, home from school: "I say, :mother, we had our singing-lesson to-day." "And how did you get o ?" " Teacher said I sang like a bird." " Really ' -
bird?" "Like a crow-!"

What biro: Miss Strickland once spent an evening with Mrs; liich- bald. It was bitterly cold weather, the fire was low, and at last she could stand it no longer, and rose to go. Mrs. Inchbald not being able to make up her mind to the extravagance of putting on more coal, but being • desirous to enjoy the talk, exclaimed, "Oh, stay a little -iOnger, and I will push all the fire to your side." "Dot brudder of mine in Chicago vhas no good," said Moses, as he dusted a pair of second-hand trousers at the door. "He close his slitore der odder day und puts on a si,n dot his wife was deadt, und he doan' keep open for two days." "Wasn't that right ?" "It vhas all right to shut oop, but vliy doan' lie say on der sign, 40n dis account I haf to dispose of dis mammoth shtock, und all goods shall be sold at ten per cent. below cost'? Vhen a peesness man's wife dies, it vhas a chance to advertise dot doan' come once in twenty years." The sergeant-major of a Scotch Volunteer corps was to be presented with a long-service and good-conduct medal. All members of the corps who had won medals were ordered to wear them on the occasion. When the battalion had formed into three sides of a square, the commanding officer glanced round the ranks, and spied one of the corps with an unusually large medal on his breast. "Galloping up to him, the officer called out, "Halo, fellow, where did you get that medal?" The private, saluting, answered, "At a plooin' match, sir." An amusing Vern in the diary of the late Sir Henry Cole is one that tells how on June 2nd,1851, the Duchess a Bent, having gone to the Great Exhibition with her daughter, was separated from her party and politely in- formed by a policeman that, if she stood on one side, she should "see the Queen pass." She was a Brooklyn girl. He was a young man from • Boston visiting at her house. In honour of his coming she had made a custard pie with her own fair hands. "Do take some," she urged at the supper toble. "1 .made it for you myself, you know." "No," said he, re- tuctantly, after an evident inward struggle ; "I cannot. If I were at home in Boston, I would; but here I dare not." "And why not ?" she urged. "Why, dearest, can you not eat it here ?" "BecauSe," he answered, with a deep-dr wn sigh, "we are now in New York, you know, and an attempt at suicide is a crime under the 'flew York laws." _ •

STAMPS ON RECEIPT.--SCUTIO---PUbliC-hOUSe, Dumbar- ton. Enter thirsty loafer. Loafer, hurriedly: If you plaze, sor, I've no money; but I'll give three stamps for a glass of whisky.—Publican, smilingly: All right, Pat, stamps are as good as money to me.—(Uives him a glass.) —Loafer, after drinking: Thank ye, sor."—(Gives three stamps on the floor with his foot.)—Publican, after a moment's reflection: Here, Pat—if you'll go over to Mac's, and do him in the same way, Plr.give you another glass.—Loafer, making for the door: Och, sor, I can't! He promised me a glass to come over and do you! The average small boy of the present day is seldom at a loss for something to say, even in the most embarrasa- ing situations. Bobby, a precocious youth of six sum- mers, had been indulging in bad language, and, in order to escape .the punishment for winch his mother had made preparations, he crawled under a barn, and re- mained there in a state of siege for the greater part of an afternoon. When his father returned at night and learned how matters stood, he made his way with much difficulty under the barn in search of the boy. "Hallo, papa," said Bobby cheerfully, as his sire approached, "have you been saying something wicked too?' "The smartest thing," writes 'A Carlton Cabby" to Vanity Fair, "I ever heard done to a cabby was this. One of my mates drove a gentleman once a two-shilling fare. Now my mate was just about to take the pledge, and, naturally .enough, he had had a last break-out on that stuff they sell at the publics that makes you drunk before it stops your being thirsty. Well, I dare say he weaved about over the road a bit. Anyhow, when he reached the end of the journey, the gent taxed him with being drunk. My mate, being an honourable man, didn't deny it. Very well,' said the gent, 'if I have you be- fore the beak, you'll get fined five shillings and have your license indorsed." Quite right, sir,' says my friend 'Well, then,' says the gent,' 'I am disposed to be lenient. Give me three shillings.' My mate hands. over the three shillings, thinking he was going to get two half-crowns back. But what does this gent do? Why, he says, Two and three is five. As you've paid the five shillings fine, I'll let you off the indorsement. Good night.' And my mate was so taken aback that he drove away, having paid the gent three shillings for driving him throe miles and a half !" SPECTRES.—Not all Verdi's countrymen have delighted to honour him. AM. Prospero Bertani, who travelled twice from Reggio to Parma to hear Aida, was disap- dointed, and frankly wrote to the composer telling him so, and asking him to refund the expenses incurred. This is the closing paragraph of his letter :—" You may now imagine, my dear M. Verdi, my regret at having spent in the two visits to Parma 32f.; add, moreover, to this the aggravating circumstance that I am dependent upon my family for support, and that this money troubles my rest as might some fearful spectre. So I turn frankly to you, and beg you will send me this sum. Here is the bill :—Railway fare to Parma, 2f. 60c.; rail- way fare back, 3f. 30c. ; theatre, Bf.; detestable supper at station, 2f. Total, 15f. 90c. by 2 31f. 80a. Hoping that you will get me clear of my scrape, I salute you cordially.—BEßTANl." And this is Verdi's reply (in- directly to his agent, M. Ricordi) :—" You can well imagine that to save a young man from the spectres that pursue him I would willingly pay the little bill that he has sent in to me. So I beg you to have forwarded to M. Prospero Bertani, 5, Via San Domenico, the sum of 27f. 80c. The amount is not that for which he asks; but, if he thinks I am going to stand him a supper into the bargain—ma, foi, non IHe can quite well sup at home. You will kindly get him to give you a receipt, and also a statement to the effect that he will never go and hear any more of my operas, and thus neither ex- pose himself afresh to the menaces of spectres nor mete the risk of paying his expenses !" The receipt was duly given. •

div.head: VOLUNTEER INSPECTION AT
div.p: VOLUNTEER INSPECTION AT

WARRINGTON. The members of the Ist Battalion Prince of Wales Volunteers, South Lancashire Regiment, Warrington and Newton, were inspected on Saturday afternoon, on a field at Arpley, by Colonel Thackwell, Orford Barracks, Warrington. The corps, which was until recently known under the name of the 9th Lanca- shire Rifle Volunteers, had during the week gone through their annual training. The Warrington Volunteers assembled at the Drill Hall soon after four o'clock in the afternoon, and here they were joined by the Newton contingent, but it was not until some time later that a start was made. The men assembled on the green in front of the Town Hall, where they formed into marching order. Thence, with two bands playing, they marched by way of Sankey-street and Parker-street to the field where the inspection took place. The weather was dull and rather threatening, but a large number of people lined the route of march, and not a few wit- nessed the subsequent manoeuvres on the field. The men looked smart and drilled well. Their dress and accoutrements were neat and clean, and the appearance they presented was altogether credit- able. The bands in attendance were the band of the regiment, and a drum and fife band that has not long been in formation, and which played well. Previous to leaving the grounds in front of the Town Hall, a photograph of the corps was taken by Mr. Birtles, of Sankey-street. The total strength of the battalion is 612, and of that number only eight were unaccounted for. The officers present were Colonel Greenall, in command, Major and Adjutant O'Leary, Major Bolton, Captains Bridge, Ridgway, Widdows, Gooch, Thomson, and Buckton ; Lieut. Baynes; Surgeon-Major Gornall, and Quartermaster Hutchinson. After one or two preliminary exercises had been gone through the Inspecting Colonel rode on to the field, and was received by the battalion in line, and with the customary present. He after- wards rode along the line and inspected every man in the battalion. The battalion was next broken into column to the right, and the men were marched past in quick time, in quarter distance column, and at the double. The battalion was then wheeled to the left, and line was formed to the left of the rear company. Major Bolton then put the battalion through manual and firing exercises. Col. Greenall was called to the front and gave the com- mand—" Right company to the front; remainder fours right,' and the battalion advanced in column. Direction was then changed to the left, quarter column was formed, and they then deployed to the left. The battalion then retired in column from the left, in rear of the right, and advanced in column and formed line to the right of the leading company. Major Bolton was now called up again. He broke the battalion into column to the right, wheeled back again into line, retired in fours from the right of companies, front-turned the column, and wheeled into line to the left. Captain Bridge then prepared the battalion for cavalry, in line from the right. He then re-formed line, formed quarter column of double companies in rear of the centre, and deployed outwards. Captain Thomson then formed square on the two centre companies, advan- ced, retired, and moved the square to a flank. He then formed column of double companies and de- ployed outwards. Captain Gooch next advanced the line and changed front to the left on the right company, after which the commanding officer took over the command and put the battalion through the attack formation. This concluded the inspection. Colonel Thackwell then addressed a few words to the men, expressing himself extremely satisfied with the steadiness of the corps, and with their neat and clean appearance. The movements had been well executed and the men had performed what they had been called upon to do in a soldier-like manner. It would be his duty to report favourably on these points. He then left the field and Colonel Greenall spoke to the men. He said that all of the eight men unaccounted for at the inspection had put in one or more drills during the week. Although he did not presume to dictate to the authorities, he hoped that at the Queen's Jubilee next year, Warrington would show its loyalty by joining with other volunteers in the Hyde Park review, if permission could be obtained. Having referred with regret to the deaths of Sergt. Bugler Buckley and Sergeant Hill, Colonel Greenall thanked the men for their attention. He had passed a pleasant week, and he hoped they had done the same. He wished always when he came amongst them that they should enjoy themselves as far as possible, and as far as was compatible with military duties. He felt that they should not separate without acknowledging to whom they were in- debted for the appearance they had that day pre- sented. There was no doubt that those who had brought about that satisfactory state of things were the members of the staff, headed by Major O'Leary, who, as all knew, was a painstaking officer. They were also indebted to Sergeant-Major Fennelly, Ser- geant-Instructors McCoy and Hill, and the other members of the staff. He again thanked them for their support, and the soldier-like appearance they had that day presented. This concluded the busi- ness of the afternoon, and the battalion was marched back to the Drill Hall.
