GENERAL 1\ EWS.
An inmate of the County Down Lunatic Asylum, Down- patrick, on Monday, drowned himself in a pond while out

for a walking exercise. Her Royal Highness the Duchess of Cambridge entered upon her 90th year on Sunday, having been born on July 25th, 1797. The venerable duchess is in the enjoyment of excellent health, and had a family party at ginner on Sun- day evening. sIIICLDE.—Some boys at play on Hackney Downs on Saturday morning observed a respectably dressed man place a revolver to his head and fire. Information was conveyed to the police, and upon a constable proceeding to the spot he found the man dead. Poomoriox.—Mr. H. B. Primrose, who has been for some time Mr. Gladstone's principal private secretary, has been appointed Secretary to the First Commissioner of Works in succession to Mr. Mitford. The salary attached to the posi- tion is £1,500 a year. Rior IN A Pnisoeie—Four hundred prisoners in the prison of La Roquette, Paris, revolted on Satarday morning. The gevernor invoked the aid of the military, and after somel trouble order was restored and the ringleaders arrested., Several prisoners were wounded in the struggle. Snnious Finis.—On Monday evening a fire occurred on the premises of Mr. David Norton, lace and hosiery bleacher and dresser, Nottingham. So fierce were the flames that the doors and shutters of houses 40 feet distant were set on tire. The entire premises and contents were destroyed. The damage is estimated at from £15,000 to £20,000. Execuricier —At Shrewsbury, on Monday morning, Wm. Samuels was executed for tbe murder of William Mabbots, whom he poisoned with strychnine at Welshpool. Samuels slept badly during the night, ate little or no breakfast, and had to be supported on to the scaffold. He made a full coo- fession of the crime, at which he expressed regret. Berry was the executioner. "Music IN Naw YORK."—Not before nine in the morn- ing, and not after the same hour at night, may the wander- ing organ grinder make the streets of New York resound , hereafter. A police order imposing these limits on the tar- rel-organist also directs the arrest of any person who beats a drum, blows a horn, or makes similar noisy demonstra- tions on the highway for advertising purposes. SHOCKING FATALITY.—A shocking fatality occurred at I the new post office at Leicestershire, on Tuesday. A work- I man named Bryan Feeley, belonging to Yorkshire, was in the top part of the building, when he fell through an opening in the floor, striking some joists with his head. On being picked up he was quite dead, his neck havieg been broken by the fall. The deceased was aged 32, and unmarried. IRE Wure,_4( COAL TRADEI —Notices were Tuesday posted at the Ocean Collieries, Rhondda Valley, announcing a re- duction of wages of 2i per cent, for the ensuing three months. Notices for a reduction in wages have now been served upon the miners in most of the colliery districtsl throughout the Principality in consequence of a great de- preciation in the Welsh coal trade. For some months past mest of the collieries have only worked about half-time, and matry of the coal owners have been compelled to clods their works. GENEROUS AND MODEST.—An anonymous donor has just presented to the Worcester Infirmary £5,000 on condition that his name shall not be divulged during his life. He had made a will bequeathing this sum to the institution at his death, but on second thoughts decided to hand over the , amount while living, by which step he gave to the in- firmary the heavy duty which would otherwise be levied on the bequest. The amount is to be invested in Consols, and the proceeds to go annually to the infirmary, which is about to be enlarged. Ourie " WooDEN WALLS."—One piece of ancient history has to be recosded and received with regret. The last of the wooden walls of Old England, her Majesty's ship, Velture, was disposed of on Monday. The Vulture was one of the , last wooden gen-vessels built about 18 years ago for the I Royal Navy before the introduction of composite ship- building, and has had a considerable amount of foreign ser- vice. She was last employed on the East Indies station, where she took a prominent part in the suppression of slavery, capturing several dhows engaged in that nefarious tree-

Ade. THE MIIDER TRIAL IN CORH—The trial of Timothy Hurley, labourer, for the murder of John Regan, a boycotted farmer, in West Cork, was resumed and concluded on Tues- day, at Cork Assizes. Deceased's daughter swore that she 14w the prisoner run away after shooting her father from behind a hedge whilst he was engaged gardening. Other witnesses swore that on the evening Regan was murdered, horns were sounded on the hill sides proclaiming victory over Regan. The prisoner was tried at the last assizes, when the jury disagreed. The present jury found him not guilty, and he was discharged. PROPOSED SHORT TIME IN THE COTTON SPINNINO MILLS. —The Cotten Spinners' Association met in Manchester on Tuesday, and passed a resolution expressing a decided opinion in favour of adopting short time in the cotton spin- ning mills of Lancashire; inviting the co-operation of dis- trict associations, and convening a meeting of the entire trade to consider the situation. A resolution was also passed regretting that the Liverpool Dock Board showed little disposition to protect the interests of cotton consumers and urging a reconsideration of the questions of weigh- ing and marking hales, and protecting them from the weather. FATAL FIGHT BETWEEN BROTHERS.—At Dresden, near Longton, on Sunday evening, a tragedy occurred which ended in the death of William Rushton, 32 years of age. A younger brother of the deceased, named Henry, lodged with his father, next door to the house of William, and during the latter's absence on Sunday evening Henry en- , tered his brother's house, and a quarrel arose between him and William's wife. William was sent for, and on his arrival said to his brother' " I want thee," and Henry re- plied, "I am ready for thee." Blows followed. and Wil- liam fell to the ground, mortally stabbed, death taking place a few hours later. Henry, who is only 19 years of age, made off. RRPORTRD IMPRISONMENT OF MDME. SARAH BERNHARDT. --It is reported that Mdme. Sarah Bernhardt has been getting into troultle in Rio Janeiro. According to the story, as received by M. Sarcey. at Paris, there was among the miscellaneous company provided by her impresario to ac- company her on her South American tour a certain artist named Mdme. Noirmont. The lady having had a difference , with the great tragedienne during a rehearsal of Adrienne Lecourrear resolved summarily to quit the company. On Mdme. Bernhardt expostulating a lively dispute nsued, whieh ended with that lady punishing her recalcitrant colleague by the administration of a horsewhip. The con- sequence was a summons before the magistrate, which is stated to have resulted in the imprisonment of Mdme Bern- hardt. GREAT JEWEL ROBEZRY.—At the County Petty Sessions at Wolverhampton on Monday, James Donald Wildsmith, 39, was charged with stealing a quantity of silver plate and jewelry, value £2,000, the property of the Misses Perry, The Werge Hall, Tettenhall. The prisoner had been several years in the employ of the Misses Perry and their late brother Captain Perry, as confidential servant and butler. During the absence of his mistresses from the hall in May last, the prisoner, yielding to sudden temptation, committed the robbery now charged against him. and absconded to London. From there a few days afterwards he returned the plate and jewelry, per railway, addressed to the Misses Perry, and with it a letter, in which he expressed contrition for the offence, attributing it to drink, and asked to be for- given in consequence of his long service. Miss Perry was desirous of withdrawing the charge, but the Public Prosecu- tor refused permission, and the prisoner was committed to the assizes.

RELIGIOUS INTOLERANCE IN IRELAND.—A case of religi- ous intolerance (a Dublin correspondent says) was reported on Monday from New Ross. Mrs. Daubeny. of London, being desirous of perpetuating the memory of her „father, the late General Clayton Brown, determined on erecting a fountain as the best mode of effecting her object. She pre- sented the fountsin to the Town Commissioners of New Ross, in which town her deceased father had long been known. The Commissioners accepted it, and thanked Mrs. Daubeny for the gift. With the fountain Mrs. Daubeny sent a number of copies of St. John's Gospel: A few of these were taken by the townspeople, and about 60 copies, consti- tuting the balance, were returned to Mrs. Daubeny, with a curt note from the chairman of the Commissioners. At the next meeting of the Board this action on the part of the chairman was condemned but it is stated, under the haftence of the priests, tile Roman Catholic Commissioners who repudiated the conduct of the chairman have been obliged to apologise, and a resolution has since been passed directing , that a text of Scripture on the base of the fountain should be erased. The Catholics charged Mrs. Daubeny with send- ing over poisonous stuff in the shape of Proteetast tracts, and denounced five of the Catholic Commissioners as guilty of religious profligacy. The text to be erased is from St. John—" If any man thirst let him come unto Me and drink." It is regarded as calculated to wound Catholic feeling. It has also been proposed that an ornamental harp on the fountain shall be removed and a statue of the Virgin Mary substituted. SHOCKING DEATH PROM HYDROPHOBIA.—)n Saturday an inquest was held at Lastock, Cheshire, touching the death of George Henry Jones, six years old. On June sth the deceased and two playmates were gathering watercress in a field belonging to Mr. Beswick, a farmer in the neigh- bourhood. Mr. Beswick and a lad named Dalton were in the field, carting away potatoes. On seeing the boys, Mr. Beswick shouted to them to be off, and they ran away. There were two ckgs in the field; and one of them ran after the boys and bit the deceased severely on the arm and leg. They did not hear anyone setting the dog at them, nor did they hear anyone call the dog back. Dalton's evidence was to the effect that the dog ran playfully after the deceased and his playmates. One of them, a boy named Buckley, struck the dog with a basket, and the dog Own bit the de- ceased. Mr. Beswick took the deceased home and washed the wounds, and witness sucked them. Mr. Beseick thee took deceased to the surgery of Dr. Joynson, Northwich. The same evening, at the request of the father of the de- ceased, the dog was shot. The father of the deceased de- posed that under the treatment of Dr. Joynson the wounds healed up. In about a fortnight afterwards deceased began to rave. On Monday, when out for a walk, he "snapped and hacked with his teeth " when facing the wind, and he was greatly alarmed when he saw a dog running after some cows. He became worse and worse till Wednesday, when after intense agony, during which he kept shouting" Bes- wick and the dogs are coming," he died.—Police-constable Egerton deposed that Dr. Joynson had informed him that the deceased had undoubtedly died from hydrophobia. Several jurymen remarked upon the absence of Mr. Beswick, and at their suggestion the inquest was adjourned to secure his attendance.
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY. JULY 31, 1886.

CON*RBOATIONAL UNION OF ENGLAND. —The Rev. Alexeselet Xfa-ck.ennal, of Bowden, has accepted the chair- manship of the Union, to which he was invited by the com- mittee, in place of Mr. Samuel Morley, whose illness has prevented his acceptance of the office. Mr. Mackennal is well known throughout this district as secretary of the Northern Board of Education, and as the successful minister of the Congregational Church at Bowdon, Cheshire He received his theological training at Hackney College, and is a graduate of London University. ILLITERATE VOTERS.—A Parliamentary return. moved for by Mr. 8. Leighton, has been issued by the HOM 9 Office, showing the number of persons who voted as illiterates at; the General Election of 1885, and specifying the constitutn- , cies in which their votes were recorded. The number of votes polled in England and Wales was 3,705,103, of which 80.430 were illiterates; in Scotland, 447,588 Votes, of which 7.708 were illiterates ; and in Ireland, 450,906, of which 98,404 were illiterates. In the 66 Erish county contests con- tests there were recorded 373 863 votes, of which 92 822 were illiterates. In the 13 Irish borough counties 77,043 votes were recorded, of which 5.582 were illiterates. In tke 37 Scotch county contests there were 254,624 votes re- corded, of which 6012 were illiterates ; while in the 27 borough contests there were 192,964 votes, of which 1,696 were illiterates. The return does .not separate the English counties from the boroughs. In the City of Loud-qa there were 33,009 votes recorded, of which 20 were illitera-es ; in Edinburgh, 26,827 votes and 118 illiterates: and in Dub- lin, 31,846 votes and 869 illiterates.

SERIOUS ENCOUNTER. WITH POACHERS.—On Monday, At Wigan County Petty Sessions, James Bennett, collier, was charged with night poaching at Wiustanley.—alfred Hum- phreys, one of the gamekeepers on the Winstanley estate, said that on Saturday morning, about a quarter to one, he was in Winstanley Park, along with two other keepers and an assistant. Hearing the screaming of rabbits, they went in the direction of the sounds, and met nine or ten men. Moat of them fell back, but the prisoner called out "Come on chaps, there are only three of them." Prisoaer threw a stone, which hit one of the keepers on the face. The men then made a rush, and the prisoner then gave witness a severe blow on the hank of the head which felled bim to the ground. He get up and caught hold 'of the prisoner's leg, and they fell to the groutid together, and the prisoner tried to bite his ringer. Fie .held .the prisoner notwithstanding kicks and blows.' 'Eventually the rest of the pa:tenets ran away, and the other keepers coming to witness's assistance they secured the prisoner. .Pegs and nets, were found upon the prisoner, and on the ground there were ether nets and bags, one containing six and the other seven rabbits.— Prisoner was remanded; an aPplication for bail being re- fused.

ALLEGED BRUTAL Wm; MURDER —Ott Sunday morn- ing, Peter Kiernan, 40 years of age, a labourer, of 76, Pun- the-street, Bootle, was taken into custody on suspicion of having caused the death of his wife. It appears that aboat six o'clock on Saturday evening Kiernan returned from work, and on reaching home be sent for a pint of beer, which he, a Mrs Hartley. and the deceased woman drank in company. Shortly afterwards Kiernan and his wife went Out and did not return until after eight o'clock. Neither husband nor wife was then drunk, but were decidedly under the influence of intoxicants. They quarrelled over some ttifling matter, and Kiernan turned on his wife and struck her a violent blow in the face, knocking her down. About seven o'clock on Sunday morning Mrs Hartley called from her room to Kiernan, and asked him bow his wife was. He instantly replisd that she was all right, but correcting this statement a moment afterwards, said "She's dead." The police were communicated with, and on entering the room they found the woman dead in bed, and in her everyday attire. Life had apparently been extinct for some hours. A closer scrutiny disclosed several pools of blood on the floor of the room. The woman's face was found to have been bruised and cut, and was clotted with blood, and shockingly disceloured.—Kiernan was taken before the magistrates on Monday, and committed to the Liverpool Assizes on a charge of manslaughter. EXTRAORDINARY FATALITY.—On Monday, at Enfield Petty Sessions, Edward Fenn, bootmaker, was charged, on his own confession, with causing the death of his son Ed- ward, aged five years, by throwing a cherry stone down his throat. The prisoner; on being placed in the dock, seemed much affected, and his wife, who was weeping on her en- trance into court, became hysterical, and had to be carried away prostrate.—P.C. Agg deposed that on Monday after- noon prisoner went to him and said, "I have choked my son."—Mr. Bowles: What state did he appear in f.-Witness: He seemed in great distress, and was crying very much. I said to him, "How did you choke him ?" and he replied, "I was playing with him with cherry stones. trying to throw them into his breast." I then asked him how he knew the boy was dead, and he answered, "I am quite sure, because he was black and cold before I left the house." I then took him to the police-station, where he was charged.—The other testimony showed that prisoner is a respectable man, and that after dinner on Sunday be was endeavouring to pitch cherry stones down the neck of the deceased, the collar of his shirt being open. Several attempts having been made, the next stone thrown went into the boy's mouth, and lodged in his throat, drawn there by strong inward breathing at the instant. The lad began to choke, and died before assistance could arrive. Dr. Shaw found the cherry stone sticking in the throat and removed it, but the unfortunate lad had been dead for some time.—The Bench were informed that notice of the occurrence had been given to the coroner, and prisoner was remanded on bail to await the result of the in- quest. EARL GR,IIIVILLE ON HOME AND FOREIGN AFFAIRS.— Earl Granville presided on Monday at the annual meeting of the members of the City Liberal Club. His Lordship said: There is one all-absorbing political question on which Ide not propose to enter this afternoon. The question as to what is the right policy with regard to the government of Ireland has been so fully discussed lately, in and out of Parliament, that I doubt whether anything useful or new can be said on the subject till men's minds have had time to get somewhat calmer, and especially until we have, in some authoritative form, the information of which is the rival— or the rivals—of that policy which Mr. Gladstone and his colleagues submitted to Parliament, and which has bean re- jected by the majority of the constituencies in England. That decision'has led to the resignation of Mr. Glad- stone and his colleagues, a resignation which has even slightly anticipated the period at which formerly it used to be considered the constitutional time. Our course is justi- fied by two recent precedents; but in any case we thought that, having proposed our plan for re-establishing peace and order in Ireland, and finding ourselves in face of the impos- sibility of carrying it out, no time ought to be lost in trans- ferring to others the power and responsibility of attempting this great work. On the formation of his Government, Mr. Gladstone was much pressed to produce his plan without delay. We wish to avoid depriving our succesrors of any of the time which they may use in preparing theirs. (Hear, hear.) At such a moment, I should be sorry to say one word which could in any degree add to the difficulty of their task, and, as I dare say, there are even some in this room who hold different shades of opinion on the subject, I should be sorry to initiate a debate. (Hear, hear.) But you will perhaps allow me to say only, as regards myself, that I have always been strongly in favour of largely-ex- tended self-government in Ireland; that up ton somewhat recent period, I wished for Lord John 4ussell's proposal, viz., self-government for each of the four provinces— (cheers)—but having been convinced by Liberals who dis- agree with me that this plan, good or bad, was impossible, chiefly from the want of suport either in Ireland or in Great Britain, I have arrived; by a process of exhaustion, to consider that no other policy is possible excepting one based on the same principles as we have proposed. (Cheers.) I feel certain that this policy will eventually prevail, and I only trust, under such favourable circumstances as would have accompanied its being agreed to this year. (Cheers.) I am happy to say that, with regard to the different depart- ments of the Government, there are none in a state which does not make the transfer of them to our successors very satisfactory. Foreign affairs have not been without their difficulties, greater. perhaps, than meet the eye of the super- I ficial observer, but Lord Rosebery has coped successfully ' with them. Lord Granville then briefly reviewed our rela- tions with foreign countries. A FEW REASONS WHY THE VACCINATION ACTS SHOULD BE REPEALED.

Sir,—As tunny candidates for Parliament have been re- cently questioned and interviewed upon this important social and political question in various parts of England, may I venture to state a few of the reasons which create general dislike of the existing law. 1. The law enforcing vaccination was needlessly passed ire Parliament with much precipitation in 1853 at the in- starece of medical men, who promised as its undoubted cer- tain result the speedy extinction of small-pox in two or three years. The Registrar-General's returns show that there has been no diminution of that disease except what is due to the sanitary amelioration, and small-pox epidemics are still of frequent occurrence in many of the large centres of population. 2. The promoters of vaccine compulsion maintained that the operation was harmless in its nature, wholly unattended with danger' and incapeble of producing other aisaases than cow-pox. But the Registrar-General's returns prove the contrary, and show that all blood diseases which are inecul- able have largely increased since vaccination was enforced; and further, that daring the past four years 251 deaths are officially certified to be directly due to vaccination. 3. The medical advocates of vaccination represent the opponents of the law as comprising only ignorant fanatics, whose opinions should be treated with silent contempt, as the opinions of a minority. The truth is that anti-vaccina- tors are found in every rank in society, and comprise well- known philosophers, University professors, statisticians, chiefs of hospitals, and eminent physicians and sanitarians. 4. The vaccine propagandists assert that the great bulk of the population are favourable to the maintenance of the law, the repeal of which they say would be a national calamity. To test the truth of this assertion, and to ascer- tain the real opinions of the people on this momentous ques- tion, a plebiscite of householders has been made in 36 towns, town wards, districts, and villages in nearly every part of England, and the returns show that 90 per cent, of the vot- ing householders are averse to the vaccination laws alto- gether, aed more than 70 per cent, have no faith in the efficacy of vaccination itself, while over 1,500 cases of in- jury and death are reported, in many cases with all circum- stantial detail by eye-witnesses. Small-pox is essentially a filthy disease, developed by over-crowding and:other insani- tary conditions, and against which vaccination affords no defence whatever. Although this mischievous and costly mistake originated with some inferior members of the medi- cal profession, the responsibility of continuing it rests hence- forth with the enfranchised democracy, who ought t 3 see that their -views are fitly represented in Parliament. —Yours faithfully, WILLIAM TEBB. National Liberal Club, Charing Cross, London, July 26, 1886.

THE GUARDIANS AND VACCINATION. Sir,—lt must be conceded that the Earlestown anti- waocinators scored a notable victory at the last meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians. The time was, and that net very long ago, when the Guardians would not par- ley for a moment with anti-vaccination. The law was on their side, the law must be obeyed, and that was enough for them. Like Lord Salisbury, they believed in resolute government, and defiance of the law was not to be condoned for a moment. But now The native hue of resolution Is sicklied o'er, to. The persistence of the anti-vaccinators has won the day. The Guardians hesitated, doubted, considered, and at length, .ander pretence of a council of war with the Local Govern- ment Board, beat a strategic retreat. The Guardians are a representative body, and they were never truer to their representative character than in this action of theirs in regard to anti-vaccination. There can be no doubt that a fastly increasing number of people are be- ginning to have the same opinion as to vaccination that Mr. Greening and some other members of the Board showed they had. These people admit that there is a heavy weight of authority on the side of vaccination, but they are extremely doubtful whether vaccination by coercion is a wise thing. The Mayor, no doubt, is cor- seized with the indignation of a superior mind when he finds that people who live in cottages and cannot quote poetry and the sayings of Confucius and other philosophers, are presumptions enough to have opinions of their own on matters of this kind. Has he not the whole of the "faculty," with a few exceptions, on his side? But it is to be feared that there are perverse individuals who will have it that the opinion of the "faculty " is not everything even in res- pect to vaccination. They may even remember that it was the simple eeuntry people of Gloucestershire who first dis- covered the efficacy of vaccination, and that the oelief in it was for long enough treated by the learned doctors as a popular superstition, or—as the Mayor, if he lived then, would probably have characterised it—as an exhibition of vulgar "fanaticism." We know that Dr. Jenner was ad- monished not to let it be known to his learned brethren that he believed in vaccination lest he should lose the great re- putation he had gained amongst them by a long for- getten essay on the—cuckoo. It would, therefore, be to disregard past lessons if we put too much importance on the opinion of the medical profession, even on a subject which is so much within their particular province as vaccination. It is a mistake to think that in order to sympathise with anti- eaccinators it is necessary to disclaim all belief in vac- cinatioo. It is quite possible to have the fullest belief in Jenner's doctrine, and yet at the same time think that vac- cination is unnecessary, just as it would be to 'think that the adoption of any special preventitive of the plague or " hlack death" is unnecessary. If one is of epinion that the general sanitary conditions of the country have so far advanced that they would effectually prevent any serious outbreak of small-pox, it would be perfectly consistent for a thorough believer in vaccination to Join in the protest of anti-vaccinators against subjecting children to the needless dangers which everybody knows attend inoculation. Warrington, July 28. J. T. ROYALTIES.

Sir,—lt needs no gift of prophecy to foretell that the citadel ef the great land monopoly which will be subject to the first regular assault of the advancing democracy of England is that of royalties. The feeling that royalties clog the wheels of industry in this country, and that they are in themselves a monstrous injustice is wonderfully pre- valent in the minds of tile "masses," and that feeling will doubtless, in a not very distant future, carry into political Power men pledged to deal very thoroughly with them. While, however, there seems to be remarkable unanimity in regard to the necessity for something being done with royalties, there is not the same unAnimity as to what this eomething should be. There are great variances as to the "method and plans," and seeing that "methods and plans" are everything in practical politics, the need for con- sideration and discussion is manifest. There ara not a few who greatly favour a root and branch mode of treatment of royalties; they cry out that they should be "abolished" and swept away entirely. A. very simple plan this, no donbt; simple .but unworkable, and indeed irrational. These very drastic reformers, strong believers in the efficacy of legislation, would perhaps be mighty incredulous we'd scornful were they tekl that all the acts of all the legisla- tures of Europe. and the rest of the world too, for that matter, could not " abolish " one jot or tittle of royalties. Legislatures may redistribute royalties—that is take from one and give to another—in anyway they lik, but they can do nothing in the way of "abolition." Royal- ties, as we know, are a form of rent—a payment made for the use of mother earth. The farmer pays for the use of the surface of the earth, while the miner pave for the use of the earth that lies beneath the surface. The payment of

A FAMILY POISONED.—A family named Crippe, residing on a farm near Rochford, Essex, has been poisoned through eating pudding in which vermin-killer had been used in mistake for baking powder. The mother, who made the pudding, died on bunday morning; but the husband, son, and servant, although suffering severely from the effects of the poison, are expected to recover. BOATING DISASTER. A boating accident occurred on Sunday at Kilcummin, on the west coast of Ireland. It is customary for a "pattern " to be held at the place On this particular Sunday of July, and hundreds of visitors as- sembled on Sunday to take part in the sports and festivities provided. Amongst them was a party of four, consisting of Thomas Williams, Peter Egan, James Delahunty. and Anne l‘PLoughlin, all of whom were under the influence of liquor when they went to the boat in which they were to return home. After getting some distance from land the boat became submerged, and the whole of her occupants were drowned, one man who clung to the boat for a little time being too much intoxicated to retain his hold.

MURDER IN TRELAND.—A man named Whelan has been found dead at Callan, Kilkenny county, under circumstancos which point to his baying been murdered. A hatchet was found with which it is believed the crime was committed. The murder is stated to have been due to agrarian causes. A person named Tobin has been arrested in connection with the affair.

SCALDING FsTlarry.—On Thursday morning, Mr. Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest on the body of Anthony Dunleavy, two years of age, son of Patrick Dunleavy, 14- bourer, 18. Fox-street, St. Helens.—Sarah Dunleary, 15 years of age, sister to deceased, stated that she was about to wash up the dimner things, and had placed a pan of boil- ing water on the floor. Deceased and his sister asked for a drink of water. She gave them a drink, and deceased was dancing about when he caught the handle of the pan, upset it and splashed the contents over him.—A verdict of "Acci- dental death" was returned.

the latter is called "royalty," but it is essentially the same as that of the agriculturist. Now we all know that the pay- ment of rest arises from causes over which legislators have no control. As long as agricultural land varies in fertility and mines in richness, and as long as the demand for the products of agricultural lands and mines forces the bringing into use of inferior land and mines so long will somebody or other get the benefit of rent. The causes of rent are, first, the varying productiveness of natural agencies; second, the growth of population, which forces recourse to natural agencies which are of inferior productiveness. Over the first of these causes legislatures can of course have no con- trol, and with regard to the second cause it is safficient to point out that Malthusian doctrines, although very sedu- lously preached for many years past, have done nothing to repress human instincts. It might be just a little interest- ing to trace in a few lines the effects of an attempt to "abolish" royalties. To do this let us consider the case of three mines, one of which, being of an inferior character, paid the bare cost of working; another, somewhat richer, pays £5OO a year royalty to the landowner, while the third, being richer, still pays £l,OOO a year royalty. An edict, we will say, goes forth that royalties are to be abolished—to be paid no lon- ger. By this enactment the poorest of the three mines will not be affected. It paid no royalties before, and it will con- tinue to be exempt. Bat how about the £5OO and £l,OOO a year? These sums having been taken from the landlord to whom have they to be given? If you turn them over to the capitalist, or capi- talists, who works the mine you simply change the royalty-receiver but not abolish the royalty. If yon order that these sums of money are to be annually distributed amongst the workmen engaged at the twlo mines, hew does the matter stand ? Previous to the change of policy, the workmen at each of the three mines would, doubtless, be receiving the current wages for that sort of employment, but if at one mine £5OO, and at another £l,OOO, additional to the ordinary pay were to be distributed annually an unjust advantage would be given to certain workmen over others. And further than that they could only be secured in their advantage by rigorously restricting the competition for em- ploy.nent which would immediately begin at the two favoured mines, and especially at the more favoured of the two; so that in the end the only result of the intended " abolition " of royalties would be the setting up of a larger body of royalty-receivers. A few considerations like these show, I think, that the question of royalties is not quite so simple as some people seem to imagine. It is not merely a question of abolishing or not abolishing, but a question as to who ought to have the benefit of royalties. I venture to predict that when the matter comes to be practically dealt with it will be decided that the only just method of disposing of royalties is to nationalise them. that is, to use them for the benefit of the nation as a whole.
JAQUES.

Friday's bulletin says that Mr. Rnakin's state remains similar to that of Wednesday. He has passed better nights than oreviously. A serious fire broke out on Friday afternoon at Northamp- ton, on the premises of Mr. John Wilson, ironmonger, and raged for some time. The Press Association is officially informed that the divi- dend of the Midland Railway Company for the past half- year will be at the rate of 4 per cent. per annum on ordinary stock, carrying forward £14,000. No efforts have been made in Kirkham to obtain a reprieve in the case of Police-constable Bligh, who lies under sen- tence of death for murdering his three children. The execution will take place on Monday morning next at Lan- caster.

THE PENZANCE TRAGEDY.—James Hawke, who mur- dered three persona and then shot himself, was buried on Friday morning at Penzance Cemetery, without cere- mony. It is now stated that jealousy was the motive for the crime.

FATAL FOOTBALL.—A young man named Alfred Turner, aged 23 years, of Bolton, has just died from the effects of injuries received whilst playing football. He was playing with the Little Hulton Football Club, and charged one of the players, but he injured himself so seriously in tke stomach that he died in a few hours. THIS LIVERPOOL RITUAL CASEL—The Bell-Cox case Came before the York Chancery Court again on Friday morning. Mr. Lawton then prayed that the significant might issue, and this was decreed. The significavit issues from the court to the Court of Chancery, and unless the court is moved to stay, a writ witl bz drawn up and defendant com- mitted to prison. - .

INSPECTOR OF FACTORIES APPOINTMENT.—It is an- nounced. that Mr. George Sedgwick, a working man. of Leicester, has just been appointed Inspector of Factories by Mr. Childers. Mr. Sedgwick has been for some time a general secretary of the National Union of Riveters and Finishers and a member of the Leicester School Board, and was recently made a magistrate of the borough. EXTRAORDINARY FATALITY.-011 Friday morning the infant daughter of Samuel Mayne Smith, Ibston-street, off Ashton-road, Oldham, met her death in a shocking manner. At half-past eight the child was seated on a chair with a carving knife in her hand, when she fell off. The fall caused the knife to enter her mouth so far as the throat, which it cut so dreadfully that the child died in a few mi- nutes. EI WARD BEECHER'S ESTIMATE OF GLADSTONE. 4. des- cription of Mr. Gladstone by Mr. Henry Ward Beecher, wha heard his Liverpool speech, has been cabled to New York. In concludes as follows :—" I regard Mr. Gladstone by far the most notable man in Great Britain, as by far the most comprehensively educated, the most profoundly moral and religions, the most philosophical and earnest English- speaking man on the globe." ORKNEY AND SHETLAND ELECTION.—The result of this election was declared this afternoon—
L. Lyre)) (G) M. Hoare (U)
Majority At the last general election the figures were—Lyell (L) 3,352; Dundas (C), 1,940, Liberal majority. 1,412. _.

SAD DEATH OF CHESHIRR OFFICER IN BIIRMAIL—The sad news of the death of Captain Wilbraham, in Burmah, has just been received by his father, Mr. Roger Wilbraham, of Delaneere House, Cheshire. Captain Wilbraham, who was the eldest son, and heir to the extensive estates in Cheshire, is understood, from the brief intelligence which has reached the War Office and forwarded to Cheshire, to have died from wounds received in a recent engage- ment.

NEW PEERS, &c.—The Central News is officially informed that on the recommendation of Mr. Gladstone the Queen has been pleased to approve of the creation of four new peers, viz: (1) Sir Thomas Brassey, K.C.8., (2) Sir M. A. Bus, Bart., M.P., (3) Mr. J. C. Hamilton, of Dalziell, late M.P. for South Lanarkshire, (4) Sir Henry IThring, K.C.B. Her Majesty has also approved of the following Baronetcies —(1) Mr. F. T. Mappin, M.P., (2) Mr. C. M. Palmer, M.P., (3) Mr. J. D. Love Jones Parry, of Mailryn Castle, Pwllheli, (4) Mr. James Kitson (Leeds). DAMAGES FROM THE LANCASHIRE AND YORKSHIRE RAILWAY.—At Liverpool Assizes on Friday, Mary Ann Clayton, of Wigan, brought an action against the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway for damages for personal injuries. She was descending from a carriage at Moses Gate, and in consequence of there being some tar on the step she fell, and was insensible for 20 minutes. She broke a rib and in- jured two others, and was confined to bed for a month. The defence was that the accident was due to plaintiff's negli- gence. The jury awarded £B2. DEPARTURE OF MR. GLADSTONE FOR OSBORNE.—The Press Association states that Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone left Downing-street on Friday morning in a closed carriage and drove to Waterloo station, where the right hon. gentleman, who carried with him his despatch box, took the 9-30 train for-Portsmouth, en route for Osborne, where be will have an audience of the CI-teen, returning to London the same even- ing. Mrs. Gladstone, after seeing her husband off, returned to Downing-street. There was co demonstration at the station. The train was due at Portsmouth Harbour station a few minutes after noon, and Mr. Gladstone would reach Osborne about one o'clock. It is understood Mr. Glad- stone's visit to Osborne is for the purpose of submitting to her Majesty a list of the honours which, in accordance with custom, the retiring Premier proposes to bestow. It is not thought that he will deliver up the Privy Seal, so that he will have to accompany his colleagues to Osborne on Tuesday. A later telegram says :—Mr. Gladstone lunched at Osborne, and, after an audience of her Majesty, left Cowes at half-past three for London, via Portsmouth.

div.head: RIOTS AT AMSTERDAM.
div.p: THE RIOTS AT AMSTERDAM.

AMSTERDAM, FRIDAY, 10-20 A.M.—The municipality, acting in concert with the military commandant, have taken precautionary measures to prevent any disturbances to-day at the funeral of the persons killed in last Monday's rioting. Since three o'clock this morning detachments of soldiers and police have occupied positions in 19 different quarters of the city and the cemeteries, enabling them to act with advantage against any attempt at disorder. Most of the bodies have been claimed from the hospital, and are being buried at the expense of friends of the dec3ased. The fune- ral of the remainder will be at the cost of the municipality. Up to the present everything is quiet.

div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JULY 31, 1886.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JULY 31, 1886.
WARRINGTON.

A SUCCESSFUL ART STUDENT.—Among the sue- cessful exhibitions at the Exhibition of National Competition Prize Works at South Kensington Museum, there are three full-sized portions of carpets based upon Persian precedents and excel- lently adapted for reproduction in the actual ma- terials by H. Allen, a student of the Warrington School of Art. A gold medal has been awarded for this exhibit.

SUDDEN DEATH AT BANK QUAY.—Mary Hamblett (59) wife of John Hamblett, Atherton-street, off Powys-street, Bank Quay, died suddenly on Mon- day. In the morning she appeared to be in her usual health, but, whilst resting on a sofa, and when speaking to her husband, she suddenly expired. Deceased had been under medical treatment for twelve months, having suffered from bronchitis and heart disease. An inquest was not considered neces- 6ary. THE SUICIDE NEAR FLIXTON STATION.—Mr. F. Price, district coroner, held an inquest on Tuesday afternoon at the Bird in Hand Inn, near Flixton, on the body of Benjamin Johnson, 23, pupil teacher, of Shaw View, Flixton, who committed suicide on the railway by throwing himself in front of a train near Flixton Station. Several witnesses were examined, and the jury found that the deceased committed suicide whilst under temporary insanity.

MUSIC IN THE PARK.—On Thursday evening Mr. Fletcher's band discoursed a selection of music in the Park under the conductorship of Mr. William Waterfield ; and last evening the band of the Ist Volunteer Battalion (Prince of Wales Volunteer) South Lancashire Regiment occupied the grand- stand under the conductorship of Mr. Thomas Arm- strong. The weather on neither evening was par- ticularly favourable, but, notwithstanding, there were good attendances of spectators, and the efforts of the musicians were evidently appreciated. HAINES'S, for Ladies' and Gentlemen's newest styles.—

SUDDEN DEATH AT LATCHFORD.—CharIotte Mor- ris (29), wife of Albert Morris, 19, Barry-street, Latchford, died suddenly on Monday afternoon. After having dinner she went to the backdoor of a neighbour's house, where the neighbour was en- gaged removing a load of coal. Deceased com- menced to help her, and suddenly exclaimed "Oh my wind's gone." She was taken into the house and died almost immediately afterwards. Mr. Yates, coroner, held an inquest touching the death at the golden Lion Inn, Knutsford-road, on Wednes- day morning. A verdict that death resulted from heart disease was returned.

SUDDEN. DEATH AT WHITECROSS.—On Thursday evening a man named Thomas Carty, 33 years of age, Who lived at 18, Wakefield-street, and was a coal heaver at Whitecross Ironworks, died suddenly whilst engaged at his work. He was unloading a waggon of coals, and wheeling them a distance of a dozen yards up an incline. While waiting for a bar- row to be filled, deceased was seen to rest his hand on a railway waggon, and afterwards to fall to the ground. He died at once, without spekking. De- ceased is described as having been a very steady man, and was always considered to enjoy robust health.

SUCCESS OF LOCAL MUSICIANS. - Among the names of those who have been successful in the recent pianoforte examination, conducted by the National Society of Professional Musicians, is that of Miss Ethel Hall, of Hamilton House School. Miss Hall is one of three pupils from this school who passed the theoretical examination of the same so- ciety last year, the others being Miss W. M. Smith and Miss E. A. Richardson. The name of Miss Annie Podmore of Warrington, is also announced amongst the list Of awards published in the " Manchester City News" of July 24th, in connection with the early summer examination held at Manchester under the auspices of the Society of Professional Musicians. Miss Podmore, who has been under the tutorship of Dr. Hiles, has secured a pass certificate in the advanced stage.

WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.—A sitting of this court was held on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes. The cause list comprised 78 original plaints, and 20 judgment summonses. The only case of interest was one in which Mr. Thomas Litton, corn merchant, Warrington, sought to re- cover the sum of £l7 18s. 10d. from Mr. Richard Killsall, farmer, of Cow-lane, Burtonwood, for corn sold and delivered. Mr. Percy Davies appeared for the defence. The goods were delivered between the 20th of November, 1879, and the Ist of June, 1883, and defendant had paid £8 on account; and the sum claimed was now owing. Defendant paid is. 10d. into court in satisfaction of the plaintiff's claim. For the defence Mr. Davies submitted that the debt had not been proved, and pointed out that neither •Mr. Robinson nor Mr. Isherwood, who had been called to prove the case for the plaintiff, would swear that the money was owing. Mr. Davies sub- mitted a number of receipts for goods supplied to defendant in 1882, one of which was for .£l7 Bs. 6d., which was receipted by plaintiff. After hearing evidence his Honour ruled that the receipts produced were simply invoices, and said it could not be con- tended that the defendant had paid his accounts regularly, as it was admitted that certain items of the account claimed were owing. Judgment would be givon for plaintiff for the amount claimed.

LOYAL ORDER OF ANCIENT SHEPHERDS (ASHTON UNITY).—The members of the Pride of Latchford Lodge, Warrington District, celebrated their anni- versary at their lodge-house, Brother Thomas Ire- land's, Cheshire Cheese Inn, Latchford, on Saturday, when a large number of members and friends sat down to an excellent dinner. The chair was taken by Brother John Hartley, who was supported by Pro. Cor. Sec. Abel Henry Mather, P.M. Peter Kirk- man, Brother Henry Craddock, and Brother Chorley. The vice-chair was occupied by W. M. James Smith Burgess.—The Chairman proposed "The Loyal Order of Ancient Shepherds,' coupling with the toast the Warrington District; and in response the Pro. Cor. Sec. Abel H. Mather stated that it was a pleasure to him to be present at that annual gather- ing, for he considered that such gatherings tended to cement the brotherhood more firmly together. The district was financially in a better position now than at any time since it was established, for after paying .£603 13s 5d for sick pay, £lBO for death claims, £l9O 2s 44 for management, and .£l2l 7s for medical attendance, they were now worth £2,748 14s id, which he considered ought to be gratifying to the members when they took into consideration the state of trade.—The Chairman sub- sequently gave "The Pride of Latchford Lodge " ; and in response Secretary Isaac Jones stated that during the last five years their income had been such as to enable them to add to their funds the sum of .£46, after paying £76. —The Chairman pro- posed the lodge surgeon, Dr. Cannell, who had been the medical officer of the lodge for the past ten years. Dr. Cannell acknowledged the toast.—Dur- ing the evening a framed emblem of merit was pre- sented to P.M. William Millington, for past services, and songs and Lancashire readings were given by Bros. Burgess, Hartley, Millington, and Board- man. }hymn's, for Army Bluchers, at 6s 11d, great bargains. —Advt. "ALONE IN LONDON."— On Mondriy evening the new drama "Alone in London," written by Mr Robt. Buchanan and Miss Harriet Jay, was produced in ;Warrington by a new company specially organised by Messrs. Wynn Miller and J. F. Eiliston. The play may be described as of the sensational school, and yet it is not of the ordinary sensational charac- ter, the plot, which is throughout well sustained, abounding in situations which, whilst startlingly realistic, are exceedingly true to life. The scenery, which has been specially prepared for the piece, is of the most elaborate kind, and is so wonderfully I' effective, that the drama is well worth seeing as a spectacular representation. The various members lof the company seem to have been carefully selec- ted for the parts. Miss Grace Balmaine is graceful and effective as "Annie Meadows," and as "Nan," a flower girl, appears to great advantage. Miss May 1 Holt makes a great hit as "Tom Chickweed," the I touches of pathos being finely rendered. Mr. Har- rington Reynolds leaves nothing to be desired as "Richard Redcliffe " ; and the other more impor- tant parts are well sustained by Mr. M. Martyn as "John Biddlecomb." Mr. L. Meadows as " Jenkin- son," Mr. George Harley as " Spriggins," Mr. John Henderson as "Mr. Burnaby," Mr. Stanley Hope as 1" Walter Burnaby," Miss Rosamond Tennyson as "Ruth Cli,fden," and Miss Dot Henderson as "Mrs Moloney.' Mr. W. P. Dempsey created pleiaty of fun as "Charlie Johnson," and had a good partner in Miss Douglass as "Liz Jenkinson.' Consider- ing that Monday was the first occasion on which this company had played together, it must be said that the piece went with remarkable smoothness. Some little delay was occasioned on the first night with the scenery, which is of a most extensive and complicated kind, but that has since been avoided, and the drama now is exceedingly well represented. The dressing and appointments are of the best class, and there is every prospect of "Alone in London 'S having, as a drama, an extraordinary success. There have been large attendances each night, and the audiences have been demonstrative in their expres- sions of approval.

"DROPPING" A CONSTABLE.-011 Saturday night Police Constables Smith and Turner were taking a prisoner in custody from the fair ground to the police station, when a youth named Edward Grif- fin came up behind Smith and, striking him a blew behind the ear, knocked him to the ground. Smith did not see who was his assailant, but Turner no- ticed who gave the blow, and Griffin was afterwards apprehended. When he was brought before the magistrates, at the Borough Court on Monday, it was stated that there were 18 previous convictions recorded against him. He denied having committed the assault, but the Bench found him guilty, and inflicted a fine of 20s and costs or a month's impri- sonment.

THA EDUCATION ACT.—At the Borough Court, on Monday, Mr. George Riley, school attendance ofricer, summoned three persons for not regularly sending their children to school. The case of James Emp- son, glass maker, 42, John-street, was, Mr. Riley said, a troublesome one. It had been three times before the School Committee and once before the court. The boy, despite the exertions of his parents, was continually playing truant, and was accus- tomed to staying out late at nights. The parents had done all they could with him. An order was made for the youth to go to the ship Clio.—Eleanor Bennett, Old Gardens, Winwick-street, was next charged, and Mr. Riley said that in his opinion the mother was not fit to have control of the boy, who was also sent to the ulio.—Enoch Jones, forgeman, Lythgoe's-lane, was fined ss. for neglecting to send his child to school.—At the Borough Court, yester- day, an order was made for a boy named France to attend school.

THE BIRTH AND DEATH RATE OF WARRINGTON. —For week ending Saturday, July 24th, 1886.—The mean temperature was 62.5 Fahr., and therefore 4 deg. warmer than the preceding week. The maxi- mum temperature 75 Fahrenheit, was recorded on the 22nd inst., and the minimum temperature. 54 Fahrenheit, on the 24th inst. The rainfall measured .65 inches. The general direction of the wind was S.W. During the week, which was the 30th of the current year, 37 births and 21 deaths were registered. The death rate from all causes was equal to 23.5 per 1,000, against 14.8, the average of the previous four weeks, and against 6.8 the cor- responding week of last year. The deaths included 2 from diarrhcea, 3 from premature birth, 1 from whooping cough, 1 from old age,.3 from phthisis, 1 from heart disease, 1 from parturition, 4 from brain disease. One case of typhoid fever was reported ' under the requirements of the Act of Parliament.— Jrto. H. GORNALL, Medical Officer of Health.

SWINE FEVER. Inspector Norman told the Borough Magistrates at their sitting on Monday that there were at present no less than four out- breaks of swine fever in the borough, that 11 pigs had died from the disease during the last montk, and 20 pigs had been attacked. He had that morn- ing received information that a herd of about eight pigs had become affected. Mr. Norman gave this information after prosecuting in a case in which Samson Green, of Winwick-road, was charged with not giving notice of the existence of swine fever on his premises. On the 29th nit, Mr. Norman said, defendant notified to him that he had a herd of swine, and that some of them were unwell. He visited defendant's premises on the following morn- ing, and found that the animals were suffering from swine fever. A declaration was made and defendant was told that he should have reported the matter earlier. Afterkards Mr. Norman again visited the premises, and found the carcase of a pig buried in the ground, about two inches from the surface. The carcase was examined by a veterinary surgeon, who certified that it had been affected with swine fever. The summons was taken out because in- formation had not been given regarding the pigs. The Bench ordered that defendant should pay costs, „i 1 us 6d.

I ALLEGED VIOLENT ASSAULT.—At the Borough Court on Monday a man named Andrew Williams was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Hill-street, and with assaulting Thomas Hines by kicking him at the same time and place. The cir- cumstances of the case were stated by Chief Con- stable Hunt, who said that shortly after eleven I o'clock on Saturday night Police Constable Plaice was on duty in Buttermarket-street, and, acting I upon information received, proceeded to Hill-street. There he found Thomas Hines, of 8, Hill-street, lying on the ground bleeding profusely from the face, and apparently in an insensible state. Pri- soner was pointed out in the crowd a 3 the man who had kicked Hines in the head and face. Dr. Can- , nell attended to the injured man, who was unable to appear. The assault, Mr. Hunt said, was a very savage one, and he asked for a remand. Constable Plaice spoke to the condition of Hines after the assault. The man, he said, had received five wounds one of which was about an inch and a half in length. Prisoner told the Bench that he, on Saturday night, engaged a bed at the house of Hines, and the people in the house persuaded him to buy drink. The only row he remembered after- wards was one between Hines and his wife. After- ' waris he was assaulted and turned out of the house. The remand was granted. At the Borough Court, yesterday morning, Williams was again charged. CHe was defended by Mr. A. Browne. Chief Con- ' stable Hunt said that complainant, who lived at 8, Hill-street, was well known to the Court. Prisoner was a foreman working at the Vulcan Ironworks, and nothing was known against him, except the story told .by the complainant Hines. Prisoner's wife and family lived at Crewe.. Mr. Hunt briefly I explained the circumstances, and evidence was then called as to the assault. Mr. Browne contended that the parties had been drinking together, a quarrel followed, and Hines was injured in falling. The Bench fined prisoner ss, including costs, for drun- kenness, lOs and costs for the assault, and orderedl that he pay lOs as the doctor's fee. The money - was paid. GARDEN PARTY AT LATCHFORD.—On Tuesday and 'Wednesday a garden party was held at S. , James's Vicarage. Latchford, in aid of the St. James's Mission House and Day Nursery, which is . ' situate in Knutsford-road. The party is an annual event, but this year a special effort was made to . raise funds, it being desired to get together the amount of no. The fete opened on Tuesday after- noon, but there was not a large attendance, two other garden parties that were being held in the same , neighbourhood militating against it. The arran;e- , ments were under the care of the Rev. F. and Mrs. Slater, assisted by members of the congregation. The grounds in the evenings were illuminated by 500 small lamps, and a variety of games was intro- duced. There was also a sale of work. Music was supplied by the Volunteer and the Workhouse bands, and instrumental trios were played by Messrs. Pearson, Bond, and Ford, which were greatly appreciated. Messrs. Atkinson, Scarisbrick, Coggins, and Stirrup provided a considerable amount of fun by their negro minstrel entertainments. They were got up in the usual nigger costume, and were very amusing. A special attraction on Wed- nesday was a baby show. There were not, how- ever, many babies submitted for competition. The prizes were awarded as follows :—Thomas Uns- worth, 17 months old, weight 29 lbs ; William Har- greaves, 8i months old, weight 25 lbs; Dora Perry, 5 months old, weight 18 lbs ; and Frederick J. Par- sonage, 31 months old, weight not taken. CONSERVATIVE CLUB.—The annual meeting of the Warrington Conservative Club Buildings Company, Limited, was held at the Club, in Sankey street, on Wednesday evening, Captain S. Reynolds presiding. There was a good attendance of members. Mr. J. L. Tunstall read the annual report of the directors, which stated that the share capital had been taken up to the extent of 6,544 shares' on which the sum of £5,791 17s 6d had been paid, leaving a balance outstanding of £752 2s 6d, most of which was not yet due. The number of shareholders was 739, up- wards of 600 of whom were working-men. This showed an increase of 83 members for the past year. The whole of the premises were at present let at a rental of £375 per annum. The share capital was increased last year from £6,000 to £7,5C03 and 544 of the additional shares had so far been taken up. Taking into consideration the expenses yet to be in- curred in decorations and street making, the direc- tors were of opinion that if 456 further shares were issued, making a total share capital of £7,000, the share list might be closed, and the remaining 500 shares reserved for future issue in case of need. The directors urged the shareholders to subscribe the amount asked for, or to get their friends to do so, inasmuch as a f!onsiderable saving would thereby be effected in bank interest. The profit and loss account showed a disposable balance of £316 18s Id. The directors recommended the payment of a divi- dend for the past year after the rate of 5 per cent per annum. This would absorb a sum of £272 19s sd, and leave £43 8s 8d to go in reduction of the preliminary expenses account. The retiring direc- tors, Capt. Reynolds, Messrs. J. Roberts, R. T. Smith, Thos. Sutton, and John Thornton were re-elected, and thanked for their past services on the motion ' of Mr. John Pierpoint, seconded by Mr. Smethurst. In the course of an address, Captain Reynolds ex- pressed the opinion that the Conservative majori- ties at the two last Parliamentary contests were to a great extent attributable to their having such a club, with such a large number of shareholders.

div.head: FRODSH AM-
div.p: FRODSH AM-

VIOLENT ASSAULT.—At Eddisbury Petty Sessions, on Monday. Thomas Gaytor, labourer, of Newton, Frodsham, was mama •ned for assaulting Allan Lovett, at Sutton.—Mr. J. E. Fletcher appeared for complainant, and said that the cosnolainant was the lock tenter at Sutton Lock, and as inch it was his duty to warn off trespassers on the Navigation. He bad several times warned the defendant for fishing in the river, and on the 2nd July he again found Gaytor fish- ing at the wear. He went to him and ordered him off. De- fendant refused to go, and after some little altercation Gaytor struck him a violent blow in the rib,. He then trie4 to throw witness into the lock, and afterwaids struck him a second and a third blow in the eye, which prevented him from seeing for a fortnight. —This statement was borne out in evidence by the complainant, James Miller, and Thomas Yarwood.—Defendant, who did not appear, was fined £5 and £1 2a 6d costs, in default two months' imprisonment with hard labour. A FRODSHAM MAN AND HIS WIFS FROM THE WORK. HousE.—On Monday, at Eddisbury Petty Sessions, Ellen Whitby, of Frodsham, was summoned for using threatening I language towards her husband on the sth July.—Defendant did not appear, and P.C. Povey stated that she was now co- habiting with another man at Ruccorn.—ln answer to the Bench, the complainant said he had been married leas than 12 months to the defendant. He was previously married some 29 years. He had got a" bad lot," and he was going to get" ()urea" her some way or other. She had taken his clothing out of the house many a time.—Mr. Cooke: She has gone away, and is not likely to trouble you any more, perhaps.—Complainant: I am not going to have her. I want to know what to do if she comes and will stop.—De- fendant was hound over to keep the peace for six menthe, herself in £2O, and two sureties in £lO each, in default two months' iinprisonntent.—ln answer to the Bench, complain- ant said that his wife came out of the workhouse and lived with him come three weeks or a month before they were married. She was right enough then.

div.head: POLITICA L SITUATION.
div.p: THE POLITICA L SITUATION.
THE NEW CABINET.

It is officially stated that the following Ministerial ap- pointments have been made : Prime Minister and First Lard of the Treasury Lord Salisbury. Lord Chancellor Chancellor of the Exchequer and Lc .der of the House of Com- mons Lard R. Churchill. Foreign Minister Lord Idelesleigh. Irish Secretary Sir M. Hicks-Beach. Lord President of Council Lord Cmnbroak. Home Secre4try Mr. H. Mathews. Secretary of State for the Colonies Mr. E. Stanhope. Secretary for War Mr. W. H. Smith. First Lord of the Admiralty Lard G. Hans:Mon. Chancellor of the Duchy of Lan- caster Lord Chancellor of Ireland Lord Ashbourne. So far as settled up to the present, THE NEW MINISTRY

Includes— Lord Lieutenant of Ireland Lord Londonderry. Attorney-general Sir R. Webster. Solicitor-general Bit John Gorst. President of the Local Govern- ment Bard Kr. H. Chaplin. Scotch 8 :rotary Mr. A. J. Balfour. Postmaster-general Mr. C. Raikes. President of the Board of Trade Mr. C. T. Ritchie. Vioa-President of Council Sir H. Holland. Chief Commissioner of Works Mr. Plunkett. Financial Secretary to the Trea- sury .Mr. W. L. Jackson. Political Secretary to the Trea- sury Mr. Akers Douglas. Payrruter-Giaeral Earl Beauchamp. Judge Ad vocate-general Mr. W. T. Marriott. Lord Advocate Mr. J. if. Mac ionald. Attorney General for Ireland Mr.. Holmes. Solloitor General for Ireland Mr. J. G. Gibson. Hon. 8. Herbert. Junior Lords of Treasury Mr. Dalrymple.

Regarding additions, there is good reason to believe that the other appointments below mentioned, in addi- tion to those officially announced, will prove to be cor- rect : Indian Secreteiry Sir R. Cross.

Colonial Secretary Colonel Stanley. Secretary to the Board of Trate Baron de Worms rx Mr. Porwood. Secretary Local Government Board Under-Seeretary Home Office Mr. Stuart Wortley. The chief secretaries in most instances will hare a choice in the selection of tbe under-secretaries, and therefore we may not hear of their appointment for a day or two. A London correspondent writing oa Thursday night says: The Cabinet is not yet completed, but little remains to be done, and the Queen ought to have the list of the leading Ministers before her in the course of to-morrow. The great surprise of to-day has been found in the appointment of Mr. H. Matthews, Q.C., to the Home Office. This is the reward of a distinguished electoral success at Birmingham, and is calculated to create not a little astonisbment. Mr. Matthews is, however, an able man, and he ought to do well, spite of the want of official experience. I stated last night that Lord Cranbrook would probably return to the office of Lord President, and this is confirmed to-city. Lord Halabary has also got his re-appointment as Lord Chancellor. I hear that Sir R. A. I Cross is likely to go to the India Office, though the matter is not yet settled. On the other hand, it ia certain that the right hon. gentleman is not to be shelved, as reported— neither will he go to the peers. Sir F. Stanley has been designated to-day as the successor of Lord Kimberley; but it appears much more likely, if he is again to be in the Cabinet, that he will return to his old post at the Colonial Office. LA.TEST APPOINTMENTS.

The Central News says it was thought that as soon as he had disposed of the Chancellorship of the Exchequer and the Foreign and Irish Secretaryships, Lord Salisbury would have found little if any difficulty in completing his Cabi- net, but the necessity for finding a place for Mr. Matthews not only upset all outside speculations, but obviously added immensely to the Premier's embarrassments. Practically the whole of Thursday was occupied in adjusting the rival claims of Mr. Raikes and Mr. Matthews, and Friday has been almost entirely taken up with the efforts to find places for, or to satisfy otherwise, the seven or eight nn- placed statesmen, all of whom in person or through their friends have put forward pretensions to Cabinet rank. Very little progress was made up to dinner time, only one Cabinet appointment, that of Viscount Cranbrook to be Lord President of the Council, ',sing definitely settled; but in the coarse of the afternoon the friends of Sir R. Cross confidently assailed that he would receive the Indian secre- taryship. In that event there is little doubt that Mr. Stan- hope would go to the Colonial Office. None of the remain- ing legal pests in the administration were allotted on Friday afternoon except of Judge Advocate General, which has been again given to Mr. Marriott.

Sir R. Cross was the first caller at Arlington-street on Friday morning. He remained with the noble Marquis for about twenty minutes, Mr. Stanhope being present a part of the time, and remaining after the right hon. gentleman had left. Mr. Arthur Balfour called shortly after one o'clock, but only remained a quarter of an hour. He proceeded to the Carlton Club, where he had interviews with several leading members of the party. At half-past two Lord Randolph Churchill paid a flying visit to Lord Salisbury, and after a few minutes' con- versation drove off to the Carlton. The appoint- ment of Mr. Matthews to the Home Secretary- ship has engrossed attention at the Conservative clubs, al- most to the exclusion even of speculation on the remaining vacancies in the Cabinet. The rank and file party were entirely unprepared for such an appointment, and it cannot be denied that it has given rise to a feeling akin to disaffec- tion. In the absence of a more feasible explanation, it is generally assumed that Mr. Matthews owes his sudden ad- vancement much more to his well-known friendship with Lord R. Churchill than to his own admittedly great abili- ties. Mr. Matthews distinguished himself in the D'.lke case, and he sat many years ago as M.P. for Dungarvan, being elected as a "Liberal Conservative." Though an English- man, he was a Roman Catholic, and his creed, which stood in his way in England, constituted his principal claim on the Irish electors.

HAYDOCIC FOOTBALL Ciam—On Tuesday evening the following members of the Haydock (late Temperance) Foot- ball Club received handsome silver medals with gold cen- tres, representative of a football, which were awarded to them as the winners of the first prize in the football contest at the remt Ashton Recreation's Society's sports :—Jobn Taylor, goal; T. Hatton, R. Whittle, and T. King, backs; J. Blackie, John Moran, and P. Twist, forwards. The medals were presented in the pavilion, near the field belonging the club, and the presentation was made by Mr. W. Tunstall, chairman of the committee.

The will of Mr. Michael Hughes. formerly of Sherdley Hall, St: Helens, but late of No. 41, Grosvenor-place, and of Huntley Lodge, Huntley, in the county of Aberdeen, who died on April 24 last, was proved on the 3rd inst., by Mrs Ellinor Mary Hughes, the widow, and Michael James Hughes, the son, the acting executors, the value of the personal estate in the United Kingdom amounting to upwards of £B2OOO. The testator gives all his plate to his said son ; his furni- ture. pictures, hooks, jewellery, household effects, horses, carriages' live and dead stock. and £3OO to his wife; and there are bequests to his brother, William Edward, and to his three sisters. All his real estate and the residue of his personal estate he settles upon his wife, for life, with re- mainder to his son, Michael James, for life, with remainder to his first and other sons successive:3', according to their respective eeniorities is tail male.
